translations.title: A Towering Sequence
translations.explanation: A sequence is an ordered list of terms. The position of a term matters: changing the order makes a different sequence. A recursive rule tells you a starting term and how to obtain each next term from the previous one. In the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, you move one disc at a time between three pegs, never placing a larger disc above a smaller one. Count the fewest moves for each number of discs and explain why the count follows a repeatable rule rather than merely guessing the next value.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A sequence has a first term and an order; for example, 2, 5, 11, 23, ... can be defined by \(a_1=2\) and \(a_n=2a_{n-1}+1\) for integers \(n\ge2\). For the minimum-move Tower of Hanoi sequence, let \(T(n)\) denote the minimum number of legal moves for \(n\) discs. \(T(1)=1\), and \(T(n)=2T(n-1)+1\) for \(n\ge2\): transfer the \(n-1\) smaller discs, move the largest disc once, then transfer the smaller stack again. The resulting counts are 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ...; neither consecutive differences nor consecutive ratios are constant. Always specify what \(n\) counts and where the sequence begins.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — a recursive list. Start at 3 and repeatedly double the current value and subtract 1. The first five terms are \(3,5,9,17,33\), since \(2(3)-1=5\), \(2(5)-1=9\), \(2(9)-1=17\), and \(2(17)-1=33\). A complete description states both the first term and the rule; saying "double and subtract 1" alone leaves the starting number unknown.

Example 2 — legal Tower of Hanoi moves. One disc needs one move. For two discs, move the small disc to a spare peg, move the large disc to the destination, and move the small disc on top: 3 moves. For three discs, the two smaller discs must first leave the largest disc (3 moves), then the largest disc moves once, then the smaller stack moves back on top (3 moves), for \(3+1+3=7\) moves. Repeating this argument gives \(T(4)=2(7)+1=15\) and \(T(5)=2(15)+1=31\). This same decomposition also proves that fewer moves are impossible: the largest disc cannot move until every smaller disc is elsewhere, and restoring the stack needs another full transfer.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define the term: \(T(n)\) counts minimum legal moves needed for \(n\) discs. 2. Establish the base case \(T(1)=1\). 3. To move the largest disc, first move the \(n-1\) smaller discs to the spare peg: \(T(n-1)\) moves. 4. Move the largest disc once, then restore the smaller stack: \(T(n-1)\) more moves. 5. Write \(T(n)=2T(n-1)+1\); compute \(T(2)=3\), \(T(3)=7\), \(T(4)=15\). 6. Verify the recurrence explains both the construction and the lower bound; do not mistake the move count for the number of discs.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not treat the disc count n as the number of moves. Do not place a larger disc onto a smaller one when testing a proposed move sequence. A recursive rule needs an initial term. The Tower of Hanoi counts are not geometric: 3/1 is 3 whereas 7/3 is not 3. They are not arithmetic: successive differences are 2, 4, 8, ... rather than constant.
translations.quickSummary: A recursive sequence specifies where to start and how to calculate the next term. For Tower of Hanoi minimum moves, \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T(n-1)+1\); the first five terms are \(1,3,7,15,31\). Explain each term using the legal-disc-move constraints.

translations.title: Introducing Geometric Sequences
translations.explanation: In a geometric sequence, every term comes from multiplying the preceding term by the same fixed number, called the common ratio or growth factor. This can represent repeated growth or repeated shrinking. Compare consecutive terms, organize a pattern in a table, and plot its values against the term number or number of actions. The important question is whether multiplication by one factor works at every step, not whether the terms merely increase or decrease.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(a_1\) is the first term and \(r\) is a fixed ratio, a geometric sequence satisfies \(a_n=r\,a_{n-1}\) for integer \(n\ge2\), equivalently \(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\). For nonzero previous terms, compute \(r=a_n/a_{n-1}\) and check it stays constant. Ratios \(r>1\) give increasing positive sequences, while \(0<r<1\) give decreasing positive sequences. A repeated paper cut that doubles the piece count but halves the area of each piece creates two different geometric sequences. For a paper of area \(80\) square inches, after \(n\) cuts (with \(n=0\) at the start), the count is \(P(n)=2^n\) and each piece has area \(A(n)=80(1/2)^n\). The product \(P(n)A(n)=80\) stays constant.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — determine the growth factor. The sequence \(45,15,5,5/3,\ldots\) has ratios \(15/45=1/3\), \(5/15=1/3\), and \((5/3)/5=1/3\). It is geometric with \(r=1/3\). The fifth term is \(5/9\). In contrast, \(2,4,7,11\) has varying ratios and is not geometric.

Example 2 — repeated cutting. Start with a rectangle measuring 8 by 10 inches, with total area 80 square inches. After 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 rounds of halving and stacking, the number of pieces is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, while the area of one piece is 80, 40, 20, 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25 square inches. At six cuts, \(64\times1.25=80\), confirming area conservation. The graph of each sequence consists of separate points at nonnegative whole-number cut counts; do not draw a physically meaningful line between half-cuts.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Label the sequence and starting index; the paper example begins at \(n=0\). 2. Divide each nonzero term by its predecessor and compare the quotients. 3. If a constant \(r\) exists, write the recursive rule and compute missing terms by multiplication or division. 4. In the paper model use \(P(n)=2^n\) and \(A(n)=80(1/2)^n\), so \(P(6)=64\) and \(A(6)=1.25\). 5. Verify \(P(n)A(n)=80\) for each checked \(n\), and label graph axes and units. 6. State explicitly that only nonnegative integer cut counts are allowed in this context.
translations.commonMistakes: A constant difference is evidence of an arithmetic sequence, not necessarily a geometric one. When the sequence decreases, a positive common ratio can still describe it (for example r=1/2). Do not divide by a previous term of zero. The whole sheet's area remains 80 square inches even though each piece gets smaller; do not confuse area per piece with total area. Use n=0 for the uncut sheet if that is how the model is indexed.
translations.quickSummary: Geometric sequences multiply each term by a constant factor. After \(n\) repeated paper halvings, \(P(n)=2^n\) pieces each have area \(A(n)=80(1/2)^n\); their product is always \(80\) square inches.

translations.title: Different Types of Sequences
translations.explanation: Arithmetic and geometric sequences describe two different kinds of repeated change. An arithmetic sequence adds the same difference each step; a geometric sequence multiplies by the same factor each step. A table and a graph help determine which rule fits: equally spaced points on a straight line suggest constant differences, while a curved pattern may suggest multiplication. Use the actual term numbers when comparing table rows, especially if some positions are missing.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: An arithmetic sequence has \(a_n=a_{n-1}+d\), where \(d\) is the constant common difference, and the explicit form \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\) for \(n\ge1\). A geometric sequence has \(a_n=r\,a_{n-1}\) and \(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\) for \(n\ge1\). Consecutive differences determine an arithmetic pattern; consecutive ratios determine a geometric pattern when denominators are nonzero. Some sequences are neither; a constant nonzero sequence is both arithmetic (difference 0) and geometric (ratio 1). When table entries skip positions, divide the change by the number of steps before identifying the per-step difference.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — classify three sequences. For \(A=30,40,50,60,70,\ldots\), successive differences equal 10, so \(A(n)=30+10(n-1)\). For \(B=0,5,15,30,50,\ldots\), differences 5, 10, 15, 20 vary; the ratios also fail to give a common factor, so \(B\) is neither. For \(C=1,2,4,8,16,\ldots\), every term doubles, so \(C(n)=2^{n-1}\).

Example 2 — nonconsecutive rows. A table gives \(f(1)=2\), \(f(2)=6\), and \(f(5)=18\). The difference from term 1 to 2 is 4. From term 2 to term 5 there are three steps and the total increase is 12, so the per-step change is \(12/3=4\), consistent with \(f(n)=4n-2\). The implied missing entries are \(f(3)=10\) and \(f(4)=14\). The displayed values look like multiples of 3 from one listed row to the next, but those rows do not represent equally spaced term numbers; a common ratio cannot be inferred from them. These three values alone do not prove every unobserved term follows the pattern, so the proposed rule is a model to check against the task context.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Write down the term numbers, not just the values. 2. For consecutive entries, calculate differences \(a_{n+1}-a_n\); if constant, identify \(d\). 3. When all relevant denominators are nonzero, compare ratios \(a_{n+1}/a_n\); if constant, identify \(r\). 4. If the table jumps from \(n=2\) to \(n=5\), count three steps before comparing a proposed rule. 5. Write and test the equation against all observed points: for \(f(n)=4n-2\), values at 1, 2, 5 are 2, 6, 18. 6. Classify as arithmetic, geometric, both, or neither with a written justification.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not confuse a constant increase with a constant multiplier. Do not treat adjacent table rows as consecutive terms if the input indices skip values. The sequence 0, 0, 0 is arithmetic (difference 0) and can also be generated geometrically, although ratios 0/0 cannot be used to identify its factor. A few data points may support but do not uniquely determine an infinite rule without an additional pattern assumption.
translations.quickSummary: Arithmetic: add a fixed difference \(d\); geometric: multiply by a fixed factor \(r\). With \(a_1\) at index 1, the explicit forms are \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\) and \(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\). Use index spacing and show evidence for the classification.

translations.title: Using Technology to Work with Sequences
translations.explanation: A spreadsheet can build a sequence by referring to earlier cells, and graphing technology can plot the resulting term-number/value pairs. Enter the starting value once, enter a formula in the next row that refers to the previous cell, then fill down to apply the pattern. Arithmetic rules add a constant; geometric rules multiply by a constant. Plot a sequence at whole-number term positions as discrete points, and use spreadsheet differences and ratios to test a conjectured pattern.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: In a typical spreadsheet, typing \`=A1+3\` into cell A2 calculates a value three greater than cell A1; filling the formula down updates relative references to A2, A3, and so on. Typing \`=B1*0.5\` in B2 repeatedly halves the column's previous value. Differences can be checked using \`=A2-A1\`, and ratios using \`=B2/B1\` when the denominator is nonzero. A scatterplot pairs each integer term number \(n\) with its output \(a_n\); the domain of a sequence is typically discrete, not a continuous interval. A graph with one output for each allowed input represents a function.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — arithmetic spreadsheet. Enter 10 in A1 and \`=A1+3\` in A2. Fill down to A5: the values are 10, 13, 16, 19, 22. In B2 enter \`=A2-A1\` and fill to B5; each difference is 3. The plotted points (1,10), (2,13), (3,16), (4,19), (5,22) lie on a straight-line pattern but are five separate data points.

Example 2 — geometric spreadsheet. Enter 16 in C1 and \`=C1*0.5\` in C2. Filling to C5 yields 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Enter \`=C2/C1\` in D2 and fill down to D5; each ratio equals 0.5. For the independent sequence 700, 70, 7, 0.7, the ratio is 0.1 at every step, not a constant subtraction. Check how one formula responds after changing the starting cell; relative references make all later values update.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Put the first term in a chosen starting cell (A1 = 10). 2. Enter a relative-reference formula in the next row (A2: \`=A1+3\`) and press Enter. 3. Fill down four rows; verify the sequence 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 by arithmetic. 4. In a separate column compute consecutive differences or ratios using the previous row, guarding against division by zero. 5. Build a graphing table with term number n and value a(n), then plot one point per valid term index. 6. Label inputs and outputs and confirm that changing the initial value updates dependent cells as intended.
translations.commonMistakes: A spreadsheet formula normally begins with =; otherwise software may treat it as text. A fixed reference such as $A$1 is not the same as a relative reference A1 when filling down. Never divide by a previous term of zero to estimate a geometric ratio. Connecting discrete sequence points with a continuous line can imply inputs that are not part of the problem. Formula syntax may differ by spreadsheet locale; check the calculated values.
translations.quickSummary: Use cell references and fill-down formulas to generate many sequence terms. Difference formulas identify arithmetic patterns and ratio formulas identify geometric patterns. Graph the integer-indexed terms as discrete points with meaningful axis labels.

translations.title: Sequences are Functions
translations.explanation: A sequence is a function that assigns one output to each allowed whole-number position. You can use a function name and a starting term to describe a sequence recursively, instead of writing out every value. In a growing triangular dot pattern, step n contains all dots from step n−1 plus a new row of n dots. The term number is an input; the number of dots is its output. State the domain explicitly, because a non-integer step such as step 2.5 does not describe this discrete pattern.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Function notation for a sequence identifies both the input and output: \(D(n)\) is the number of dots at step \(n\). For a triangular-dot pattern, \(D(1)=1\) and \(D(n)=D(n-1)+n\) for integers \(n\ge2\). The first five terms are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. A recursive definition requires a base value plus a rule whose inputs stay inside the domain. Arithmetic example: \(A(1)=99\), \(A(n)=A(n-1)-3\); geometric example: \(G(1)=80\), \(G(n)=G(n-1)/2\). A sequence has a discrete input domain such as \(\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) or \(\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) depending on the context.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — count growing dots. A triangular pattern has 1 dot at step 1, then adds a row of 2 dots, then a row of 3, and so on. The table is \((n,D(n))=(1,1),(2,3),(3,6),(4,10),(5,15)\). To calculate step 4, use \(D(4)=D(3)+4=6+4=10\), not \(D(3)+3\). These values are neither arithmetic nor geometric because successive differences are 2, 3, 4, 5 and successive ratios vary.

Example 2 — describe two recurrences. For \(99,96,93,\ldots\), define \(A(1)=99\), \(A(n)=A(n-1)-3\) when \(n\ge2\). For \(80,40,20,\ldots\), define \(G(1)=80\), \(G(n)=G(n-1)/2\) when \(n\ge2\). Check \(A(3)=93\) and \(G(3)=20\) by applying each recurrence twice.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Decide what a valid term number represents and specify its allowed integer domain. 2. Give the sequence function a name, such as \(D(n)\). 3. Find a base value: \(D(1)=1\). 4. Determine what is added or multiplied at every next step; here the new row contains \(n\) dots. 5. Write \(D(n)=D(n-1)+n\) for \(n\ge2\). 6. Calculate \(D(2)=3\), \(D(3)=6\), \(D(4)=10\), \(D(5)=15\), then compare with the visual count.
translations.commonMistakes: A recurrence without its initial value does not determine the sequence. In the triangular pattern, the new row size changes with n, so the sequence is not arithmetic. Use D(n−1), not D(n), on the right side of a recurrence if the rule depends on the preceding term. Function notation D(4) refers to the output at position 4, not 4 times D. Never use fractional term positions for discrete dot-building steps.
translations.quickSummary: A sequence is a function with a discrete input domain. Give both an initial condition and a next-term rule. For triangular dots, \(D(1)=1\) and \(D(n)=D(n-1)+n\); the first five outputs are \(1,3,6,10,15\).

translations.title: Representing Sequences
translations.explanation: The same sequence can be represented as a written description, a list, a table of term numbers and values, a discrete graph, or a recursive rule. To match representations, identify the starting term, test whether the change is additive or multiplicative, and check at least several successive values. A picture of stacked square blocks can define a sequence that is neither arithmetic nor geometric; do not force every pattern into one of those two families.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For an arithmetic sequence \(a_n=a_{n-1}+d\), the common difference \(d\) appears as equal changes between consecutive table rows. For a geometric sequence \(g_n=r g_{n-1}\), the constant factor \(r\) appears as equal nonzero consecutive ratios. A sequence defined by \(g(1)=-5\) and \(g(n)=-2g(n-1)\) alternates signs: \(-5,10,-20,40,\ldots\). A discrete graph uses the points \((1,a_1),(2,a_2),\ldots\). For stacked square arrays with \(S(n)=1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2\), an appropriate recurrence is \(S(1)=1\), \(S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2\).
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — translate descriptions. "Start at 10 and subtract 2.5 each step" produces 10, 7.5, 5, 2.5, 0, ... and can be written \(A(1)=10\), \(A(n)=A(n-1)-2.5\). "Start at −5 and multiply by −2" produces −5, 10, −20, 40; the growth factor is −2, not +2. On the graph, these values alternate above and below the horizontal axis.

Example 2 — stack of squares. Construct steps with square layers of side lengths 1, 2, 3 and 4. The total square counts are 1, \(1+4=5\), \(1+4+9=14\), and \(1+4+9+16=30\). A table \((n,S(n))=(1,1),(2,5),(3,14),(4,30)\) agrees with \(S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2\). Verify the next value \(S(5)=55\). These successive differences 4, 9, 16, 25 are not constant, and neither are the ratios.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the first term and allowed starting position. 2. Test a constant difference and, where valid, a constant ratio. 3. Convert the description to a recurrence with its base case. 4. Generate at least three terms from the recurrence and compare with the given list or visual pattern. 5. Make a table with term number as the first column, then plot the corresponding discrete points. 6. For the square-layer pattern, check \(1,5,14,30\) and predict \(55\) by adding \(5^2\).
translations.commonMistakes: A negative growth factor causes alternating signs; do not drop its minus sign. A recurrence with a changing increment, such as +n², is not an arithmetic sequence. A graph of a sequence contains separate points at allowed integer inputs; a continuous line can misrepresent the domain. Match a recurrence by its initial condition as well as its rule, not by its rule alone.
translations.quickSummary: Lists, tables, recursive formulas and discrete graphs are different representations of one sequence. Match both start and repeated change. Square layers give \(S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2\), not a constant-difference or constant-ratio rule.

translations.title: Representing More Sequences
translations.explanation: An information-gap problem asks you to decide what information is missing before calculating an answer. For a sequence, useful information may include the first term, the type of change, a growth factor or common difference, the term-number convention, and the position you want. Ask precise questions, state why each answer matters, then show a table, graph, recurrence, or equation that uses the data. Some tasks require mathematical explanation or partner discussion and should be reviewed with a rubric rather than automatically graded as one numeric answer.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: An arithmetic sequence is determined by a starting term \(a_1\) and common difference \(d\): \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\). A geometric sequence is determined by a starting term \(a_1\) and ratio \(r\): \(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\). If a prompt only says "the sequence is geometric" there is not enough information to calculate a unique fifth term. If it supplies \(a_1=20.25\) and \(r=2/3\), then \(a_2=13.5\), \(a_3=9\), \(a_4=6\), and \(a_5=4\). A table and graph must use the same indexing and units as the written rule. For information-gap tasks, record the missing inputs, your questions, and a justification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — ask for what you need. A data card states that a model is geometric but hides its starting value and multiplier. You cannot uniquely find the fifth term. Ask, "What is the first term and at what index?" and "By what factor does each new term change?" Suppose the answers are \(H(1)=12\) and \(r=2/3\). Then \(H(2)=8\), \(H(3)=16/3\), \(H(4)=32/9\), and \(H(5)=64/27\). The model is \(H(n)=12(2/3)^{n-1}\) for positive integer n.

Example 2 — compare two possible models. A card says only that the first term is 6. One model decreases by 5 each step: \(6,1,-4,-9,\ldots\). Another halves each step: \(6,3,1.5,0.75,\ldots\). Both match the starting term but not later terms. Request the difference or factor before choosing a rule. Explain in words which evidence eliminates the competing model.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Name the unknown, such as \(H(5)\). 2. List the available information, including whether the rule is arithmetic, geometric, or another recurrence. 3. Request the initial value, the index at which it occurs, and the step difference or ratio. 4. Write a proposed recurrence and compute a table using the supplied values. 5. Check the rule against any additional data and present an equivalent explicit formula when appropriate. 6. Explain what evidence would make the answer unique; when assessing dialogue or a drawing, use a criterion-based review rather than pretend it is a single numeric submission.
translations.commonMistakes: Knowing only the first term is insufficient to infer a unique sequence. Do not assume every recurrence has a fixed difference or ratio; a rule such as f(n)=f(n−1)+n² has neither. Be precise about whether numbering starts at 0 or 1. Do not treat an unobserved data card as evidence, and do not score a partner's explanation solely by matching one canned sentence.
translations.quickSummary: Determine the missing information needed for a sequence model, ask for it explicitly, then justify the rule using tables, graphs or equations. A valid arithmetic or geometric model needs both initial information and the change rule.

translations.title: The $n^{\text{th}}$ Term
translations.explanation: An explicit sequence formula calculates a term directly from its index, without evaluating all previous terms. For arithmetic sequences the formula depends on the number of equal additions; for geometric sequences it depends on the number of repeated multiplications. The index at which a sequence begins changes its exponent or subtraction offset. Compare formulas by testing them at the same allowed indices, not just by noticing similar-looking expressions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For an arithmetic sequence starting at \(n=1\), \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\); starting at \(n=0\), \(a_n=a_0+nd\). For a geometric sequence, \(g_n=g_1r^{n-1}\) or \(g_n=g_0r^n\), depending on the initial index. These can represent the same outputs after shifting indices appropriately. If paper starts with area \(80\) square inches and each cut halves the area, \(C(0)=80\) and \(C(n)=80(1/2)^n\) for nonnegative integer cuts. If a different process removes a strip of area 8 square inches per cut, \(K(n)=80-8n\) is meaningful only while the paper remains, for integer \(0\le n\le10\).
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — two paper processes. An 8-by-10-inch sheet has area 80 square inches. Repeated halving gives \(C(6)=80(1/2)^6=80/64=1.25\) square inches per remaining piece. Removing a strip of width 1 inch from the 10-inch side removes \(8\) square inches per cut, so \(K(6)=80-8(6)=32\) square inches. Therefore \(K(6)>C(6)\). Although the formulas look different, both start at 80 when \(n=0\), and both require whole-number counts in their physical models.

Example 2 — starting index matters. The list \(5,8,11,14,\ldots\) has common difference 3. If the first value is \(a_1=5\), write \(a_n=5+3(n-1)=3n+2\). If the same first listed value is called \(b_0=5\), write \(b_n=5+3n\). Thus \(a_4=b_3=14\); subtracting one in the wrong indexing convention gives a shifted sequence.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the first allowed index, either 0 or 1 in these examples. 2. Determine the starting value and the constant difference or growth factor. 3. Use \(a_n=a_0+nd\) or \(a_n=a_1+(n-1)d\) for arithmetic, and the corresponding \(r^n\) or \(r^{n-1}\) form for geometric. 4. Substitute the requested index directly. 5. For six halvings, calculate \(80/64=1.25\); for six removed strips, calculate \(80-48=32\). 6. Verify both against small indices and state physical domain limits.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not use n−1 when the first term is at n=0. An explicit formula does not require the previous term. Cutting an object in half and removing a fixed-area strip do not produce the same sequence type. A formula may make algebraic sense beyond a physical domain, but negative remaining paper area is not a valid model result.
translations.quickSummary: An explicit equation gives the \(n\)th term directly. Starting at index 0, halving paper gives \(C(n)=80(1/2)^n\); removing equal-area strips gives \(K(n)=80-8n\). Include the correct index offset and domain.

translations.title: What’s the Equation?
translations.explanation: A sequence model should match both how a quantity changes and what inputs are possible in the context. Sometimes a geometric rule is convenient in both recursive and explicit form; other patterns, such as a Fibonacci-type construction, are easiest to state recursively. Interpret what term zero or term one means before writing equations. An equation can predict a value, but the model's domain and assumptions must be stated separately.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If a quantity retains a constant fraction \(r\) after each step, use \(C(0)=C_0\), \(C(n)=rC(n-1)\) for integers \(n\ge1\), and \(C(n)=C_0r^n\). For a cake from which each person takes one third of the amount remaining, the retained fraction is \(r=2/3\), not \(1/3\). With the whole cake at \(n=0\), \(C(n)=(2/3)^n\) for integer \(n\ge0\). A Fibonacci-type rule has two initial values: \(F(1)=F(2)=1\), \(F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)\) for \(n\ge3\). It is neither arithmetic nor geometric.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — sharing cake. Before anyone arrives \(C(0)=1\). After person 1 removes one third, \(C(1)=2/3\). After person 2 removes one third of what remains, \(C(2)=(2/3)(2/3)=4/9\). Then \(C(3)=8/27\), \(C(4)=16/81\). The recursive formula is \(C(n)=(2/3)C(n-1)\) with \(C(0)=1\); the explicit formula is \(C(n)=(2/3)^n\). Only nonnegative integer numbers of people are allowed, and the idealized model assumes each successive person takes exactly a third of the remainder.

Example 2 — adjoining squares. If consecutive square side lengths are 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... because each new side matches the sum of the preceding two sides, then \(F(1)=F(2)=1\) and \(F(6)=8\). A fixed multiplier does not produce these values: \(2/1\ne3/2\). The recurrence uses two preceding terms, so giving just one base value would be insufficient.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Choose a quantity and define its unit and initial index. 2. Determine what fraction or amount remains after each step. 3. For cake, write \(C(0)=1\) and multiply by \(2/3\) at each arrival. 4. Compute the first four noninitial values \(2/3,4/9,8/27,16/81\); check against \(C(n)=(2/3)^n\). 5. For a Fibonacci-type pattern, specify two initial conditions before adding the preceding two terms. 6. State which indices make sense, and explain which model is easier to evaluate or justify.
translations.commonMistakes: Taking one third of the remainder does not mean the fraction left decreases by a fixed one third of the original. The retained factor is 2/3, not 1/3. Do not treat the cake as a continuous real-number function of the number of people without explaining the domain. Fibonacci-type rules need two initial terms and are not generally geometric.
translations.quickSummary: Translate contextual repeated change into a model with a defined domain. Cake remaining after \(n\) one-third removals is \(C(n)=(2/3)^n\) for integer \(n\ge0\). Some patterns need two-term recurrences rather than a simple explicit rule.

translations.title: Situations and Sequence Types
translations.explanation: Use observed differences, ratios, pictures, and context to choose a sequence model. An additive amount each year suggests an arithmetic sequence; a fixed percentage change suggests a geometric sequence. A growing shape may follow a polynomial pattern that is neither. Write an equation, label the time or step variable, and use the formula to make comparisons. Do not claim a real-world pattern must continue forever simply because its first few points fit.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: With an initial value \(A(0)\) and a fixed increase \(d\), \(A(n)=A(0)+dn\) is arithmetic. With an initial value \(B(0)\) and a fixed growth factor \(r\), \(B(n)=B(0)r^n\) is geometric. A factor \(r=1.5\) is a 50% increase per period, not 150%. For the population-model task, \(A(n)=23000+6000n\) and \(B(n)=3125(1.2)^n\), where \(n\) counts whole years after 1990. For a black rectangle of \(n\) rows and \(n+1\) columns, \(B_{\mathrm{sq}}(n)=n(n+1)\), which is neither arithmetic nor geometric; a surrounding white border with \(4n+6\) squares forms an arithmetic count.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — model two populations. Population A has values 23,000, 29,000, 35,000 for years 0, 1, 2, so its common difference is 6,000 and \(A(n)=23000+6000n\). Population B has values 3,125, 3,750, 4,500, so its factor is 1.2 and \(B(n)=3125(1.2)^n\). At year 21, \(A(21)=149000\) and \(B(21)\approx143766\), so A is still greater. At year 22, \(A(22)=155000\) and \(B(22)\approx172519\); under these models B first overtakes A at \(n=22\), corresponding to 2012. This is a mathematical projection, not a guarantee about real populations.

Example 2 — growing square counts. Suppose a black interior forms an \(n\)-by-\((n+1)\) rectangle surrounded by white squares. The number of black squares at steps 1, 2, 3 is 2, 6, 12, modeled by \(n(n+1)\). The white border count is 10, 14, 18, modeled by \(4n+6\). At step 4: black 20, white 22. At step 5: black 30, white 26, so black first exceeds white in the shown positive-integer pattern at step 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify time/step index and starting value. 2. Test equal consecutive differences for an arithmetic candidate and constant nonzero ratios for a geometric candidate. 3. Write \(A(n)=23000+6000n\) and \(B(n)=3125(1.2)^n\) for the population data. 4. Evaluate both for successive integer years until their ordering changes; verify years 21 and 22. 5. For the square pattern, count \(n(n+1)\) black and \(4n+6\) white squares and check the observed first three steps. 6. Explain the context, valid index set, percentage interpretation, and limits of extrapolation.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not interpret the geometric factor 1.2 as 120% growth; it is a 20% increase. Exponential growth may eventually exceed linear growth even if the exponential model starts smaller. A small data table does not guarantee the rule forever. For the square pattern, distinguish the rectangular area n(n+1) from a linear border count; not every sequence is arithmetic or geometric.
translations.quickSummary: Choose additive, multiplicative or other rules using evidence. Model two example populations by \(A(n)=23000+6000n\) and \(B(n)=3125(1.2)^n\); within the discrete model, \(B\) first exceeds \(A\) in year 2012.

translations.title: Adding Up
translations.explanation: Sometimes a situation requires the sum of several sequence terms rather than the value of one term. For a geometric sequence, successive contributions scale by a fixed factor. Write out the terms relevant to the story, keep track of which quantities are already distributed and which remain, and add using common denominators. At this point, you can calculate a short geometric sum directly without assuming a general infinite-series formula.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: The partial sum of a sequence is \(S_n=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n\), not just the last term \(a_n\). For a geometric sequence with first term \(a\) and ratio \(r\), the terms are \(a,ar,ar^2,\ldots\). In a repeated four-way paper split, someone who receives one quarter of the paper still held at each round receives contributions of \(1/4,1/16,1/64,\ldots\) of the original, so the first three contributions total \(1/4+1/16+1/64=21/64\). The last retained remainder after three rounds is \(1/64\). Conservation gives \(3(21/64)+1/64=1\).
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — add short fractional sequences. Evaluate \(1/2+1/4+1/8+1/16\). A common denominator of 16 gives \(8/16+4/16+2/16+1/16=15/16\). If every term were tripled, the four-term sum would also triple to \(45/16\). This is a finite sum, not a claim that the series goes on forever.

Example 2 — paper-sharing rounds. A person has one full sheet. At each round they divide the sheet still held into four equal parts, give one new part to each of three friends, and keep one part. Each friend receives \(1/4\) of the original in the first round, \(1/16\) in the second and \(1/64\) in the third. After three rounds each friend owns \(21/64\) of the original. The original owner holds \(1/64\) and the check \(3(21/64)+1/64=64/64\) confirms that no area disappeared or was counted twice.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify whether the task asks for one term or for accumulated terms. 2. Define each round's contribution as a fraction of the ORIGINAL quantity. 3. For three four-way divisions, list \(1/4,1/16,1/64\) for each recipient. 4. Convert to denominator 64 and add \(16/64+4/64+1/64=21/64\). 5. Multiply by the number of recipients and include the remainder: \(3(21/64)+1/64=1\). 6. State the number of rounds; do not claim the short sum equals an infinite limit.
translations.commonMistakes: The last distributed piece is not the total amount a recipient has received; earlier contributions must be added. A fraction of the remaining sheet differs from the same fraction of the original sheet. Use a common denominator for exact addition. Do not apply an infinite geometric-sum expression where the task asks for only three or four rounds.
translations.quickSummary: A partial sum adds several sequence terms. In three four-way paper-sharing rounds, each of three recipients collects \(1/4+1/16+1/64=21/64\) of the original; \(1/64\) remains with the original owner.

translations.title: Let’s Make a Box
translations.explanation: Build an open-top box by removing equal square corners from a rectangular sheet and folding the sides upward. If the original sheet is 3 by 8 inches and the cutout squares have side x inches, the folded box has height x, length 8−2x and width 3−2x. Volume depends on all three dimensions. Graph the volume as a function of x, restrict the graph to physically possible cutouts, and estimate the largest achievable volume.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Volume is \(V(x)=x(L-2x)(W-2x)\). For a 3-by-8-inch sheet, \(V(x)=x(3-2x)(8-2x)=4x^3-22x^2+24x\) cubic inches. The physical domain is \(0<x<1.5\), since both base sides must remain positive. Distinguish the input giving the greatest volume from that maximum output. A cubic polynomial is defined for all real inputs algebraically, even when negative dimensions make its values physically meaningless.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: With a half-inch cutout, the box dimensions are 2, 7 and 0.5 inches, yielding volume \(2\cdot7\cdot0.5=7\) cubic inches. With a 1-inch cutout, the dimensions are 1, 6 and 1, yielding 6 cubic inches. Example 2: An accurate graph on \(0<x<1.5\) peaks near \(x=2/3\), where \(V(2/3)=(5/3)(20/3)(2/3)=200/27\approx7.407\). Original Edulytiks extension: \(V'(x)=4(3x-2)(x-3)\) verifies that \(x=2/3\) is the only interior maximum.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Let x be the corner-square side length. 2. Subtract 2x from the original length and width, then set the folded height to x. 3. Multiply to obtain \(V=x(3-2x)(8-2x)\). 4. Enforce \(0<x<1.5\); outside this interval no nondegenerate box exists. 5. Evaluate several feasible choices and graph only the feasible portion. 6. Check \(x=2/3\) gives \(200/27\) cubic inches and state both the optimum input and the resulting volume.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not subtract x only once from a base dimension: both corners take away x. A tall box need not have the greatest volume because its base shrinks. Cutout x=2 is not a feasible real box from a 3-inch-wide sheet. Do not use negative or zero heights, confuse square inches with cubic inches, or claim an algebraic maximum outside the physical domain.
translations.quickSummary: An open-top box cut from a 3-by-8-inch sheet has \(V(x)=x(3-2x)(8-2x)\), \(0<x<1.5\). Its largest volume is \(200/27\approx7.407\) cubic inches at cutout side \(x=2/3\) inch.

translations.title: Funding the Future
translations.explanation: Use powers of a variable to model an account with money deposited at different times. Just as place-value notation writes \(329=3(10^2)+2(10)+9\), a polynomial can track several deposits accruing interest for different numbers of years. Let x=1+r, where r is the annual interest rate as a decimal; a deposit earns one factor of x for every complete year after it is made.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For an initial $300 deposit and additional deposits of $500 after year 1, $250 after year 2 and $400 after year 3, all evaluated at the end of year 4, \(C(x)=300x^4+500x^3+250x^2+400x\). Exponents count actual interest periods, not the number of deposits. \(x=1+r\) is a dimensionless annual growth factor, while C(x) is measured in dollars. The fixed-rate model excludes bank fees and variable interest; \(r=0.05\) corresponds to \(x=1.05\), not \(x=0.05\).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Draw a year-by-year timeline showing the initial deposit, three later deposits, and the year-4 endpoint. 2. Count each gift's growth periods: 4, 3, 2, and 1. 3. Multiply the deposits by \(x^4,x^3,x^2,x\), respectively, and add. 4. Confirm the formula equals $1450 when x=1. 5. Substitute x=1.05 for a 5% annual rate, keeping full precision until rounding to cents. 6. If solving a target balance from a graph, convert the plotted x back to rate r=x−1.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not assign the same fourth power to all gifts, because later deposits earn interest for fewer years. A rate of 5% is 0.05; use growth factor 1.05. The x-axis is the growth factor rather than dollars or interest percentage. Do not use the bank polynomial to infer guaranteed real investment performance.
translations.quickSummary: The polynomial \(C(x)=300x^4+500x^3+250x^2+400x\) models a sequence of deposits through four years. Each exponent is the number of years the corresponding deposit earns interest, and \(r=x-1\).

translations.title: Introducing Polynomials
translations.explanation: Describe what makes an expression a polynomial in one variable, then match polynomial equations to graphs using degree, coefficients, and possible turning points. In standard form, terms are collected by descending whole-number exponents. The degree of a nonzero polynomial is its largest remaining exponent. On a graph, a relative maximum is higher than nearby outputs, and a relative minimum is lower than nearby outputs; neither necessarily represents a global extreme.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Write \(p(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0\), where exponents are nonnegative integers and \(a_n\ne0\). The leading term is \(a_nx^n\), the leading coefficient is \(a_n\), and the constant term is \(a_0\). Collect like terms first. \(x^{1/3}\), \(x^{-1}\), and \(\sqrt{x}\) are not polynomial terms in x. A nonzero constant polynomial has degree 0; the zero polynomial has no uniquely defined degree. A real polynomial of degree n has at most n−1 turning points.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(4-x^2+x^3-4x=x^3-x^2-4x+4\) is degree 3 with leading coefficient 1 and constant 4. \(2x^4+x^2-5.7x+2\) is degree 4. \(x^2+7x-x^{1/3}+2\) is not polynomial because the fractional exponent is disallowed. \(3x^2-3x^2+7=7\) is degree 0 after combining terms. Example 2: \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) has a relative high point at \((-1,2)\) and a relative low point at \((1,-2)\); it has no global maximum because outputs grow without bound for large positive x.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Check every exponent is a nonnegative integer. 2. Distribute and combine like terms before identifying the degree. 3. Reorder the polynomial to read leading term and constant term. 4. Match candidate graphs using intercepts and number/shape of turns. 5. For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), evaluate values near x=−1 and x=1 to verify the local high and low points. 6. Explain why local extrema need not be absolute extrema.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not count canceled high-degree terms when determining degree. Fractional exponents make an expression nonpolynomial even if the other terms have valid powers. A relative maximum may not be a function's largest value overall. A fourth-degree polynomial may have fewer than three turns: a degree sets an upper bound, not an exact required count.
translations.quickSummary: A polynomial is a finite sum of nonnegative integer powers times constants. In standard form, the largest nonzero exponent gives degree. Relative maximum and minimum describe neighboring graph behavior, not necessarily global extremes.

translations.title: Combining Polynomials
translations.explanation: Investigate whether adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing elements of a number or expression set always produces another element of that same set. Integers and polynomials stay within their respective sets under addition, subtraction and multiplication. Test examples, then justify why these operations always preserve the polynomial form. Comparing division exposes a counterexample to this closure property.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Polynomials are closed under addition and subtraction because like-degree terms combine to produce valid coefficients. They are closed under multiplication because the product \(x^m x^n=x^{m+n}\) still has a nonnegative integer exponent for \(m,n\ge0\). They are not closed under general division, since \(1/x\) is not a polynomial. Even integers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, whereas odd integers are not closed under addition because odd + odd is even.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(7+9=16\), \(7-9=-2\) and \(7\cdot9=63\) are integers, but \(7/9\) is not an integer. Example 2: Let \(p=2x^2-3x+1\) and \(q=x^2+4x-5\). Then \(p+q=3x^2+x-4\), \(p-q=x^2-7x+6\), and \(pq=2x^4+5x^3-21x^2+19x-5\). Each is a polynomial. However \(p/x=2x-3+1/x\) for x≠0 is not polynomial, and x=0 stays excluded from the quotient.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Choose which set you are investigating. 2. Add two polynomial expressions by collecting like terms. 3. Subtract while distributing the minus sign across every term. 4. Multiply each term of the first polynomial by every term of the second and combine. 5. Generalize by using the exponent rule \(x^m x^n=x^{m+n}\). 6. Refute closure under division using \(1/x\), noting x=0 is excluded.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not infer a universal closure law from a single successful example: justify it from the structure of polynomial terms. Multiplication requires cross terms and negative signs matter. Polynomials do not remain polynomial under every quotient; a denominator containing x can introduce negative exponents. A rational expression's excluded values still matter after simplification.
translations.quickSummary: Polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication always yield polynomials; division does not necessarily do so. The proof comes from combining polynomial coefficients and adding nonnegative integer exponents.

translations.title: Connecting Factors and Zeros
translations.explanation: A polynomial's zeros are inputs where its output equals zero, which correspond to its horizontal-axis intercepts. Factored form makes many zeros directly visible. Use the zero-product property: if a product of real factors is zero, at least one factor is zero. Compare nearly identical factored polynomials to see which intercepts stay fixed and which move when a factor changes.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(x)=(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)\), zero-product reasoning gives zeros \(a,b,c\). The horizontal-intercept coordinates are \((a,0),(b,0),(c,0)\). The vertical intercept is separately \((0,f(0))\). Multiplying f by any nonzero constant changes its nonzero outputs but preserves the zeros. A factor must equal zero, not merely be negative, for a product to equal zero.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=(x+5)(x+1)(x-3)\) has zeros −5, −1, and 3. Its y-intercept is \(f(0)=5\cdot1\cdot(-3)=-15\). Check \(f(3)=0\), but \(f(2)=7\cdot3\cdot(-1)=-21\), so 2 is not a zero. Example 2: \(g(x)=(x+5)(x+1)(x-2)\) instead has zeros −5, −1, and 2, and \(g(0)=-10\). The first two roots do not move; the third does. \(h(x)=-2g(x)\) keeps g's zeros even though it reflects and stretches the graph.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Record all factors from the given product. 2. Set each factor equal to zero and solve its linear equation. 3. Turn root values into points on the horizontal axis. 4. Calculate the vertical intercept by evaluating the function at x=0. 5. Substitute a root to verify the product vanishes. 6. Compare two expressions factor by factor and note changed or unchanged roots.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not report the zero x=−5 as x=+5 simply because the factor is x+5. A zero is an input, while an x-intercept is the point (x,0). Changing a nonzero outside multiplier does not change root locations. The vertical intercept f(0) is usually different from the horizontal-axis intercepts.
translations.quickSummary: Factored form makes zeros visible. \(f(x)=(x+5)(x+1)(x-3)\) has roots −5, −1 and 3, and its graph has y-intercept −15.

translations.title: Different Forms
translations.explanation: Standard and factored forms of a polynomial expose different information about the same function. Factored form displays zeros, while standard form shows the degree and leading term. Expand carefully to demonstrate equivalence. Then compare graphs of polynomials that differ by a nonzero constant multiplier: their roots remain at the same horizontal positions even as their vertical output values change.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For the 14-by-8.5-inch box, \(V(x)=x(14-2x)(8.5-2x)=4x^3-45x^2+119x\). Algebraically the roots are 0, 7, and 4.25; however the physical domain is \(0<x<4.25\). For \(f(x)=(x-2)(x+3)(x-7)\), \(g(x)=\tfrac12f(x)\) has the same roots and half the output value at each x. Changing multiplication by a nonzero k preserves roots and degree, but negative k also reverses the sign of every nonzero output.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Expand the box: \((14-2x)(8.5-2x)=119-45x+4x^2\), so \(V=4x^3-45x^2+119x\). At \(x=1\), factored evaluation yields \(1(12)(6.5)=78\) and standard form yields \(4-45+119=78\) cubic inches. Root 7 is algebraically correct but outside the physical domain. Example 2: \(f=(x-2)(x+3)(x-7)=x^3-6x^2-13x+42\), while \(g=\tfrac12f\) has y-intercept 21 instead of 42, and both have zeros 2, −3 and 7. \(h=(3x-6)(x+3)(x-7)=3f\) triples the vertical output.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the factors and expected zeros. 2. Distribute the factors to rewrite the function in standard form. 3. Match results at a sample input such as x=1 for the box. 4. From the leading term, identify degree and coefficient. 5. Restrict box inputs to positive x less than half the shortest sheet dimension. 6. For a nonzero constant multiplier, keep the same zero inputs and multiply all y-values by that constant.
translations.commonMistakes: An algebraic zero of a polynomial can be physically impossible in a real-world model. Do not discard the factor x while expanding a volume expression. Two equivalent algebraic forms represent the same graph. A positive vertical scaling leaves zero locations unchanged; it does not shift x-intercepts. Do not label a cubic polynomial's full real domain as the box's feasible domain.
translations.quickSummary: Equivalent forms expose different polynomial features: \(x(14-2x)(8.5-2x)=4x^3-45x^2+119x\). A nonzero vertical scale changes outputs but not zeros.

translations.title: Using Factors and Zeros
translations.explanation: Use factored equations to plan a useful graphing window and to build a polynomial from desired horizontal intercepts. Each factor x−a supplies a zero x=a. A constant multiple changes the graph's heights but not the zero locations. Look carefully at every root before choosing an x-range: a narrow window may make a cubic resemble a parabola or omit important intercepts.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(p(x)=k\prod_i(x-r_i)\) with nonzero k, then every \(r_i\) is an x-intercept. To show all real roots, a viewing window must extend below the smallest and above the largest root, with reasonable margins; adjust vertical range for the curve's scale. For \(M(x)=(x+3)(2x-5)\) and \(K(x)=3M(x)\), both have zeros −3 and 2.5, but \(K(0)=3(-15)=-45\) while \(M(0)=-15\). To create zeros −2, 0, 4, choose \(Q(x)=x(x+2)(x-4)\); any nonzero multiple also works.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(p(x)=(x+1)(x-2)(x+15)\) is degree 3 with zeros −15, −1 and 2. The window \(-10\le x\le8\) misses −15 and can give a misleading picture; choose \(-18\le x\le5\) and then adjust the vertical scale by evaluating the function. Example 2: \(Q(x)=2x(x+2)(x-4)\) has zeros −2, 0 and 4. Check \(Q(1)=2(1)(3)(-3)=-18\) and \(Q(4)=0\). Multiplying Q by −1 changes its orientation without moving zeros.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Factor the equation and list every real zero visible from its linear factors. 2. Include all zeros plus a margin in the horizontal range. 3. Evaluate outputs, including \(f(0)\), to choose a vertical range wide enough to see the curve. 4. For given desired roots, write one factor x−r per root. 5. Multiply by a convenient nonzero coefficient and check each root by substitution. 6. Compare the graph and the algebraic zero set to detect hidden intercepts.
translations.commonMistakes: A screen that looks parabolic need not represent a quadratic; a missing far-left or far-right zero can change the interpretation. A vertical stretch does not require moving the horizontal window, but it may require a wider vertical range. Roots are inputs, not vertical-axis intercepts. There are infinitely many polynomial expressions with a prescribed set of roots.
translations.quickSummary: Use factored expressions to choose viewing windows and construct equations from desired roots. For zeros −2, 0 and 4, \(Q(x)=x(x+2)(x-4)\) works, as does every nonzero constant multiple.

translations.title: End Behavior (Part 1)
translations.explanation: End behavior describes what happens to a polynomial's outputs at inputs farther and farther to the left or right. When the leading coefficient is positive, even-degree polynomials rise in both directions and odd-degree polynomials fall to the left and rise to the right. Compare large positive and negative inputs to see why the highest-power term dominates while lower powers may temporarily affect the visible graph.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a nonzero polynomial with positive leading term \(ax^n\), \(a>0\), large positive inputs give large positive outputs. For large negative inputs, an even n also gives positive outputs; an odd n gives negative outputs. Lower-degree terms change details near the middle but not this end behavior. A term with a huge lower-degree coefficient may dominate moderate inputs; eventually the highest power dominates as the magnitude of x increases. Infinity is a direction of unbounded values, not a number that can be substituted into an equation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=x^3+4x^2-x-4\) has leading term \(x^3\), so outputs fall without bound as x gets farther left and rise without bound as x gets farther right. \(g(x)=x^4-10x^2+9\) has leading term \(x^4\), so both distant ends rise. Example 2: \(p(x)=-0.01x^3+25422x^2+8x+26\) can give positive outputs for moderate negative x even though the cubic leading term is negative. At sufficiently large negative x, the \(-0.01x^3\) term becomes positive and dominates; for sufficiently large positive x it becomes negative and dominates. This counterexample is an original extension illustrating why small tables may mislead.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Write the expression in descending degree and combine like terms. 2. Identify the leading term. 3. Compare the sign of the leading term for large positive x and large negative x. 4. For positive leading coefficient, even degree means up on both ends; odd degree means down-left/up-right. 5. Calculate representative outputs at larger magnitudes and explain why lower-degree terms become relatively less important. 6. Describe directions precisely rather than trying to evaluate a function at infinity.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not decide degree from the largest coefficient; it comes from the largest exponent with a nonzero coefficient. A table at x=−1 and x=1 cannot establish end behavior. The sign of negative x raised to an even power differs from an odd power. Avoid calling infinity an input value, and distinguish the current graph window from behavior at very large magnitudes.
translations.quickSummary: For a positive leading coefficient, even-degree polynomials rise at both distant ends; odd-degree polynomials fall on the far left and rise on the far right. The leading term determines the behavior regardless of temporary middle-range features.

translations.title: End Behavior (Part 2)
translations.explanation: The sign of the leading coefficient combines with degree parity to determine a polynomial's two distant ends. A negative leading coefficient reflects the basic positive-leading-term pattern vertically, so both ends fall for even degree and the far-left end rises while the far-right end falls for odd degree. Use this structure to match equations to graph shapes and to construct examples that satisfy stated end-behavior conditions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Even degree with positive leading coefficient: both far ends rise; with negative leading coefficient: both fall. Odd degree with positive leading coefficient: far left falls, far right rises; with negative leading coefficient: far left rises, far right falls. The polynomial \(x(x+3)(2-x)\) has leading term \(-x^3\), so it exhibits the last pattern. A constant expression like \(5(x+3)-5x=15\) has degree zero and remains at output 15; simplify before classifying.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=-2x^4+3x^2+7\) has even degree 4, negative leading coefficient and both ends going downward. A different equation \(g(x)=-x^3+2x\) has odd degree and negative leading coefficient; its far-left outputs rise, while its far-right outputs fall. Example 2: Expanding \(x(x+3)(2-x)=x[(x+3)(2-x)]=-x^3-x^2+6x\) shows the leading coefficient −1, even if the graph is zoomed in. By contrast \(1-3x+5x^4\) rises at both ends. \(5(x+3)-5x=15\) is constant, not linear.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Expand or simplify enough to find the highest surviving power. 2. Decide whether its degree is even or odd. 3. Decide whether the leading coefficient is positive or negative. 4. Apply the corresponding far-left and far-right end directions. 5. Test an expression by substituting large positive and negative inputs. 6. To create an equation with a desired pattern, choose a correctly signed leading term and add at least one lower-degree term if required.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not treat an unexpanded factor (2−x) as having a positive leading coefficient: its leading term is −x. Do not rely on a graph window that omits the distant ends. After simplification, (5(x+3)-5x) is constant and does not have odd-degree end behavior. A negative coefficient on a lower-degree term does not change the end behavior when the leading coefficient is positive.
translations.quickSummary: Degree parity and the leading coefficient's sign determine end behavior. For example, \(-x^3+2x\) rises to the far left and falls to the far right; \(-2x^4+3x^2+7\) falls at both ends.

translations.title: Multiplicity
translations.explanation: Multiplicity measures how many times a factor occurs in a polynomial expression. When a zero has odd multiplicity, its graph crosses the horizontal axis; when it has even multiplicity, the graph touches the axis and turns back. The familiar roots still give horizontal intercepts, but the powers of the factors help decide how to sketch the curve between and around them. Use the degree and leading coefficient to complete a rough sketch of the two distant ends.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(p(x)=k(x-a)^m\cdots\), then a is a zero with multiplicity m provided the remaining factors do not also vanish at a. A factor with even multiplicity makes the polynomial keep the same sign as x moves across that root; an odd multiplicity reverses the sign. Multiplicity 1 typically crosses with nonzero slope, multiplicity 2 touches and turns, and multiplicity 3 crosses with flattening. Total degree is the sum of multiplicities of the shown linear factors (assuming nonzero k). End behavior also depends on the sign of the leading coefficient.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=(x+1)(x-3)^2\) has roots −1 (multiplicity 1) and 3 (multiplicity 2). It crosses the x-axis at −1 but touches and turns at 3. Its leading term is \(x^3\), so the distant left side falls and right side rises; \(f(0)=9\). Example 2: \(g(x)=(x-3)^3\) has a triple root at 3 and changes sign there, with a flattened crossing. By contrast \(h(x)=(x-3)^2\) never becomes negative, and 3 is its minimum. A polynomial with three distinct real zeros that is nonnegative for all real x must give each zero an even multiplicity, so its degree is at least 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Factor the polynomial and record every distinct root. 2. Count how many copies of each factor occur. 3. At odd-multiplicity roots draw a crossing; at even-multiplicity roots a touch-and-turn. 4. Compute total degree and leading coefficient from the factors. 5. Decide the two end directions using parity and leading sign. 6. Plot the vertical intercept and one point between neighboring roots to verify the sign of each segment.
translations.commonMistakes: Multiplicity is not the number of distinct intercepts: a double root is still just one x-coordinate. A cubic root may cross while appearing almost flat near the axis. A factor squared cannot by itself change the sign of a product. Avoid sketching a graph crossing at an even-multiplicity zero or touching without crossing at a simple root.
translations.quickSummary: Factor multiplicity controls local zero behavior. Odd multiplicities cross the axis; even multiplicities touch and turn. Combine these facts with degree, leading sign and sample points for a credible polynomial sketch.

translations.title: Finding Intersections
translations.explanation: To find where two polynomial graphs intersect, solve for inputs at which they have the same output. Instead of setting either function equal to zero, set the two function expressions equal to each other and simplify. Linear and quadratic pairs may intersect at zero, one, or two distinct points, or coincide along an entire graph. Substitution supplies exact answers when factorization or the quadratic formula is convenient; graphing technology can check or estimate more complicated intersections.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: An intersection \((x,y)\) satisfies both \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\), so solve \(f(x)-g(x)=0\). Check every candidate by substituting it back into both functions and reporting the common y-coordinate. If the difference is a nonzero constant, there are no intersections. If the difference is identically zero, every allowed graph point is common. For a quadratic-vs-line system, there may be 0, 1, or 2 real intersections depending on the resulting quadratic discriminant.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=x^2-7\), \(g(x)=2\) intersect where \(x^2-7=2\), so \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\); the points are \((3,2)\) and \((-3,2)\). Example 2: Solve \((x+7)(x-4)=x-4\). Moving all terms to one side gives \((x-4)[(x+7)-1]=(x-4)(x+6)=0\). Thus \(x=4\) or \(x=-6\); since the common right-side function is \(g(x)=x-4\), the intersections are \((4,0)\) and \((-6,-10)\). Example 3: \(5x^3+6x^2+4x=5640\) has x=10 as a verified intersection because substituting gives 5640; do not assume without further analysis that no other solutions exist.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define both graph functions with their allowed input domains. 2. Write \(f(x)=g(x)\) and move everything to one side. 3. Factor or use an equation-solving strategy; for the second example factor \((x-4)(x+6)\). 4. Solve each factor equation, giving x=4 and x=−6. 5. Substitute both inputs into either function to find y-values 0 and −10. 6. Verify the points satisfy BOTH original equations; use a graph to inspect any missing or closely spaced intersections.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not confuse x-intercepts, which satisfy f(x)=0, with intersections of f and g, which satisfy f(x)=g(x). An x-value alone is not a complete intersection point; report y too. If dividing both sides by x−4, you might wrongly discard the valid solution x=4. A graphing window can hide intersections, and numerical solutions require checking.
translations.quickSummary: Intersections solve \(f(x)=g(x)\). Factor carefully, check each input in both original functions, and report ordered pairs. Two polynomial graphs can intersect at several or no points, or coincide completely.

translations.title: Polynomial Division (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Divide a polynomial by a linear expression by working backward from multiplication. Organize terms by descending powers, determine the leading quotient term, multiply the divisor, and subtract to find what remains. A factor diagram is one way to display the work; the essential mathematical claim is verified by multiplying the divisor by the proposed quotient and adding any remainder.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For dividend \(P(x)\) and nonzero divisor \(D(x)\), division yields \(P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x)\) where the remainder has smaller degree than \(D\). If \(D(x)=x-a\), the remainder is constant. When \(R=0\), \(x-a\) is an exact polynomial factor. When interpreting the rational quotient \(P(x)/(x-a)\), the original input \(x=a\) remains excluded even if algebraic cancellation leaves a polynomial expression.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Divide \(x^3+5x^2+2x-8\) by \(x-1\). The quotient starts with \(x^2\), leaving \(6x^2+2x-8\); add \(6x\), leaving \(8x-8\); add 8, leaving 0. Hence \(x^3+5x^2+2x-8=(x-1)(x^2+6x+8)=(x-1)(x+2)(x+4)\), with roots 1, −2, −4. Example 2: \(2x^2+7x+6=(x+2)(2x+3)\). Multiply \(x+2\) by \(2x+3\) to check \(2x^2+4x+3x+6=2x^2+7x+6\).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Write the dividend with all powers in order, including zero coefficient placeholders when necessary. 2. Divide the highest term of the dividend by the highest term of the divisor to choose the next quotient term. 3. Multiply the full divisor by that term and subtract the result. 4. Repeat until the remainder has degree lower than the divisor. 5. For \(P/(x-1)\), obtain quotient \(x^2+6x+8\) and remainder zero. 6. Multiply back and, when factoring P, use the quotient's own factors to locate all zeros.
translations.commonMistakes: Subtract the entire product of divisor and quotient term, not only its leading term. Keep missing powers as zero coefficients to avoid column shifts. Exact division by x−a does not authorize evaluating the original rational expression at x=a. A zero remainder proves divisibility; a nonzero remainder must remain in the final answer.
translations.quickSummary: Polynomial division reverses multiplication: \(P=DQ+R\). In this example \(x^3+5x^2+2x-8=(x-1)(x+2)(x+4)\), so division by \(x-1\) has remainder 0.

translations.title: Polynomial Division (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Polynomial long division organizes the same inverse-multiplication reasoning as an area diagram, but uses columns of descending powers. Each step chooses a term to eliminate the highest remaining power. Repeat until the leftover expression has lower degree than the divisor. A nonzero remainder is legitimate and belongs to the division identity; it does not mean the entire division is invalid.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Given \(P(x)\) and nonzero \(D(x)\), long division produces \(P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x)\), with \(\deg R<\deg D\) when \(R\ne0\). Write each polynomial in descending powers, insert zero-coefficient terms if a power is missing, and subtract the entire row of products with correct signs. For a linear divisor \(x-a\), the remainder is a constant, and the expression \(P(x)/D(x)=Q(x)+R(x)/D(x)\) is defined only where \(D(x)\ne0\).
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Divide \(2x^3+7x^2+7x+2\) by \(x+1\). \(2x^3/x=2x^2\), subtract \(2x^3+2x^2\) to leave \(5x^2+7x+2\). Next \(5x^2/x=5x\), subtract \(5x^2+5x\) to leave \(2x+2\). Finally subtract \(2(x+1)\). Quotient \(2x^2+5x+2\), remainder 0. Verify \((x+1)(2x^2+5x+2)=2x^3+7x^2+7x+2\). Example 2: Divide \(x^2+1\) by \(x-1\). Quotient \(x+1\), remainder 2; indeed \((x-1)(x+1)+2=x^2+1\). For the rational expression, x=1 is excluded.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Align all terms by descending exponent. 2. Divide leading dividend term by leading divisor term to obtain the next quotient term. 3. Multiply divisor by that term and subtract every term of the product. 4. Bring down the next degree and repeat. 5. Stop when the remaining polynomial has lower degree than the divisor. 6. Verify the dividend equals divisor times quotient plus remainder, and retain excluded denominator inputs in rational interpretations.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not stop simply because a constant remains: its degree must be compared with the divisor's degree. A remainder 2 means the divisor is not a factor, but the division identity still works. Missing degree columns or missed negative signs produce wrong quotients. Never erase denominator domain exclusions after converting a rational expression to quotient-plus-remainder form.
translations.quickSummary: Long division returns \(P=DQ+R\), with remainder degree less than divisor degree. Exact factors have \(R=0\); for \((x^2+1)/(x-1)\), quotient \(x+1\), remainder 2 and x=1 remains excluded.

translations.title: What Do You Know About Polynomials?
translations.explanation: Apply several polynomial representations together: use a known factor, an equation in standard form, and information from a partner to construct a factorization and sketch the graph. The purpose of the information gap is to ask which additional details are needed rather than guessing them. A reliable solution records the polynomial's degree, known factors, zeros with multiplicities, leading sign, and enough additional data to determine the remaining factors.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(P(x)=x^3-7x+6\), a possible factorization is \((x-2)(x+3)(x-1)\), revealing distinct zeros 2, −3, 1. To verify, expand \((x-2)(x-1)=x^2-3x+2\) and multiply by \(x+3\) to obtain \(x^3-7x+6\). The leading coefficient is positive and degree 3, so the graph falls to the far left and rises to the far right. A polynomial's degree 3 and known factors x and x+4, with exactly two x-intercepts, could indicate one repeated zero, but the information alone does not uniquely specify its scale or multiplicities without an extra condition.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Starting with \(P(x)=x^3-7x+6\) and the known factor \(x-2\), divide to get \(x^2+2x-3\), which factors to \((x+3)(x-1)\). The zeros are 2, −3, and 1; \(P(0)=6\) is the vertical intercept. Example 2: A degree-3 polynomial has factors x and x+4, exactly two distinct real intercepts (one negative), and a negative leading coefficient. Two possible expressions are \(-x^2(x+4)\) and \(-x(x+4)^2\), showing why additional information about multiplicity is needed. Both have only zeros 0 and −4 and satisfy the given leading-sign requirement.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the supplied data card or source equation and list known factors and degree. 2. Identify the missing information needed to finish factoring, such as a coefficient or additional root. 3. Ask an explicit question about that datum and explain why it matters. 4. Divide by known factors and factor any remaining quadratic. 5. Confirm by multiplication and substitution at each zero. 6. Sketch intercepts, touching/crossing behavior and two distant ends; where multiple answers remain possible, state that the problem is underdetermined.
translations.commonMistakes: Knowing two roots does not generally specify a unique cubic. Do not assume a known factor reveals multiplicity unless its repeated occurrence is given. Factorization by an assumed root needs a remainder-zero check. Partner explanation and graph reasoning need an argument or rubric, not automatic exact-string grading.
translations.quickSummary: Use polynomial division and source information to recover missing factors, verify an equivalent standard form, and sketch the zeros/end behavior. Ask for any information that is required before claiming a unique answer.

translations.title: The Remainder Theorem
translations.explanation: The Remainder Theorem connects the value of a polynomial at a number to division by a linear expression. Rather than performing every division, evaluate the function at the appropriate input. A zero remainder is exactly the condition for a linear factor. Use this fact to find an unknown coefficient in a polynomial or to decide which proposed factors are valid, then justify the result from the division identity.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Dividing a polynomial \(P(x)\) by \(x-a\) gives \(P(x)=(x-a)Q(x)+r\), with constant remainder r. Substitute \(x=a\): \(P(a)=(a-a)Q(a)+r=r\). Therefore \(\mathrm{remainder}=P(a)\); in particular \(x-a\) divides P exactly if and only if \(P(a)=0\). This proves both directions of the factor theorem without relying on a plot. For x+3, use a=−3, not +3.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(x)=x^4-ux^3+24x^2-32x+16\) has \(x-2\) as a factor. Then \(f(2)=16-8u+96-64+16=64-8u=0\), so \(u=8\). Re-substitution verifies a zero remainder. Example 2: \(P(x)=x^2+1\) divided by x−1 leaves \(P(1)=2\), so x−1 is not a factor. Example 3: \(A(x)=6x^2-7x-5\) has \(A(2)=24-14-5=5\), so division by x−2 leaves remainder 5 without completing long division.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Put the proposed divisor into the form x−a and identify a. 2. Evaluate the polynomial at a using correct signs and exponents. 3. For a known factor, set P(a)=0 and solve the resulting equation for an unknown coefficient. 4. For the source example, compute f(2)=64−8u and obtain u=8. 5. Substitute the answer back and check f(2)=0. 6. For a nonzero evaluation, report the nonzero remainder and explain why the divisor is not an exact factor.
translations.commonMistakes: For divisor x+3 the tested input is −3, not +3. A zero of a polynomial is a number a, while its factor is the expression x−a. Do not infer that P(a)=0 proves a factor without maintaining the polynomial setting. If the remainder is nonzero, division still produces a quotient and remainder; the divisor is simply not an exact factor.
translations.quickSummary: The remainder from dividing \(P(x)\) by \(x-a\) is \(P(a)\). Thus \(x-a\) is a factor exactly when \(P(a)=0\). For \(x^4-ux^3+24x^2-32x+16\), factor x−2 requires \(u=8\).

translations.title: Minimizing Surface Area
translations.explanation: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials with a denominator that cannot be zero. Explore this type of function by designing closed cylindrical cans with a fixed volume but different radii and heights. A larger radius means a shorter cylinder, but it also changes the areas of the top and bottom. Combine the formulas for cylinder volume and surface area to find a single function of radius, then use the physically valid domain to estimate the least material needed.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a closed cylinder with radius r, height h, and fixed volume \(V=452\) cubic centimeters, \(V=\pi r^2h\) gives \(h=452/(\pi r^2)\) for \(r>0\). Total exterior area is \(S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\), so \(S(r)=2\pi r^2+904/r\) square centimeters. The domain is \(r>0\), since radius zero would make the formula undefined and negative radius is physically impossible. The formula has a polynomial part plus a rational term; as r becomes very small or very large, required area grows.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: With r=2 cm and volume 452 cubic centimeters, \(h=452/(4\pi)=113/\pi\approx35.97\) cm, and \(S(2)=8\pi+452\approx477.13\) square centimeters. With r=4 cm, \(h=452/(16\pi)\approx8.99\) cm, and \(S(4)=32\pi+226\approx326.53\) square centimeters. Example 2: A graph of \(S(r)=2\pi r^2+904/r\) for positive radii has a minimum near r=4.16 cm. Original Edulytiks calculus extension: \(S'(r)=4\pi r-904/r^2=0\) implies \(r^3=226/\pi\), so \(r\approx4.159\), \(h=2r\approx8.318\), and minimum area is approximately 326.04 square centimeters. This analytic optimization is supplemental to the source's table-and-graph task.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Start with the fixed-volume equation \(\pi r^2h=452\). 2. Solve for height h, retaining r>0. 3. Substitute h into the closed-cylinder area \(2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\). 4. Simplify to \(S(r)=2\pi r^2+904/r\). 5. Evaluate several positive radii, such as 2, 4 and 5 cm, and graph the positive-domain curve. 6. Identify the lowest plausible surface area, report radius and corresponding height, and check that their volume remains 452 cubic centimeters.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not use only lateral area 2πrh: a closed can also has two circular ends. A fixed volume does not mean the height stays fixed as radius changes. Domain r=0 is excluded; cancellation or limiting interpretation cannot make a radius-zero can real. Surface area is in cm², volume in cm³. A manufacturer may prefer other dimensions for strength, packaging or usability even if they use more material.
translations.quickSummary: For fixed closed-cylinder volume 452 cm³, \(h=452/(\pi r^2)\) and \(S(r)=2\pi r^2+904/r\), with \(r>0\). The minimum is near radius 4.16 cm and height 8.32 cm, using about 326.04 cm² of material.

translations.title: Graphs of Rational Functions (Part 1)
translations.explanation: A rational function is a ratio of polynomial expressions with a denominator that must not equal zero. This lesson focuses on how a vertical asymptote arises when the function becomes unbounded near an excluded denominator zero. For a 10-mile ride, t(r)=10/r gives the number of hours needed at speed r miles per hour, so the physical domain is r>0. As r approaches 0 from the positive side, t(r) increases without bound; r=0 is not an allowable speed and the vertical line r=0 is an asymptote. Sketch the decreasing first-quadrant curve using a labeled rate axis and a time axis.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For f(x)=N(x)/D(x), exclude D(x)=0 from the domain. An uncanceled denominator root can produce a vertical asymptote when outputs become unbounded; cancellation can instead give a removable hole. For t(r)=10/r on r>0, t(8)=1.25 hours, the vertical asymptote is r=0, and t(r) decreases as r increases. The curve stays in the first quadrant because both speed and travel time are positive. For (x−2)/(x+1), x=−1 is the vertical asymptote, x=2 is the zero, and y=1 is the horizontal asymptote. Use sample values from each interval around excluded inputs when sketching.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 (ten-mile ride): t(r)=10/r. At 8 mph, t(8)=10/8=1.25 hours=75 minutes. At 20 mph, t(20)=0.5 hours. To finish in 45 minutes (0.75 hours), solve 10/r=0.75, so r=40/3≈13.33 mph. For a sketch, plot (r,t)=(5,2), (10,1), (20,0.5), then draw a decreasing curve approaching r=0 but never touching it. Example 2 (algebraic graph): f(x)=(x−2)/(x+1). The graph has x-intercept x=2 because the numerator vanishes there, a vertical asymptote at x=−1 because the denominator vanishes without cancellation, and horizontal asymptote y=1 because the leading coefficients have ratio 1. A few points: f(0)=−2, f(1)=−1/2, f(−2)=4. These points locate branches on either side of x=−1.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the numerator, denominator, input units, and excluded denominator zeros. 2. Check whether numerator and denominator share a factor: a canceled factor gives a hole, not necessarily an asymptote. 3. For an uncanceled pole, examine values approaching it from the left and right to see which way each branch grows. 4. Find intercepts by setting the numerator to zero (and respecting excluded inputs). 5. Compute several points across every domain interval, noting signs and rates of change. 6. Sketch continuous branches only where the function is defined; label asymptotes as dashed lines and state physical-domain restrictions when present.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not plot a value at a zero denominator or mark every excluded input as an asymptote: if factors cancel the result may be a removable hole. Do not put zero speed in the ten-mile travel-time graph. Do not connect branches across a vertical asymptote. Do not confuse 10/r with 10r; faster speed means less time for fixed distance.
translations.quickSummary: Determine excluded denominator zeros, asymptotes, intercepts and representative points. Sketch branches on permitted intervals. For t(r)=10/r with r>0, the curve decreases in the first quadrant and approaches r=0 without touching it.
