translations.title: Understanding Rational Inputs
translations.explanation: Exponential function inputs need not be whole numbers. A half-decade represents five years, and a fractional exponent represents the amount of growth occurring over that fraction of the time unit. Use the known growth factor for a full interval to infer the factor for half or another fractional interval. The resulting output can be exact as a radical or approximate as a decimal; always give the units and the calendar date represented by the input.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(P(d)=P_0b^d\) and d counts DECADES, then d=1/2 means five years and \(b^{1/2}=\sqrt b\) is the half-decade factor. For Florida's estimated 1840 population of 54,500 and 60% modeled growth per decade, \(P(d)=54500(1.6)^d\). Thus \(P(1/2)=54500\sqrt{1.6}\) in 1845, and \(P(2)=54500(1.6)^2\) in 1860. A constant positive factor applies to every equal-length interval in an exponential function.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The equation \(x^2=5\) has two real values ±√5; among positive exponential outputs, \(5^{1/2}=\sqrt5\) is the single positive value. The equation \(p^3=10\) has unique real value \(\sqrt[3]{10}=10^{1/3}\). Example 2: With \(P(d)=54500(1.6)^d\), the 1850 population estimate is \(P(1)=87200\), while 1860 is \(P(2)=139520\). For 1845 use d=1/2: \(54500\sqrt{1.6}\approx68,938\). Moving a half-decade forward multiplies by √1.6 rather than by 1.6 or adding half the 60% growth percentage.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the time variable's unit: a decade is 10 years. 2. Convert the requested date to elapsed decades since 1840. 3. Write \(P(d)=54500(1.6)^d\) using the 60% growth factor. 4. At d=1/2, rewrite \(1.6^{1/2}\) as \(\sqrt{1.6}\). 5. Multiply to obtain an approximate population and label people as the unit. 6. Verify the half-decade estimate is between the starting and full-decade values and explain the constant-growth assumption.
translations.commonMistakes: A 60% decadal increase means factor 1.6, not 0.6. Five years is one half of a decade, so the factor is (sqrt{1.6}), not 1.3 unless explicitly using a different linear approximation. Population models are approximations; fractional inputs interpolate under an exponential assumption, not measurements taken every instant.
translations.quickSummary: For \(P(d)=54500(1.6)^d\) with d in decades since 1840, 1845 corresponds to d=1/2 and estimated population \(54500\sqrt{1.6}\), while 1860 gives 139,520.

translations.title: Representing Functions at Rational Inputs
translations.explanation: Convert an exponential rule written for one time unit into an equivalent rule for a different time unit. A population growing 50% per decade does not grow 50% each year: the annual factor must compound over ten years to produce the decadal factor. Fractional exponents provide the exact conversion. Compare the models at a decade, a year, and an intermediate date to verify the same predicted amount.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(f(d)=A b^d\) with d measured in decades since a start date, then in years t with d=t/10, the same model is \(g(t)=A b^{t/10}=A(b^{1/10})^t\). The yearly growth factor is \(b^{1/10}\). For \(b=1.5\), the yearly factor is \(1.5^{1/10}\approx1.04138\), or about 4.138% annual increase, NOT 5%. For Nigeria's example, an estimated 95.3 million in 1990 and 122.4 million in 2000 imply decade factor \(122.4/95.3\), and under a constant exponential model the 1995 amount is the geometric mean \(\sqrt{95.3\cdot122.4}\) million.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(f(d)=5000(1.5)^d\) represents a city population d decades after 5,000 people. The same rule in t years is \(g(t)=5000(1.5^{1/10})^t\). At t=5, \(g(5)=5000\sqrt{1.5}\approx6123.72\), and at t=10 it equals 7,500, matching f(1). Example 2: For Nigeria's modeled population, the decade factor is \(122.4/95.3\approx1.28437\). The annual factor is \((122.4/95.3)^{1/10}\), about 1.0253. The midpoint 1995 estimate is \(95.3(122.4/95.3)^{1/2}=\sqrt{95.3\cdot122.4}\approx108.00\) million.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Name the original time unit and new time unit. 2. Convert years t to decades d=t/10. 3. Replace d in the original \(A b^d\), obtaining \(A b^{t/10}\). 4. Use the exponent identity \(b^{t/10}=(b^{1/10})^t\). 5. Calculate the yearly growth factor and annual percent as 100(factor−1)%. 6. Verify equivalence by evaluating both models at 10 years, and optionally at five years using a square root.
translations.commonMistakes: Divide the EXPONENT time count by ten, not the base itself. A 50% growth over ten years does not mean exactly 5% compounded growth each year. The midpoint of exponential growth is a geometric mean, not an arithmetic mean. A population value stated in millions must remain in millions unless explicitly converted to people.
translations.quickSummary: Changing decades to years transforms \(A b^d\) into \(A(b^{1/10})^t\). A 50%-per-decade model has annual factor \(1.5^{1/10}\approx1.04138\), and five years correspond to multiplication by \(\sqrt{1.5}\).

translations.title: Changes Over Rational Intervals
translations.explanation: Exponential functions multiply by the same factor over any two equal-length intervals, even when the interval is fractional. For \(h(x)=4^x\), a one-unit increase multiplies the output by 4, while a half-unit increase multiplies by \(\sqrt4=2\). The same reasoning applies to a machine's depreciating value at six-month intervals, provided the annual depreciation rate remains constant.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(t)=Ab^t\), the ratio \(f(t+\Delta)/f(t)=b^\Delta\) is independent of starting time t, when A,b>0. Thus a half-year multiplier is \(b^{1/2}\), a one-third-year multiplier \(b^{1/3}\), and a two-year multiplier \(b^2\). For machine value \(V(t)=16000(0.85)^t\), with t in years since purchase, each year retains 85% of value, and each half-year retains \(\sqrt{0.85}\) of the prior value. This is a deterministic value model; a real machine's resale market need not follow it exactly.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(h(x)=4^x\) satisfies \(h(x+1)=4h(x)\), \(h(x+2)=16h(x)\), and \(h(x+0.5)=2h(x)\) for every real x. Example 2: The machine starts at $16,000 and after a year is worth $13,600, so annual factor is \(13600/16000=0.85\). Its year-2 value is \(16000(0.85)^2=$11560\); its year-3 value is $9826. At half a year, \(V(0.5)=16000\sqrt{0.85}\approx$14,751.27\), while \(V(1.5)=13600\sqrt{0.85}\approx$12,538.58\). Each six-month interval applies the same multiplier.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Name the annual factor b using consecutive one-year values: b=13,600/16,000=0.85. 2. Set the full exponential equation \(V(t)=16000(0.85)^t\). 3. Translate six months to \(\Delta=0.5\) years. 4. Use \(V(t+0.5)=V(t)\sqrt{0.85}\). 5. Evaluate both \(V(0.5)\) and \(V(1.5)\), checking that their ratios to the preceding whole-year values equal the same factor. 6. Include dollar units and the constant-depreciation assumption.
translations.commonMistakes: An 85% retention factor means 15% depreciation, not 85% depreciation. Half-year retention is √0.85, not 0.85/2. Equal fractional intervals have equal multiplicative ratios, but not equal dollar losses as the base value changes. Do not confuse the time-step interval with the exponent at the observation date.
translations.quickSummary: For \(f(t)=Ab^t\), every interval of length \(\Delta\) changes the output by factor \(b^\Delta\). Machine value \(16000(0.85)^t\) changes by \(\sqrt{0.85}\) every half year.

translations.title: Writing Equations for Exponential Functions
translations.explanation: Find the defining equation of an exponential function when the useful information comes as two input-output pairs instead of consecutive table rows. Decide what values you must request from an information-gap data card, then explain how their input spacing determines the growth factor. The key is that \(y=ab^x\) multiplies by \(b^{x_2-x_1}\) between input x1 and input x2, so a ratio of outputs alone is not always the ONE-step factor.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(x)=ab^x\), positive a,b, two exact points \((x_1,y_1)\), \((x_2,y_2)\) with \(x_1\ne x_2\) and positive outputs determine \(b=(y_2/y_1)^{1/(x_2-x_1)}\), then \(a=y_1/b^{x_1}\). Ask for the two input coordinates and outputs, not just the difference in y-values. A constant base greater than 1 indicates growth, while 0<b<1 indicates decay. A student explanation and information request may need a reasoning rubric rather than automatically graded free-text.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Suppose a data card reveals \(f(1)=6\) and \(f(3)=24\) for a positive exponential model. Their input gap is two, so \(24/6=4=b^2\), yielding b=2 and a=6/2=3. The equation is \(f(x)=3(2)^x\); verify f(1)=6 and f(3)=24. Example 2: \(64^{1/3}=4\), \((8^2)^{1/3}=4\), \((2^3)^{2/3}=4\), and \(8^{2/3}=4\), despite distinct notations. If two values are separated by one half step and their ratio is 3, the full-step factor is 9 because \(b^{1/2}=3\).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Ask what two input positions and outputs are known. 2. Calculate the input separation \(\Delta x\). 3. Divide the later output by the earlier to find the factor over that separation. 4. Solve \(b^{\Delta x}=y_2/y_1\), respecting b>0. 5. Substitute one point to recover a. 6. Check both original points using the new equation and explain what information was essential.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not use the ratio 24/6=4 as a one-step factor when inputs differ by TWO; the one-step factor is 2. Do not confuse initial value a with the output at x=1 unless x=0 is given. If either output is nonpositive, a positive exponential (ab^x) may not fit the data. A pair of points does not determine a unique general function without the exponential-family assumption.
translations.quickSummary: Two points determine a positive exponential model by their output ratio and input difference. If f(1)=6 and f(3)=24, then \(b^2=4\), \(b=2\), \(a=3\), so \(f(x)=3\cdot2^x\).

translations.title: Interpreting and Using Exponential Functions
translations.explanation: Radioactive decay follows an exponential model when a fixed fraction of an isotope remains after each half-life. Interpret half-life as the time required for a starting quantity to drop to half, not the time needed for it to disappear entirely. Use the carbon-14 half-life of 5,730 years to estimate the age of a sample or amount remaining at fractional numbers of half-lives; explain how the evidence supports or challenges an antiquity claim.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If mass M0 decays with half-life H, the remaining mass after t years is \(M(t)=M_0(1/2)^{t/H}\), for t≥0. The factor over a shorter interval \(\Delta t\) is \((1/2)^{\Delta t/H}\). Carbon-14 half-life H=5730 years means 25% remains after 11460 years (two half-lives). The model estimates an isotope fraction assuming an appropriate initial concentration and closed system; contamination, altered starting conditions and measurement uncertainty may affect conclusions about real artifacts.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A fossil begins with 3 picograms of carbon-14. After 5730 years it retains 1.5 picograms; after 11460 years it retains 0.75. After 1910 years, exactly one third of a half-life, it retains \(3(1/2)^{1/3}\approx2.381\) picograms. Example 2: A microbe colony doubles every six hours, so its one-hour factor is \(2^{1/6}\), because six consecutive applications multiply to 2. A bacteria population halving every four hours has one-hour factor \((1/2)^{1/4}\). An alleged 2500-year-old papyrus retaining 85% of its initial carbon-14 is inconsistent with the simple closed-system model, which predicts about 74% at that age; this discrepancy alone does not establish the entire artifact's history.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify starting isotope quantity and its half-life. 2. Express elapsed time as number of half-lives t/H. 3. Use \(M=M_0(1/2)^{t/H}\) with consistent years. 4. For 1910 years, t/H=1/3 and compute \(3(1/2)^{1/3}\). 5. For two half-lives, multiply by (1/2) twice to obtain one quarter of the starting mass. 6. For an artifact claim, compare modeled remaining fraction with observed fraction and discuss assumptions and uncertainty.
translations.commonMistakes: Half-life does not mean an element vanishes after one interval; half always remains. Carbon-14 decay is not a fixed subtraction of picograms each year. Before interpreting a lab fraction, specify the baseline initial amount and units. A difference between modeled and observed fractions calls for investigation, not automatic proof of fraud.
translations.quickSummary: For half-life H, \(M(t)=M_0(1/2)^{t/H}\). Carbon-14 with H=5730 years retains 25% after 11460 years; a 3-picogram sample retains about 2.381 picograms after 1910 years.

translations.title: Unknown Exponents
translations.explanation: When the variable is in an exponent, ordinary linear equation operations cannot simply isolate it. Start by reasoning with known powers, drawing a table or estimating graph intersections. In a repeated subdivision, the number of smallest pieces multiplies by four each step, so solving for a step means finding the exponent on 4. Exponential change in continuous time may require a noninteger exponent, motivating the logarithms developed next.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A repeated four-way subdivision beginning with one trapezoid at step 0 produces \(N(n)=4^n\) smallest pieces after integer n≥0 steps. A value \(4^n=262144\) can be solved by recognizing \(262144=2^{18}=4^9\), so n=9. For general b>0 with b≠1, an equation \(b^x=c\) with c>0 has one real solution, which can be estimated from a graph or later written as a logarithm. Be careful that the task's step count is discrete, while many population or cooling models have continuous inputs.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: In a trapezoid subdivided into four similar trapezoids at each step, step 4 contains \(4^4=256\) smallest shapes; step 10 contains \(4^{10}=1,048,576\). To locate 262,144 shapes, note \(4^8=65536\) and \(4^9=262144\), so step 9. Example 2: Solve \(3^x=20\) approximately. Since \(3^2=9\) and \(3^3=27\), the unique real x lies between 2 and 3. Numerical graph refinement gives \(x\approx2.727\); this is an approximation of the exponent, not a claim x must be whole. Example 3: \(\sqrt{3x}=12\) instead can be solved algebraically as 3x=144, x=48, illustrating a different kind of unknown.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Decide whether the variable is the BASE, the EXPONENT or an argument inside a root. 2. For a subdivision count, define the starting step and growth factor \(N(n)=4^n\). 3. Compare the target with a table of integer powers of four. 4. Identify \(4^9=262144\), then substitute to check. 5. For a target that does not equal a known power, use bracketing or a graph to estimate the exponent. 6. Distinguish whole-step construction counts from continuous-time exponential models.
translations.commonMistakes: The equation 4^n=262144 requires solving for an exponent, not dividing 262144 by 4 once. The sequence starts with one object at n=0, so step n has 4^n pieces. A noninteger exponent can make sense for a continuous exponential model but not for the count of complete subdivision steps. Do not assume every unknown exponent is an integer.
translations.quickSummary: Unknown exponents can be found from known powers or graph estimates. A four-way subdivision has \(4^n\) pieces at step n; 262144 pieces occur at step 9.

translations.title: What is a Logarithm?
translations.explanation: A logarithm expresses the exponent needed to reach a positive quantity using a chosen exponential base. In the base-ten log table, the outputs 1, 2 and 3 occur at inputs 10, 100 and 1000 because \(10^1=10\), \(10^2=100\), \(10^3=1000\). Nonpower values such as 50 need an exponent between 1 and 2, which a table or calculator can estimate. The logarithm notation gives an exact name for that exponent even when its decimal form is approximate.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(b>0,\ b\ne1,\ x>0\), \(\log_b x\) is the unique real number y satisfying \(b^y=x\). In this introduction b=10. Therefore \(\log_{10}1000=3\), \(\log_{10}1=0\), \(\log_{10}0.1=-1\), and \(\log_{10}50\approx1.69897\). The argument of a real logarithm must be positive; \(\log_{10}0\) and \(\log_{10}(-2)\) are undefined as real numbers. A decimal displayed to four digits such as 1.6990 is an approximation, not an exact exponent.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(10^w=1000\) gives \(w=3=\log_{10}1000\). Since \(10^1=10\) and \(10^2=100\), the solution to \(10^y=50\) is between 1 and 2, named exactly \(y=\log_{10}50\) and estimated as 1.699. Example 2: The table gives \(\log_{10}9\approx0.9542\), so \(10^{0.9542}\approx9\). It gives \(\log_{10}90\approx1.9542\); multiplying the argument by ten adds 1 to the exponent because \(90=9\cdot10\), but this pattern must be explained with exponent rules.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the exponential base, here 10, and the positive target value. 2. Read \(10^y=x\) as the equation to solve for y. 3. Rewrite it as \(y=\log_{10}x\). 4. For familiar powers compute exactly; e.g. \(10^3=1000\). 5. For other targets bracket the exponent between nearby known powers. 6. Test a decimal estimate by substituting it into the original exponential equation, with approximate-equality notation.
translations.commonMistakes: The logarithm is an exponent, not division by 10. (log_{10}50) is NOT 5, and 1.699 is approximate rather than an exact rational value. The argument x must be positive for a real logarithm. Do not mix a base-ten table with a base-two or natural-log table unless the base changes explicitly.
translations.quickSummary: A base-ten logarithm answers an exponent question: \(\log_{10}x=y\) means \(10^y=x\). Thus \(\log_{10}1000=3\), and \(\log_{10}50\approx1.699\).

translations.title: Interpreting and Writing Logarithmic Equations
translations.explanation: Logarithms work in any valid base, not only 10. Translate the statement "the logarithm base b of x equals y" into the equivalent exponential equation \(b^y=x\), then use a base-two table or familiar powers to evaluate. The base and argument play different roles; writing an exponential equation in logarithmic form does not change its solution.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For base \(b>0,\ b\ne1\) and argument \(x>0\), \(\log_b x=y\iff b^y=x\). In base 2, \(\log_2 1=0\), \(\log_2 8=3\), \(\log_2 16=4\), \(\log_2 32=5\). For a nonpower, \(\log_2 15\) lies between 3 and 4, approximately 3.907. With base 5, \(\log_5 25=2\) because \(5^2=25\). For \(2^y=70\), the exact solution is \(y=\log_2 70\), larger than 6 since \(2^6=64\).
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Translate \(\log_{10}(100000000)=8\) into \(10^8=100000000\). Likewise \(\log_2 16=4\) means \(2^4=16\), and \(\log_5 25=2\) means \(5^2=25\). Example 2: Using a base-two table, \(\log_2 15\approx3.9069\) and \(\log_2 40\approx5.3219\). To solve \(2^y=5\), write \(y=\log_2 5\approx2.3219\). It is correct to leave the value in logarithmic notation when the table's decimal is only an estimate.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Locate the base written after log and the positive argument inside it. 2. Define y as the desired exponent. 3. Translate \(\log_b x=y\) into \(b^y=x\) or reverse. 4. Evaluate exact powers before using decimal estimates. 5. For an unknown exponent, name it exactly as a logarithm, e.g. \(\log_2 5\). 6. Verify by raising the base to the estimated exponent and comparing with the target.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not interpret (log_2 16) as 16 divided by 2; it equals 4. In (log_5 25), the base is 5, not 25. The table's decimal 3.9069 for log₂15 is approximate. Negative or zero real arguments are not allowed, and a logarithmic equation with base 1 is not a valid logarithm.
translations.quickSummary: Equivalent logarithmic and exponential equations contain the same relationship: \(\log_b x=y\iff b^y=x\). For example \(\log_2 16=4\) and \(2^4=16\).

translations.title: Evaluating Logarithmic Expressions
translations.explanation: Evaluate logarithms both mentally and with technology, and justify which of two logarithmic values is larger. Powers of ten make some common logarithms exact, while other positive arguments give approximate decimal outputs. A log in base greater than one increases with its positive argument, so comparing two logs with the same base often requires comparing only their arguments. Keep the base visible when using calculators.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For the common logarithm \(\log x=\log_{10}x\), \(\log10=1\), \(\log10000=4\), \(\log0.1=-1\), \(\log(1/1000)=-3\). For b>1, \(\log_b x\) increases as x increases. For \(0<b<1\), it decreases instead, so the direction of comparisons reverses. A calculator's \(\log\) usually means base 10 and \(\ln\) means base e. If only a different base is offered, the change-of-base identity is \(\log_b x=\ln x/\ln b\), provided the inputs are valid; this is a calculator extension, not a requirement to memorize a new logarithm law in this lesson.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Evaluate \(\log10=1\), \(\log10000=4\), \(\log0.1=-1\), and \(\log0.001=-3\), since the respective powers are 10¹, 10⁴, 10⁻¹, and 10⁻³. Example 2: \(\log_2 10\approx3.32193\), because \(2^{3.32193}\approx10\). The estimate \(3+1/3\) is close but not exact: \(2^{10/3}=8\sqrt[3]2\approx10.079\), which exceeds 10. Example 3: \(\log_2 40>\log_2 15\) because 40>15 and base 2>1; a calculator confirms values about 5.322 and 3.907.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify whether the logarithm is common, natural, or another base. 2. Evaluate known powers exactly, especially positive and negative integer powers of ten. 3. For an unfamiliar argument, estimate between nearby powers. 4. Use a calculator to refine the approximation if allowed. 5. When comparing logs of the SAME base greater than one, compare positive arguments directly. 6. Verify the chosen exponent by computing the corresponding exponential and explain rounding.
translations.commonMistakes: A negative logarithm can be perfectly valid: log10(0.1)=−1. A negative argument is not valid for real logarithms. A decimal calculator value is typically an approximation. Do not compare logarithms with different bases by their arguments alone, and remember a base between zero and one reverses monotonicity.
translations.quickSummary: Logarithms name exponents: \(\log10=1\), \(\log0.1=-1\), and \(\log_2 10\approx3.322\). For the same base above one, larger positive inputs produce larger log values.

translations.title: The Number $e$
translations.explanation: The number \(e\) is a positive mathematical constant of approximately 2.71828. It can be used as a base of an exponential function just as 2 or 10 can, and it appears naturally in many models. Explore its value through graphing and the expression \((1+1/n)^n\) for increasingly large positive n. In this introductory lesson, the goal is to recognize and interpret the constant e, not to construct an entirely new theory of continuous growth.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Euler's number \(e\approx2.718281828\) is irrational and positive. Its natural logarithm satisfies \(\ln e=1\), and \(e^0=1\). For large positive integers n, \((1+1/n)^n\) approaches e, although finite values are not exactly e. For example n=1 gives 2, n=2 gives 2.25, and n=10 gives about 2.59374. If \(f(t)=400(0.5)^{0.1t}\), the 0.5 factor applies over ten time units; likewise \(400(2)^{0.1t}\) doubles over ten units. The value of e is not exactly 2.7 or 2.718.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — limit pattern: \(n=1\) gives \((1+1)^1=2\), n=2 gives \((1+1/2)^2=2.25\), n=10 gives \((1+1/10)^{10}\approx2.593742\), and n=100 gives \((1.01)^{100}\approx2.704814\). These values grow toward about 2.718, but none equals e exactly. Example 2 — interpreting models: A population of 400 doubling every 10 hours can be modeled by \(P(t)=400(2)^{t/10}\), while a medicine amount of 400 mg decreasing 25% every ten hours can be modeled by \(M(t)=400(0.75)^{t/10}\). Replacing these bases with e would require an equivalent exponent coefficient; e is not a generic replacement for any growth factor without changing the exponent.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read e as a constant, not a variable or an engineering unit. 2. Evaluate \((1+1/n)^n\) for several positive n, recording the numeric outputs. 3. Compare their approach to 2.71828 rather than claiming they equal it. 4. Graph \(e^x\) at x=0 and x=1 to see outputs 1 and about 2.718. 5. Match a supplied exponential equation to its actual growth or retention factor and time interval. 6. Label base, exponent and units clearly while leaving deeper derivations for later work.
translations.commonMistakes: The constant e is not exactly 2.718: it has a nonterminating, nonrepeating decimal expansion. ((1+1/n)^n) approaches e as n increases but is not identical for finite n. The common logarithm uses base 10, whereas the natural logarithm uses base e. A model using factor 0.75 cannot use e as an unchanged base with the same exponent.
translations.quickSummary: Euler's number \(e\approx2.71828\) is a natural exponential base; \((1+1/n)^n\) approaches e for large positive n. Interpret e-based functions without confusing their base or units.

translations.title: Exponential Functions with Base $e$
translations.explanation: Exponential models written using base e are often presented as \(P e^{rt}\), where P is the starting amount and r is a continuous growth or decay rate. Compare this with \(P(1+r)^t\), which compounds by a fixed rate per whole period. For the same small positive r, the two curves are close but not identical. Use a calculator to evaluate e-powers correctly and interpret whether a negative r describes decay.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(t)=P e^{rt}\), P>0 and real r, \(f(0)=P\). Over an interval Δt, the multiplicative change is \(e^{r\Delta t}\); the effective one-period growth factor is \(e^r\), not exactly \(1+r\) except as a small-rate approximation. With r>0 the function increases, with r<0 it decreases, and with r=0 it is constant. For exponential expressions \(P(1+r)^t\), the corresponding per-period factor is 1+r when positive. Keep units consistent: if r is per year, t is measured in years.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: \(10e^{1.1}\approx30.04166\); \(5e^{(1.1)(7)}\approx11041.74\). Enter exponent parentheses as intended because \(5e^{1.1\cdot7}\) differs from \((5e^{1.1})\cdot7\). Example 2: For \(f(t)=400e^{-0.1t}\), at t=0 there are 400 units and after 5 time units \(f(5)=400e^{-0.5}\approx242.61\). Compare positive-rate models \(100e^{0.05t}\) and \(100(1.05)^t\); after one year the first is about 105.127 and the second exactly 105, so using the same rate number does not make the formulas equal.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify initial amount P, rate coefficient r and time unit. 2. Evaluate the exponent rt before applying the e-power function on a calculator. 3. Multiply the resulting factor by P. 4. For a negative rate, check the output is below its initial amount when t>0. 5. Compare \(e^r\) and \(1+r\) to explain why continuous and per-period models differ. 6. State the modeled quantity and assumptions without treating a smooth curve as a guaranteed forecast.
translations.commonMistakes: The letter e is a number, not a variable or "times ten." Parentheses matter: (e^{(1.1)(7)}) is not (e^{1.1}cdot7). A negative rate makes the exponential factor positive but less than one, not a negative population. Continuous 5% growth does not mean exactly the same as compounding 5% once per year.
translations.quickSummary: The model \(P e^{rt}\) starts at P and multiplies by \(e^{r\Delta t}\) over time interval Δt. A negative r represents decay; \(e^{0.05}\) is close to but not exactly 1.05.

translations.title: Solving Exponential Equations
translations.explanation: A natural logarithm undoes exponentiation with base e. Once a positive exponential expression has been isolated, apply \(\ln\) to solve for the exponent, then isolate the unknown variable by ordinary algebra. Use the exact logarithmic expression until a context calls for a rounded approximation. This lesson extends earlier base-ten and base-two logarithms to equations using e.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For x>0, \(\ln x=\log_e x\) is the real exponent y such that \(e^y=x\). Therefore \(\ln(e^y)=y\), \(\ln1=0\), and \(e^{\ln x}=x\) when x>0. To solve \(P e^{kt}=Q\) with P,Q>0 and k≠0, divide by P and take natural logs: \(t=\ln(Q/P)/k\). A real logarithm cannot be applied to a zero or negative argument. When the variable also occurs outside the exponent, this simple isolation method may not apply directly.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — check a proposed solution: \(5e^{3a}=90\) gives \(e^{3a}=18\), \(3a=\ln18\), and \(a=\ln18/3\approx0.96346\). Substituting \(e^{3a}=18\) confirms the original product 90. Example 2: \(2e^{0.4t}=100\) gives \(e^{0.4t}=50\), so \(t=\ln50/0.4\approx9.7801\) time units. The answer is positive because the target value exceeds the initial value for a positive rate. Example 3: \(\ln(e^5)=5\), whereas \(e^{\ln5}=5\).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the exponential term containing the unknown. 2. Divide away any positive constant multiplier to isolate \(e^{kt}\). 3. Check that the isolated right-hand side is positive. 4. Apply natural logarithms to both sides. 5. Simplify \(\ln(e^{kt})=kt\), then divide by k when k≠0. 6. Substitute the exact result or a sufficiently precise approximation into the original exponential equation.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not take the natural log of a negative isolated value and claim a real solution. (ln x) is not a log with base ten; its base is e. The equation (e^{3a}=18) has (a=ln18/3), not (ln(18/3)). Do not round early enough to undermine substitution accuracy.
translations.quickSummary: Natural logarithms solve unknown e-exponents. For \(5e^{3a}=90\), the exact answer is \(a=\ln18/3\) and the approximation is 0.96346.

translations.title: Using Graphs and Logarithms to Solve Problems (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Graphs and logarithms provide two ways to determine when an exponential amount reaches a target. A graph shows the horizontal input coordinate where a curve meets the target line, while the logarithm yields a precise equation for that coordinate. In continuous growth models, the natural log is especially convenient because it inverts base e. Interpret the answer with time and quantity units, and distinguish an exact crossing time from an approximate graph reading.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(t)=A e^{rt}\) with A>0 and r≠0, to reach a positive target K solve \(A e^{rt}=K\), hence \(t=\ln(K/A)/r\). If r>0, targets K>A occur at positive t, while targets K<A occur at negative t in the mathematical extension. A graph of f and the horizontal line y=K intersects at the same t. A population can be modeled by this equation for t≥0 only if the context permits the corresponding elapsed time. Always check graph axes and scales.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For \(f(t)=e^t\), \(f(3)=e^3\approx20.09\), \(f(4)=e^4\approx54.60\). The curve reaches 30 between t=3 and 4; solving \(e^t=30\) gives \(t=\ln30\approx3.401\). Example 2: A modeled colony starts with 100 bacteria and grows as \(P(t)=100e^{0.03t}\), t in hours. To reach 200 bacteria, \(e^{0.03t}=2\) and \(t=\ln2/0.03\approx23.105\) hours. On a graph, the crossing of P and y=200 should appear near 23.1 hours.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define the exponential model and positive target. 2. Graph the function on a domain containing the target crossing and draw the horizontal target line. 3. Estimate t from the graph to check scale. 4. Algebraically divide by A to isolate the exponential. 5. Apply \(\ln\) and solve \(t=\ln(K/A)/r\). 6. Substitute to verify the target and report the time in correct units.
translations.commonMistakes: Reading the y-coordinate 200 from a graph does not answer WHEN the value reaches 200; the required answer is the x-coordinate t. Natural log should be taken only of a positive ratio. A negative t in an elapsed-time scenario may be outside the model's physical domain even if the algebra has a solution. Do not confuse (ln30) with (log_{10}30).
translations.quickSummary: Graph intersections estimate the time a target is reached; natural logs solve it exactly. In \(P(t)=100e^{0.03t}\), doubling occurs at \(t=\ln2/0.03\approx23.105\) hours.

translations.title: Using Graphs and Logarithms to Solve Problems (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Compare exponential models by graphing them together and finding the time at which their outputs are equal. An intersection point \((t,y)\) means two quantities have the same value y at time t. In the original first-edition bacteria experiment, one population starts larger, but another grows at a faster rate. Use a graph for an estimate and a natural-log equation for a more precise intersection; interpret both coordinates in the experiment's units. Also check whether a mathematical crossing happens at a physically meaningful time.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For positive A,B and unequal real growth rates r,s, \(Ae^{rt}=Be^{st}\) implies \(t=\ln(A/B)/(s-r)\). Both exponential outputs stay positive. The source bacteria models are \(f(h)=24e^{0.4h}\) and \(g(h)=9e^{0.6h}\), measured in square millimeters after h hours. Equality gives \(e^{0.2h}=24/9=8/3\), so \(h=\ln(8/3)/0.2\approx4.9041\) hours. Another pair \(16e^{0.02t}\) and \(17.5e^{0.025t}\) has no crossing for \(t\ge0\), because the second starts larger and grows faster.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — experiment crossing: Set \(24e^{0.4h}=9e^{0.6h}\). Divide by \(9e^{0.4h}\) to obtain \(8/3=e^{0.2h}\); taking logs gives \(h=\ln(8/3)/0.2\approx4.9041\). Substitute in either model to get an occupied area of approximately 170.6 square millimeters. A graph's crossing near (4.9,171) is consistent with this result.

Example 2 — an impossible future crossing: Country C and Country D have models \(C(t)=16e^{0.02t}\) and \(D(t)=17.5e^{0.025t}\) million people, t years since 1980. At t=0, D is already greater, and \(D/C=(17.5/16)e^{0.005t}>1\) for all \(t\ge0\). Although extending the mathematical functions backwards creates a negative-time crossing, they never meet after 1980. Country C reaches 30 million at \(t=\ln(30/16)/0.02\approx31.43\) years after 1980.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define the two exponential equations with consistent time and output units. 2. Estimate the crossing using a graph showing both curves on the same axes. 3. Set their outputs equal: \(24e^{0.4h}=9e^{0.6h}\). 4. Divide by a positive exponential expression and apply \(\ln\) to get \(h=\ln(8/3)/0.2\). 5. Substitute h into both formulas and compare results to find the common area. 6. Check h belongs to the elapsed-time domain, and explain why a pair starting with the larger and faster-growing quantity cannot cross for later times.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not confuse the intersection's x-coordinate (time) with its y-coordinate (occupied area). Solving f(h)=171 using a rounded area may give a slightly different time than solving f(h)=g(h) exactly. Do not conclude two curves must cross just because both grow: initial values and rates matter. If the equation's solution has negative elapsed time, it is not a future crossing.
translations.quickSummary: For two exponential populations, equality occurs where their graphs intersect. The bacteria models \(24e^{0.4h}\) and \(9e^{0.6h}\) meet after \(h=\ln(8/3)/0.2\approx4.90\) hours, at roughly 171 square millimeters.

translations.title: Logarithmic Functions
translations.explanation: A logarithmic function reverses the input and output roles of an exponential function. A colony starting with 1,000 bacteria and doubling every hour has population \(x=2^h\) in thousands after h hours. If the input is instead a target population x (in thousands), then the time needed is \(h=\log_2 x\). Graph population on the horizontal axis and elapsed time on the vertical axis to see why logarithmic graphs grow slowly, have positive input domains, and do not have a horizontal asymptote.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(b>1\), \(h(x)=\log_b x\) is the inverse of \(x=b^h\), with domain \(x>0\), all real output values, \(\log_b1=0\), and a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\). When x multiplies by b, h increases by 1. For base 2, \(\log_2(2x)=\log_2x+1\); for base 10, \(\log_{10}(10x)=\log_{10}x+1\), whenever x>0. In the bacteria context, use positive population sizes; negative elapsed times may correspond to the model's extrapolation before the observation rather than future growth.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — doubling bacteria: Starting at 1 thousand, the target 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 thousand corresponds to h=0,1,2,3 and 4 hours. A target of 50 thousand needs \(\log_2 50\approx5.644\) hours; 80 thousand needs \(\log_2 80\approx6.322\) hours. Doubling the target from 50 to 100 thousand adds exactly one hour in this idealized model.

Example 2 — tenfold growth: If a second species increases tenfold each day, the time to reach x thousand from 1 thousand is \(d(x)=\log_{10}x\). Reaching 50 thousand takes \(\log_{10}50\approx1.699\) days; reaching 20,000 thousand takes \(\log_{10}20000\approx4.301\) days. After five days the projected population is \(10^5=100000\) thousand bacteria, or 100 million bacteria. Explain that the model's growth assumptions may fail at large population sizes.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Start with an exponential population model using the correct initial value and time unit. 2. For doubling every hour, write \(x=2^h\) with x in thousands. 3. Solve for time by reversing the equation: \(h=\log_2x\). 4. Evaluate known powers exactly to create graph points such as (1,0), (2,1), (4,2), and (8,3). 5. Use a logarithm calculator or graph to estimate nonpower targets such as x=50. 6. Explain the positive input domain, the slowly increasing curve, and why multiplying population by the base adds one time unit.
translations.commonMistakes: A logarithmic function's input is the target population, not the elapsed time in this inverse model. A logarithm of zero or a negative real target is undefined. A logarithm grows slowly but is not bounded above and does NOT approach a horizontal asymptote. Do not confuse 20,000 thousand bacteria with 20,000 individual bacteria.
translations.quickSummary: The inverse of \(x=2^h\) is \(h=\log_2x\) for x>0. A doubling colony takes about 5.644 hours to reach 50 thousand and 6.322 hours to reach 80 thousand; a base-ten model reaches 50 thousand in about 1.699 days.

translations.title: Applications of Logarithmic Functions
translations.explanation: Apply logarithmic relationships to the original first-edition tables of acidity and seismograph displacement. A base-ten logarithm converts multiplication by ten into an additive change of one. For pH, larger hydrogen-ion concentration corresponds to LOWER pH, whereas larger seismograph displacement corresponds to a HIGHER earthquake rating in the simplified model. These contexts are an optional mathematical introduction; authentic chemistry and seismology use additional measurement details and assumptions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For the source's hydrogen-ion concentration \(H>0\), in moles per liter relative to its standard unit, \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}H\). Each tenfold INCREASE in H decreases the pH by 1. If pH is p, \(H=10^{-p}\). The first-edition seismograph table models a Richter-type rating with \(R(d)=7+\log_{10}d\), where d>0 is displacement in meters at the specified reference setup; every tenfold increase in d increases the rating by 1. This table-based relation should not be treated as a universal modern earthquake-magnitude formula.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — acidity: Water with \(H=10^{-7}\) has pH 7. In the source table, orange juice with \(H=10^{-3}\) has pH 3, while vinegar at pH 2.4 has \(H=10^{-2.4}\approx0.003981\) mol/L. A sample with \(H=5.6\times10^{-11}\) has \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}(5.6\times10^{-11})\approx10.252\). Apple at pH 3 has \(10^3\), or one thousand, times the model's hydrogen-ion concentration of milk at pH 6.

Example 2 — earthquake displacement: The source table assigns d=10⁻⁶ meters rating 1, and d=10⁻⁵ meters rating 2. From \(R(d)=7+\log_{10}d\), a displacement of 125 meters gives \(R(125)\approx9.097\). The calculation is a classroom application of the source's stated measuring assumptions, not independent confirmation of the earthquake's recorded magnitude.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the physical quantity, its positive input and unit. 2. For acidity use \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}H\) and check \(H=10^{-7}\) gives 7. 3. To reverse the pH model, compute \(H=10^{-\mathrm{pH}}\). 4. Compare concentrations by subtracting pH values and raising ten to the resulting magnitude difference. 5. For earthquake displacement use the stated classroom model \(R(d)=7+\log_{10}d\). 6. Check one row from each source table before estimating an unseen value, and describe the limits of these simplified applications.
translations.commonMistakes: A lower pH means higher hydrogen-ion concentration, not lower concentration. The log argument H or d must be positive. A difference of three pH units corresponds to a factor of 1000 in the hydrogen-ion concentration, not a factor of three. The source's rating relation depends on a specified displacement measurement context and should not be generalized to every real earthquake.
translations.quickSummary: In the first-edition classroom models, \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}H\) and \(R(d)=7+\log_{10}d\). A change of one unit corresponds to a factor of ten in the underlying positive quantity, but the direction is opposite for pH and earthquake ratings.

translations.title: Matching up to Data
translations.explanation: Data can suggest a function family without identifying one unique equation. Start with the scatterplot of a bottle of soda water cooling on a cold day. Examine whether each candidate has a plausible temperature at time zero, decreases in the observed range, and approaches the environmental temperature. Describe graph transformations informally, then justify whether a vertical or horizontal change produces a better fit. A good fit to the observed points and a reasonable long-term shape are different criteria.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A vertical translation \(f(x)+k\) moves every point's output up by k, whereas \(f(x-k)\) shifts the graph right by k (for a positive k). In the source cooling problem, \(f(h)=45+20/(h+0.5)\) and \(g(h)=45+33(0.5)^{h+0.5}\), with h hours since the bottle was set outdoors. Both approach 45°F as h grows. However at h=0, f gives 85°F while g gives approximately 68.33°F; evaluate against the data before choosing a candidate. Model selection also requires attention to domains, measured uncertainty and context, not just an attractive curve.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — comparing candidate models: At h=0, \(f(0)=45+20/0.5=85\) °F, whereas \(g(0)=45+33\sqrt{0.5}\approx68.33\) °F. At h=1, \(f(1)=45+20/1.5\approx58.33\) °F and \(g(1)=45+33(0.5)^{1.5}\approx56.67\) °F. A scatterplot beginning near 68°F favors g at the beginning, but examine several plotted points before declaring it the better overall model.

Example 2 — transformations without changing shape: The standard parabola \(p(x)=x^2\) has vertex (0,0); \(q(x)=(x-3)^2+2\) has vertex (3,2). Its graph results from moving p three units right and two units up, with the same parabolic shape. This second example is an original Edulytiks bridge to the upcoming formal function-notation lessons.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the axes, measured units and observed range of the scatterplot. 2. Evaluate both given cooling models at h=0 and at another observed hour. 3. Compare the predictions with the plotted temperatures and the horizontal long-term trend around 45°F. 4. Describe a possible adjustment to a poorly fitting model using horizontal or vertical movement. 5. For \(x^2\to(x-3)^2+2\), identify the shift of the vertex from (0,0) to (3,2). 6. Support the model choice with numerical and visual evidence, while noting that a graph of limited data cannot prove a unique physical law.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not assume every decreasing curve fits cooling data equally well. Graphs that share a long-run value of 45°F may differ substantially at the start. A shift left/right is an INPUT change while up/down is an OUTPUT change. A model's match depends on observed time and units; extrapolated temperatures should not be treated as certain measurements. Graph-description and argument tasks need a reasoning rubric, not one forced numeric response.
translations.quickSummary: Use measured points, initial values and long-run shape to compare candidate curves. The source cooling models have equal 45°F asymptotes but different initial predictions: 85°F and approximately 68.33°F. Graph transformations can improve fit while retaining the function family.

translations.title: Moving Functions
translations.explanation: Function notation states precisely how one graph is shifted horizontally or vertically. An outside addition changes outputs and moves the graph up or down, while replacing x with x−k changes the input needed for the same output and moves the graph right by k. Represent one translation at a time using equations, tables and graph points, then interpret a bakery's changing temperature schedule without confusing a time shift with a temperature shift.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For any function f with an appropriate domain, \(g(x)=f(x)+k\) is a vertical translation by k: each original point (x,y) moves to (x,y+k). For k>0, \(h(x)=f(x-k)\) is a horizontal translation RIGHT k: (x,y) moves to (x+k,y). Conversely \(f(x+k)\) moves left k. If \(f(x)=x^2(x-2)\), then \(f(x)-5=x^2(x-2)-5\), while \(f(x-4)=(x-4)^2(x-6)\). Transform domains alongside the graph, particularly when x represents elapsed time.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — polynomial translation: Let \(f(x)=x^2(x-2)\). The graph \(g(x)=f(x)-5\) is five units lower at every x; since \(f(0)=0\), \(g(0)=-5\). The graph \(h(x)=f(x-4)=(x-4)^2(x-6)\) is four units RIGHT. The original zeros 0 (double) and 2 move to 4 (double) and 6. Both changes preserve the same basic graph shape.

Example 2 — source table: A function has \(f(-3)=-5.8\), \(f(-0.7)=0\), and \(f(2)=0\). The graph labeled g is 4 units above f, so \(g(-3)=-1.8\), \(g(-0.7)=4\), and \(g(2)=4\). For \(h(x)=f(x)-2.5\), the corresponding outputs are −8.3, −2.5 and −2.5. The table confirms that the input values do NOT change in a vertical translation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Determine whether the change affects horizontal position or vertical output. 2. If every output rises by 4, write \(g(x)=f(x)+4\). 3. Substitute known outputs to verify transformed table values. 4. If each original graph point should move right by 4, replace x with x−4. 5. Expand \(f(x-4)\) only if useful; factored form shows shifted zeros more clearly. 6. Graph or tabulate original and transformed points to check the sign of the shift and maintain the contextual input domain.
translations.commonMistakes: Subtracting 4 INSIDE the function does not move a graph four units left; it moves it right. Do not confuse (f(x)-5) with (f(x-5)). A vertical shift changes y-values without changing input positions; a horizontal shift changes point positions and can shift a contextual time interval. A negative function output does not necessarily mean a negative physical temperature when using Fahrenheit.
translations.quickSummary: For \(k>0\), \(f(x)+k\) moves a graph up k, \(f(x-k)\) moves it right k, and \(f(x+k)\) moves it left k. In the source polynomial example \(x^2(x-2)\), replacing x by x−4 shifts its zeros to 4 and 6.

translations.title: More Movement
translations.explanation: Combine a horizontal shift and a vertical shift to represent new circumstances. The original bakery temperature graph shows ovens heating a kitchen according to a clock-time schedule; if baking begins two hours earlier, the entire temperature history happens earlier. The correct new equation uses a PLUS two inside the function, because the new temperature at time x equals what the old schedule showed two hours later. The thermostat change is a separate output shift.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a function H of clock time, \(G(x)=H(x+2)\) shifts its graph LEFT two hours. In contrast \(H(x-2)\) shifts it right two hours and would represent a LATER start. Combining a horizontal movement right a and a vertical movement up b gives \(F(x)=H(x-a)+b\). In the original bakery source, the graph F shows a schedule one hour later than H and temperatures five Fahrenheit degrees higher, so \(F(x)=H(x-1)+5\) when the same base schedule shape applies. If a source graph uses a restricted time interval, specify the shifted clock domain.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — earlier bakery hours: The original kitchen oven cycle begins at 5:00 a.m. and ends at 10:00 a.m. A shift two hours earlier moves those event times to 3:00 a.m. and 8:00 a.m. With old temperature function H, the new function is \(G(x)=H(x+2)\), since \(G(3)=H(5)\). The expression \(H(x-2)\) would instead move the cycle to 7:00 a.m. through noon.

Example 2 — thawing meat: An original source decay shape \(G(t)=-62(0.85)^t\) is below zero at t=0. Add a vertical constant to fit the observed thawing data. If \(M(0)\) is approximately 13.1°F, use \(M(t)=G(t)+75.1=75.1-62(0.85)^t\). This predicts \(M(0)=13.1\)°F and \(M(4.92)\approx47.2\)°F, close to the measured 45.8°F. A shifted curve can fit approximately without passing through every noisy observation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the time of a clearly marked event on the ORIGINAL graph. 2. Determine where it should occur after the schedule change. 3. For two hours earlier, substitute x+2 inside H and check \(G(3)=H(5)\). 4. Apply any thermostat increase as an OUTSIDE addition, such as H(x)+5. 5. For the source thawing data, solve \(G(0)+k=13.1\) to obtain k=75.1. 6. Check predictions at multiple times and explain that fitting data can involve approximation, not exact interpolation.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not think that "two hours earlier" requires x−2; (H(x-2)) delays the event. A thermostat increase of five degrees changes the output, not the clock-time input. Do not confuse a vertical data-fitting adjustment with an exponential decay factor. The source's measured meat temperatures vary, so a model need not pass through every point to be useful.
translations.quickSummary: An earlier schedule uses \(H(x+2)\), while a later schedule uses \(H(x-2)\). A simultaneous right shift a and upward shift b is \(H(x-a)+b\). A source thawing model can be improved by adding a constant vertical shift.

translations.title: Reflecting Functions
translations.explanation: Reflections turn a graph into a mirror image across a coordinate axis. Reflecting across the horizontal x-axis reverses the OUTPUT values but keeps each input; reflecting across the vertical y-axis reverses the INPUT values but keeps each output. Use a table of pairs to construct both reflections, and describe why they differ. This lesson introduces the transformations geometrically and through function notation, preparing for even/odd symmetry rather than prematurely assuming a function must be even or odd.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \((x,y)\) belongs to \(y=f(x)\), then \((x,-y)\) belongs to \(y=-f(x)\), the reflection in the x-axis. Meanwhile \((-x,y)\) belongs to \(y=f(-x)\), the reflection in the y-axis. For x-axis reflection, the domain is unchanged and the range is negated; for y-axis reflection, the domain is negated and the range is unchanged. Reflections preserve distances and general shape, but can reverse whether the graph is increasing in a particular direction. The operation \(-f(x)\) does not mean \(f(-x)\) unless that is established from the function.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source point table: The original graph gives \(f(-1.5)=-4.3\), \(f(-1)=-4\), \(f(0)=-1.8\), and \(f(2.6)=3.9\). For \(g(x)=-f(x)\), the corresponding outputs are \(g(-1.5)=4.3,\ g(-1)=4,\ g(0)=1.8,\ g(2.6)=-3.9\). Their horizontal positions stay fixed. Example 2 — a different reflection: For \(h(x)=f(-x)\), the original point \((-1.5,-4.3)\) becomes \((1.5,-4.3)\), not \((-1.5,4.3)\). With \(p(x)=x^2+x\), reflecting across the x-axis gives \(-x^2-x\), while reflecting across the y-axis gives \(x^2-x\); these are distinct functions.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Choose the reflection axis before modifying an equation or point. 2. To reflect in the x-axis, keep x and negate each y-coordinate; write \(g(x)=-f(x)\). 3. To reflect in the y-axis, negate each x-coordinate and keep its original y; write \(h(x)=f(-x)\). 4. Complete the source table using these paired coordinate rules. 5. Test the algebra on \(p(x)=x^2+x\) to see the two different results. 6. State what happens to the domain and range, and explain why the reflected graph still represents a function.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not confuse the negative sign outside f with a negative input: (-f(x)) reflects over the x-axis, whereas (f(-x)) reflects over the y-axis. A point ((-1.5,-4.3)) does not become ((-1.5,4.3)) under a y-axis reflection. Changing both signs is a half-turn around the origin, not a single-axis reflection. Be attentive to asymmetric domains.
translations.quickSummary: Across the x-axis, \((x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)\) and \(g(x)=-f(x)\). Across the y-axis, \((x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)\) and \(h(x)=f(-x)\).

translations.title: Some Functions Have Symmetry
translations.explanation: Some graph shapes stay unchanged when reflected across the vertical axis, while others stay unchanged under a 180-degree turn around the origin. These are the defining pictures of even and odd functions. Investigate matching coordinate pairs to infer the patterns, using a Ferris wheel at its highest point as a contextual example of equal heights at equal times before and after the top. Classify from graph and table evidence rather than the function's name.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A function is even if \(f(-x)=f(x)\) for every pair of opposite inputs in its symmetric domain; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis. It is odd if \(f(-x)=-f(x)\), equivalent to origin symmetry. A nonzero function on a domain symmetric about zero cannot be both even and odd: both conditions imply \(f(x)=0\) at every x. An odd function defined at x=0 must satisfy \(f(0)=0\). For a graph of a FUNCTION to be symmetric about the x-axis for all its points, its outputs must all be zero, since both y and −y at the same input would otherwise violate the vertical-line test.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source Ferris wheel: At t=0 Clare is at the top, 212 feet above ground. Previous heights at t=−20,−40,−60,−80 seconds are 181,106,31,0 feet. Under the constant-speed symmetric half-turn model, heights at t=20,40,60,80 seconds repeat 181,106,31,0. Thus \(H(-20)=H(20)=181\), a local example of even symmetry about t=0. Example 2 — classify typical graphs: \(p(x)=x^2+1\) is even because \((-x)^2+1=x^2+1\); \(q(x)=x^3\) is odd because \((-x)^3=-x^3\). The function \(r(x)=x^2+x\) is neither because \(r(-x)=x^2-x\), which is generally neither r(x) nor −r(x).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the axis or center of the observed graph symmetry. 2. Use an original pair \((x,y)\) to predict the matching point: even \((-x,y)\), odd \((-x,-y)\). 3. Fill the Ferris wheel table by matching times equally distant from the peak at 0. 4. Verify the proposed even symmetry against more than one pair of input values. 5. For an odd example check whether its graph passes through the origin when zero is in the domain. 6. Explain why one isolated matching pair cannot prove a function is globally even or odd.
translations.commonMistakes: An even function need not have an even exponent in every displayed term unless the equation has been simplified and the domain supports the symmetry. A graph visually symmetric about the x-axis is generally NOT a function unless it lies on that axis. One matching value (f(1)=f(-1)) is not proof the entire function is even. For an odd function with 0 in its domain, f(0) cannot be nonzero.
translations.quickSummary: Even functions satisfy \(f(-x)=f(x)\) and have y-axis symmetry. Odd functions satisfy \(f(-x)=-f(x)\) and have origin symmetry. A Ferris wheel centered at its peak shows matching heights at equal positive and negative times in the idealized model.

translations.title: Symmetry in Equations
translations.explanation: Determine even or odd symmetry directly from an equation rather than relying only on the graph's appearance. Replace every input x by −x, simplify, and compare the resulting expression with the original function and its negative. This gives a general algebraic classification for a symmetric real input domain. It also helps reconstruct a missing half of a graph: even outputs repeat at opposite inputs, while odd outputs reverse signs.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a function whose domain is symmetric about zero, the identity \(f(-x)=f(x)\) at EVERY allowed x means even, and \(f(-x)=-f(x)\) at every allowed x means odd. To test a polynomial, substitute −x into every term and simplify. Terms of even powers are unchanged under x→−x; terms of odd powers change sign. A sum of only even powers and a constant is even; a sum of only odd powers and no constant is odd. A polynomial mixing surviving even and odd powers is generally neither. The zero polynomial is both even and odd. These classifications also require verifying domain symmetry for nonpolynomial functions.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source polynomial: \(g(x)=x^5+x\). Replacing x by −x gives \(g(-x)=(-x)^5+(-x)=-x^5-x=-g(x)\), so g is odd. At x=1 the value is 2; at x=−1 it is −2, matching origin symmetry. Example 2 — even versus neither: \(f(x)=3x^6-4x^2+7\) satisfies \(f(-x)=3x^6-4x^2+7=f(x)\), so it is even. By contrast \(h(x)=x^3+x^2\) gives \(h(-x)=-x^3+x^2\), neither h(x) nor −h(x) for all x. Check x=2: h(2)=12, h(−2)=−4, unequal and not opposites.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Check the domain: if x is allowed, must −x also be allowed? 2. Write f(−x) with parentheses around every instance of −x. 3. Simplify signs using even and odd integer exponents. 4. Compare f(−x) symbolically with f(x) and −f(x). 5. Decide even, odd, both (only the zero function in a symmetric domain), or neither. 6. Use the result to reflect an existing half-graph into the other half, verifying at least one coordinate pair.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not infer odd symmetry merely because a function has an odd-degree leading term; mixed lower-degree even terms can destroy it. Do not forget that ((-x)^2=x^2) but ((-x)^3=-x^3). A numerical match at one x cannot establish an identity for all x. For nonpolynomial functions, first make sure both x and −x belong to the domain.
translations.quickSummary: Test symmetry using substitution: even means \(f(-x)=f(x)\); odd means \(f(-x)=-f(x)\) on a symmetric domain. For \(x^5+x\) the function is odd; for \(3x^6-4x^2+7\) it is even.

translations.title: Expressing Transformations of Functions Algebraically
translations.explanation: Start with a familiar function and express described translations and reflections as a new equation. Keep track of the order of operations: transforming a graph and then reflecting it may not give the same rule as reflecting first and then translating. The square-root parent function is useful because its domain endpoint makes horizontal changes easy to observe. Use a quadratic vertex and a cooling-model context to connect the algebra with graph features and data fit.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For parent \(g(x)=\sqrt{x}\), shift left 5 gives \(g(x+5)=\sqrt{x+5}\) with domain \(x\ge-5\). Shifting down 3 gives \(\sqrt{x+5}-3\). Reflecting this completed graph across the y-axis gives \(\sqrt{5-x}-3\) with domain \(x\le5\), because replace x by −x in the WHOLE previous expression. For \(f(x)=x^2\), a left-3/up-5 translation is \((x+3)^2+5\), vertex (−3,5). In general, when a graph has vertex (h,k), the function \(a(x-h)^2+k\), \(a\ne0\), has that vertex.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source square-root transformations: \(g(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Shift left five and down three: \(p(x)=\sqrt{x+5}-3\). Reflect p over the y-axis: \(q(x)=p(-x)=\sqrt{5-x}-3\). The starting point moves from (0,0), to (−5,−3), to (5,−3). Check \(q(5)=-3\), and note that q is not defined as a real function for x>5.

Example 2 — quadratic vertices: A parabola shifted three units left and five up from \(y=x^2\) is \(y=(x+3)^2+5\). A parabola with vertex (1.5,2.6) is \(h(x)=(x-1.5)^2+2.6\); one opening down with vertex (3.2,−4.7) is \(k(x)=-(x-3.2)^2-4.7\). Each vertex is confirmed by making the squared term zero.

Example 3 — original Edulytiks cooling-fit extension: A shape \(33(0.6)^h\) can be shifted vertically toward outdoor temperature 45°F to form \(T(h)=45+33(0.6)^h\). The limiting temperature is 45°F, but the original source's measured points still determine which further translations improve the actual fit.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the parent graph and its original domain. 2. Perform each requested transformation in the stated order, writing a new expression after each step. 3. For left 5, substitute x+5 into \(g(x)=\sqrt x\). 4. Subtract 3 outside to shift down. 5. For the final y-axis reflection substitute −x everywhere inside the previous function to obtain \(\sqrt{5-x}-3\). 6. Verify the endpoint and a second graph point and check how the domain has changed.
translations.commonMistakes: A translation left five is x+5 inside the function, not x−5. When reflecting after two translations, substitute −x into the ENTIRE transformed function, not only the unshifted parent. A square-root expression is not real when its radicand is negative. The vertex of ((x+3)^2+5) is at x=−3, not +3. A formula that models data approximately is not a source-measured observation.
translations.quickSummary: For \(g(x)=\sqrt x\), left 5/down 3/reflect over the y-axis gives \(\sqrt{5-x}-3\), domain \(x\le5\). Quadratic vertex form tracks left/right and up/down translations exactly.

translations.title: Scaling the Outputs
translations.explanation: Multiply a function's OUTPUTS by a scale factor to compress or stretch its graph vertically. The original source's Hulme Arch has the same horizontal endpoints as a simple quadratic model but a much lower peak. Use the measured midpoint height to determine a multiplying factor; a second example with a radical function can require a scale factor greater than one. Distinguish changes to output height from changes to horizontal width.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: If \(g(x)=k f(x)\), the point \((x,y)\) on f becomes \((x,ky)\). For \(0<k<1\), outputs are vertically compressed toward the x-axis; for \(k>1\) stretched away from it; for k<0 they also reflect across the x-axis. The x-intercepts of f remain unchanged when k is nonzero. For a source parabola \(H(x)=x(52-x)\), the zeros at x=0 and x=52 match the arch endpoints, but \(H(26)=676\) meters while the real arch is 25 meters high. Multiply by \(k=25/676\), producing \(A(x)=\frac{25}{676}x(52-x)\), physical domain \(0\le x\le52\).
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — Hulme Arch: The ends of a 52-meter arch are at (0,0) and (52,0), with maximum height 25 meters at midpoint (26,25). The unscaled \(H(x)=x(52-x)\) has midpoint value \(26\cdot26=676\). To correct its peak, choose \(k=25/676\approx0.03698\). Now \(A(26)=25\) and \(A(0)=A(52)=0\). The shape is the same parabola, just vertically compressed. Example 2 — a radical stretch, original Edulytiks exercise: Starting from \(f(x)=\sqrt x\), a transformed graph required to pass through (9,12) needs \(g(x)=4\sqrt x\), because \(f(9)=3\) and \(12/3=4\). For k=4 the domain remains x≥0 and (0,0) stays fixed.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify horizontal intercepts or other features that already match the data. 2. Compare the predicted height with the source height at the same input; use k=target/predicted when the predicted output is nonzero. 3. Compute \(H(26)=676\) and set \(k=25/676\). 4. Multiply the full function by k to obtain \(\frac{25}{676}x(52-x)\). 5. Verify both endpoints and the midpoint. 6. Explain why scaling OUTPUTS does not change the span of the arch, while the data-model domain is limited to the actual bridge.
translations.commonMistakes: A 52-meter base is not the arch's height. The parabola (x(52-x)) reaches 676 at x=26, so leaving it unscaled is not a valid fit for the 25-meter height. Multiplying outputs by 0.037 does not shrink the horizontal base. Nonzero vertical scaling preserves zeros; scaling by zero collapses the entire graph and is a different special case.
translations.quickSummary: To adjust the source arch, scale \(H(x)=x(52-x)\) by \(25/676\) so the 52-meter span stays fixed and the peak becomes 25 meters. Output scaling changes heights, not horizontal locations.

translations.title: Scaling the Inputs
translations.explanation: Multiplying the INPUT of a function changes how quickly its graph is traversed horizontally, rather than how high its outputs are. Use the source walking-distance graph to compare a person walking the same route at different constant speeds. A speed twice as large shortens every time interval by one half; the maximum distance from home remains two miles. The expression \(f(2t)\) is therefore a horizontal compression, unlike \(2f(t)\), which doubles the plotted distance.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For k>0, \(g(t)=f(kt)\) maps each original point (t,y) to (t/k,y), so it compresses horizontally by factor k when k>1 and stretches when 0<k<1. In a source round trip of 2 miles outward and 2 miles back at 2 mph, distance from home is \(f(t)=2t\) for \(0\le t\le1\) and \(f(t)=4-2t\) for \(1\le t\le2\). At twice that speed, \(g(t)=f(2t)\) is valid for \(0\le t\le1\); its peak is still 2 miles, at t=0.5 hours, and returns to zero after 1 hour. A vertical scaling \(2f(t)\) would falsely change the destination to 4 miles.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source walk: At 2 mph Elena reaches a two-mile turnaround after one hour and home after two hours. Values include \(f(0)=0,\ f(0.5)=1,\ f(1)=2,\ f(1.5)=1,\ f(2)=0\). At 4 mph the same path is \(g(t)=f(2t)\), with \(g(0)=0,\ g(0.25)=1,\ g(0.5)=2,\ g(0.75)=1,\ g(1)=0\). The graph is half as wide but equally high. Example 2 — a slower walker: At 1 mph, \(h(t)=f(t/2)\), domain \(0\le t\le4\); the turnaround occurs at t=2 hours. The expression \(2f(t)\) instead leaves the return time two hours but gives maximum distance 4 miles, so it is not the same physical situation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the original graph's time and distance units. 2. Calculate the route duration from a two-mile outward trip at 2 mph, plus the return. 3. Identify the new speed and its multiplier k relative to the original. 4. Write the transformed function \(g(t)=f(kt)\). 5. For twice speed, evaluate at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 hour. 6. Compare horizontal times and unchanged vertical distances, and restrict the new domain to the new trip duration.
translations.commonMistakes: For (g(t)=f(2t)), the trip happens faster, not slower, because the same original output is reached at half the time. Do not confuse an input factor 2 with output factor 2. The turnaround location stays two miles from home; the graph's y-intercept and maximum do not double when only speed changes. Rescale the time domain with the input variable.
translations.quickSummary: Input scaling \(f(kt)\) changes horizontal timing by \(1/k\). For Elena's two-mile out-and-back route, doubling walking speed yields \(f(2t)\), a one-hour round trip with the same two-mile maximum distance.

translations.title: Combining Functions
translations.explanation:
This lesson combines two functions at the same input through arithmetic: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x), (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x), and (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x) where g(x)≠0. Graphs and tables allow function values to be combined without explicit formulas. In the publisher context, annual books sold per person is total annual books sold divided by the population: both are measured in millions, so their ratio has units of books per person. Combining by arithmetic is distinct from composition f(g(x)), which substitutes an output into a second function and is not the central focus of this lesson.

Edulytics original standards extension (HSF-BF.A.1.c; not attributed to the source publisher): composition builds a new function by using the output of an inner function as the input of an outer function. For two functions f and g, the composition f(g(x)) generally differs from both the product f(x)g(x) and the reverse composition g(f(x)). In a real context, the inner function’s output units must match the outer function’s input units.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
At the same input x: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x); (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x); (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x); (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x), with g(x)≠0. Domains of sums, differences and products are the intersection of the original domains; quotient domains also exclude zeros of the divisor. Interpret the units of each combined quantity, not just its numerical value. For a combined graph, read f(x) and g(x) at the SAME x before adding or otherwise combining their y-values. Composition f(g(x)) is a separate operation and should not be confused with the product fg.

Edulytics extension — composition: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)). Evaluate g first, then apply f. The composition domain consists of x in the domain of g for which g(x) lies in the domain of f. Do not substitute outputs from different x values or confuse f(g(x)) with (fg)(x). Composition is generally not commutative: f∘g need not equal g∘f. Units must chain: minutes→height in meters→temperature in degrees Celsius.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 (books per person): In 2010, 2,530 million books were sold in the U.S. and the U.S. population was 309.35 million. Let B(0)=2,530 and P(0)=309.35. Then R(0)=B(0)/P(0)=2,530/309.35≈8.178 books per person. The millions cancel. R(0) is not the total book sales or the number of people. Example 2 (function arithmetic): Let f(x)=2x+3 and g(x)=x−1. Their sum is (f+g)(x)=3x+2, so (f+g)(4)=14. Their product is (fg)(x)=(2x+3)(x−1)=2x²+x−3. Their quotient is (f/g)(x)=(2x+3)/(x−1), defined only when x≠1; at x=4, its value is 11/3. Example 3 (graph table): If f(2)=5 and g(2)=−3, the combined graph for h=f+g contains (2,2), while the graph of f−g contains (2,8); add outputs at a shared input.

Edulytics extension, Example 4 — algebraic composition: f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=3x−4. Then f(g(x))=2(3x−4)+1=6x−7, while g(f(x))=3(2x+1)−4=6x−1. At x=2, f(g(2))=5, but g(f(2))=11. This demonstrates why composition is not simply multiplication and its order matters. Example 5 — temperature of a weather balloon: its height in meters after t minutes is h(t)=1,000+2t; atmospheric temperature in degrees Celsius at height y meters is T(y)=20−0.006y. Their composition is T(h(t))=20−0.006(1,000+2t)=14−0.012t °C. At t=5 minutes, the predicted temperature is 13.94°C. The input/output units match: time→height→temperature.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
1. Identify the two functions and the desired operation (sum, difference, product or quotient). 2. Determine the common domain; for a quotient also exclude inputs where g(x)=0. 3. If expressions are supplied, combine them algebraically and simplify carefully. 4. If a graph/table is supplied, read both outputs at the same x and carry out the operation. 5. When combining real-world quantities, state the output units and interpret the result. 6. Check a sample input with both the original and simplified formulas, and validate any denominator restrictions.

Edulytics extension for HSF-BF.A.1.c: 1. Identify the outer function f and the inner function g. 2. Evaluate or simplify g(x) first. 3. Replace the input of f with the entire expression g(x), keeping parentheses. 4. Simplify f(g(x)) without changing the order. 5. Check the domain: g(x) must be defined and its value must be an allowed input to f. 6. In contexts, verify output-input units are compatible across functions. 7. Test a numeric value using separate inner and outer evaluations to confirm the formula.
translations.commonMistakes:
Do not combine inputs instead of outputs. For a quotient, exclude denominator zeros even if algebraic cancellation occurs. Do not mistake composition f(g(x)) for the product (fg)(x). Do not assume book sales and population have the same output unit just because both are measured in millions: their ratio is books per person.

Edulytics extension: (f∘g)(x) is not f(x)g(x); it is f(g(x)). In general g(f(x)) differs from f(g(x)). A physically invalid height or a mismatched output unit makes a contextual composition meaningless. Domain restrictions propagate through the inner-to-outer calculation.
translations.quickSummary:
At each permitted x, combine f(x) and g(x) by arithmetic. For division, require g(x)≠0 and interpret units. Book sales divided by population yields books per person. Composition f(g(x)) is a different skill.

Edulytics extension: build compositions by substituting the inner output into the outer function. Example f(g(x))=6x−7 and g(f(x))=6x−1 for f(x)=2x+1, g(x)=3x−4. This extension is original Edulytics content beyond the publisher lesson’s arithmetic focus.

translations.title: Making a Model for Data
translations.explanation: Model one collection of temperature data using different function families, then judge each model by more than its visual fit within a short interval. The source's bottle warms after removal from a refrigerator and gradually approaches the surrounding room temperature. A shifted/scaled quadratic can match the measured points exceptionally well in the short term while predicting implausible future cooling; exponential and rational models may better preserve the expected stable long-run temperature. A defensible model identifies parameters, units, observed range and limitations rather than claiming a single curve is uniquely true.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A transformed quadratic may have form \(q(t)=a(t-h)^2+k\), while a warming exponential that approaches ambient temperature A can be \(T(t)=A-Be^{-kt}\) for B,k>0 (or \(A-Bb^t\), 0<b<1). A rational alternative is \(R(t)=A-B/(t+c)\) for t≥0, c>0. Given a model and measured points, evaluate predictions and errors \(y_\mathrm{observed}-y_\mathrm{model}\). A small sum of squared errors within the given interval supports local fit, but a physical trend must also be sensible beyond it. All example constants below are original Edulytiks teaching data, not measurements from the publisher's graph.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — original Edulytiks extension (not source measurements): Suppose a refrigerated bottle starts at 8°C in a 23°C room. The model \(T(t)=23-15(0.6)^t\), t in hours, has \(T(0)=8\), \(T(1)=14\), \(T(2)=17.6\), and \(T(3)=19.76\), approaching 23°C from below as t increases. This expression is a vertical reflection and scaling of \(0.6^t\), followed by a shift upward by 23.

Example 2 — a misleading quadratic: \(Q(t)=8+6t-0.8t^2\) has Q(0)=8, Q(2)=16.8, but reaches its maximum at \(t=6/(1.6)=3.75\) hours and then decreases without bound for large t, which is physically unsuitable for water expected to warm toward room temperature. Thus even if Q fits a few early points, it should not be chosen without testing later time and contextual expectations.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the source data's horizontal input as elapsed hours and vertical output as temperature. 2. Select a plausible parent family: polynomial, rational, radical or exponential. 3. Apply horizontal/vertical translations and input/output scales to fit observed points. 4. Evaluate predicted outputs and compare residuals or visual deviations over the MEASURED interval. 5. Examine long-run behavior, especially whether the bottle approaches room temperature. 6. Explain the choice and limitations; label synthetic examples as Edulytiks teaching extensions rather than original source measurements.
translations.commonMistakes: The visually closest curve on a short time interval is not necessarily the best physical model. A quadratic with a downward-opening parabola eventually predicts decreasing temperature after its vertex, contrary to an object approaching a warmer room temperature. Do not treat demonstration temperatures in the Edulytiks worked example as publisher data. Fit error and physical plausibility are separate evidence categories.
translations.quickSummary: Graph transformations help fit several function families to measured data, but long-run behavior matters. For a bottle warming toward 23°C, \(T(t)=23-15(0.6)^t\) approaches the correct ambient temperature; a downward quadratic eventually becomes physically implausible.
