translations.title: Moving in Circles
translations.explanation: Circular motion creates a new type of function whose outputs repeat at regular time intervals. In the original clock lesson, a ladybug rides a second hand, so its vertical position changes but repeats after each complete minute. Define a repeating period using specific matching inputs rather than simply observing that a curve goes up and down. Use the Pythagorean Theorem to find unknown coordinates on a circle centered at the origin.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A function is periodic with positive period P when \(f(t+P)=f(t)\) for all t at which the translated inputs are allowed. The smallest positive period, when it exists, is the fundamental period. The second hand completes one full rotation every 60 seconds. For a one-foot hand with its rotation center 10 feet above ground, the ladybug's height at t seconds after pointing upward is \(h(t)=10+\cos(2\pi t/60)\) feet, an Edulytiks trigonometric expression used here as an optional preview. Every point (x,y) on a circle of radius r centered at the origin satisfies \(x^2+y^2=r^2\).
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — the source ladybug: With center height 10 feet and hand length 1 foot, at t=0 the ladybug is at 11 feet; after 15 seconds it is at 10 feet, after 30 seconds at 9 feet, after 45 seconds at 10 feet, and after 60 seconds at 11 feet. Its height repeats after 60 seconds, but not after 30 seconds because 11 and 9 differ. At t=10 seconds the hand makes 60 degrees clockwise from vertical, giving height \(10+\cos(\pi/3)=10.5\) feet.

Example 2 — coordinates on a circle: A circle centered at (0,0) passes through (−5,12). Its radius is \(\sqrt{(-5)^2+12^2}=\sqrt{169}=13\). A point on that circle with y=−4 satisfies \(x^2+16=169\), so \(x=\pm\sqrt{153}=\pm3\sqrt{17}\), unless a specified side of the circle chooses one sign.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify which part of a motion repeats and how much time a complete rotation takes. 2. Determine the center height from the fact that the one-foot hand is at 10 feet while horizontal. 3. Add or subtract the vertical component of the hand to obtain heights at each quarter-turn. 4. Check both h(0)=11 and h(60)=11 to recognize a 60-second period. 5. For a circle with known point (−5,12), calculate \(r^2=25+144\). 6. Substitute a new y-coordinate into \(x^2+y^2=r^2\) and retain both possible signs until the quadrant is known.
translations.commonMistakes: One matching pair of outputs does not prove an entire function is periodic; verify the regular repeated behavior. The ladybug height is not the hand length: its center is already ten feet above the ground. A circle with y=−4 can have two x-coordinates unless the point's side is specified. Do not confuse period (time per rotation) with amplitude (radius).
translations.quickSummary: A periodic function satisfies \(f(t+P)=f(t)\). The source second-hand ladybug repeats its height every 60 seconds, with heights 11, 10, 9, 10, 11 feet at successive quarter-turns; circle coordinates satisfy \(x^2+y^2=r^2\).

translations.title: Revisiting Right Triangles
translations.explanation: Right-triangle trigonometric ratios connect angles with the lengths of opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides. Recall which side is relative to the chosen angle, then use cosine and sine to describe coordinate points on a circle. When the hypotenuse is scaled to one unit, the adjacent and opposite side lengths become the x- and y-coordinates of a first-quadrant point.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For an acute angle A in a right triangle, \(\sin A=\mathrm{opposite}/\mathrm{hypotenuse}\), \(\cos A=\mathrm{adjacent}/\mathrm{hypotenuse}\), and \(\tan A=\mathrm{opposite}/\mathrm{adjacent}\) when adjacent≠0. If the radius/hypotenuse is r and a point is (x,y) in quadrant I, then \(\cos A=x/r\), \(\sin A=y/r\), and \(\tan A=y/x\) for x≠0. On a unit-radius circle the coordinates are \((\cos A,\sin A)\). The Pythagorean Theorem \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) checks the sides, and similar right triangles preserve these ratios.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source 8–15–17 triangle: For angle A with opposite side 8, adjacent side 15 and hypotenuse 17, \(\sin A=8/17\), \(\cos A=15/17\), and \(\tan A=8/15\). Check \(8^2+15^2=64+225=289=17^2\). If opposite and adjacent have equal positive lengths, \(\sin A=\cos A\) and \(\tan A=1\), corresponding to a 45-degree acute angle.

Example 2 — source point (9,12): The hypotenuse from origin (0,0) is \(\sqrt{9^2+12^2}=15\). Thus \(\cos G=9/15=3/5\), \(\sin G=12/15=4/5\), and \(\tan G=12/9=4/3\). Shrinking the entire triangle by factor 1/15 moves the terminal point to \((3/5,4/5)\) on the unit circle without changing the angle or its trig ratios.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Locate the right angle and identify the chosen acute reference angle. 2. Mark the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse lengths relative to that angle. 3. Verify the hypotenuse using the Pythagorean Theorem. 4. Calculate the three ratios from their defining side pairs. 5. For a coordinate point (9,12), divide both coordinates by the distance 15 from the origin. 6. Explain why \((3/5,4/5)\) gives the cosine and sine coordinates of a radius-one point.
translations.commonMistakes: The word adjacent depends on the chosen angle, not only the picture's orientation. Tangent divides by the adjacent side, so zero adjacent length makes it undefined. The coordinate point (9,12) is 15 units from the origin and is NOT already on the unit circle. Trigonometric ratios are dimensionless, even if original side lengths have units.
translations.quickSummary: For a quadrant-I right triangle, cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse, sine opposite/hypotenuse, and tangent opposite/adjacent. The point (9,12) normalizes to \((3/5,4/5)=(\cos A,\sin A)\) on the unit circle.

translations.title: The Unit Circle (Part 1)
translations.explanation: The unit circle has radius 1 and center at (0,0), so its points satisfy \(x^2+y^2=1\). Describe a point by its coordinates or by a counterclockwise rotation angle from the positive x-axis. Radian measure connects a central angle with distance around a circle: one radian subtends an arc equal to the radius. A one-foot-radius wheel rolling without slipping travels the same numerical number of feet as its angle of rotation in radians.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a radius-r circle, arc length \(s=r\theta\) when \(\theta\) is measured in radians; thus \(\theta=s/r\). A full revolution has angle \(2\pi\) radians because its circumference is \(2\pi r\). On the unit circle \(r=1\), so s=θ. The Pythagorean identity \(x^2+y^2=1\) gives unknown coordinates, subject to signs determined by quadrant. For x=3/5, y=±4/5. For y=−0.4=−2/5, x=±√21/5. These are two possible points, not unique coordinates without a quadrant constraint.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source unit-circle points: If x=3/5, \(y^2=1-9/25=16/25\), hence \(y=+4/5\) in quadrant I or −4/5 in quadrant IV. If y=−0.4, \(x^2=1-(.4)^2=.84=21/25\), so \(x=\pm\sqrt{21}/5\). Both x-sign possibilities lie below the horizontal axis.

Example 2 — rolling wheel: A bicycle wheel of radius one foot rolls without slipping through \(\theta=\pi/3\) radians. Arc length swept by its rim is \(s=r\theta=\pi/3\) feet, so its center advances approximately 1.047 feet along a straight road. After one full revolution, the distance is \(2\pi\) feet; this proportionality depends on the no-slip assumption.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. State that the unit circle has r=1 and equation \(x^2+y^2=1\). 2. Substitute one given coordinate and solve for the square of the other. 3. Take BOTH square-root signs unless the quadrant selects one. 4. Define radian measure as arc length divided by radius. 5. Use \(s=r\theta\) to calculate a rolling wheel's distance. 6. Check that a full revolution gives \(\theta=2\pi\) and \(s=2\pi r\) and preserve physical length units.
translations.commonMistakes: A coordinate on the unit circle can be negative depending on the quadrant; square rooting produces both possible signs. Radians are not linear units: arc length is r times the angle. Do not confuse a unit circle's radius with its diameter or claim a full revolution is π radians. A wheel slipping on a road need not advance exactly its swept rim distance.
translations.quickSummary: On a unit circle \(x^2+y^2=1\); x=3/5 gives y=±4/5. Radians satisfy \(\theta=s/r\), and one revolution is \(2\pi\) radians; a one-foot wheel travels \(\pi/3\) feet for a no-slip rotation of \(\pi/3\).

translations.title: The Unit Circle (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Use radians to label 24 equally spaced positions on the unit circle, one angle every \(\pi/12\) radians (15 degrees). Analyze sign patterns and symmetries rather than memorizing every coordinate independently. The same positive x-coordinate can occur in two quadrants with opposite y-signs; reference angles help infer the values of special points. Describe a point both by angle and by a coordinate pair.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Counterclockwise angles from the positive x-axis are positive. A full rotation is \(2\pi=24(\pi/12)\), so successive source positions are \(\pi/12,2\pi/12,\ldots,24\pi/12\). Coordinates at angle θ are \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). Quadrant signs are (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−) from I through IV. Standard exact points include \(\theta=\pi/6:(\sqrt3/2,1/2)\), \(\pi/3:(1/2,\sqrt3/2)\), \(\pi/2:(0,1)\), and \(\pi:(-1,0)\). Angles separated by \(2\pi\) end at the same unit-circle point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source 24-position structure: Positions 2π/12=π/6, 10π/12=5π/6, 14π/12=7π/6, and 22π/12=11π/6 share reference angle π/6. Their coordinates are respectively \((\sqrt3/2,1/2)\), \((-\sqrt3/2,1/2)\), \((-\sqrt3/2,-1/2)\), and \((\sqrt3/2,-1/2)\). All satisfy \(x^2+y^2=3/4+1/4=1\).

Example 2 — the original labeled angles: At π/3 the point is \((1/2,\sqrt3/2)\). At 5π/3 the point is \((1/2,-\sqrt3/2)\), symmetric across the x-axis. The angle 13π/12 is slightly past π in quadrant III, so BOTH coordinates are negative; their exact radical forms are optional at this stage. The angle 2π reaches (1,0) and represents the same point as 0 radians.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Divide the full circle \(2\pi\) into 24 equal angles, each \(\pi/12\). 2. Label each ray counterclockwise from the positive horizontal axis. 3. Mark special angles with familiar right triangles: π/6, π/4, π/3 and π/2. 4. Use horizontal/vertical reflection symmetries to transfer coordinate magnitudes into the other three quadrants. 5. Apply the appropriate signs and verify x²+y²=1. 6. Explain why 0 and 2π, though different angle measures, end at the same unit-circle location.
translations.commonMistakes: A 15-degree interval is (pi/12) radians, not π/15. The sine coordinate is y and cosine is x; switching them changes many angles. In quadrant III both coordinates must be negative. A negative angle may reach the same point as a positive coterminal angle, but angle measures need not lie only in [0,2π].
translations.quickSummary: Twenty-four unit-circle positions fit around \(2\pi\) radians in steps of \(\pi/12\). A point is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\); coordinate magnitudes repeat with quadrant-dependent signs and standard angle symmetries.

translations.title: The Pythagorean Identity (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Use right triangles and the unit-circle equation to establish a relationship that holds for sine and cosine at every real rotation angle. In quadrant I, cosine and sine are the horizontal and vertical legs of a radius-one right triangle. In other quadrants they are signed COORDINATES rather than unsigned side lengths. This observation leads directly to the Pythagorean Identity and allows you to decide whether a suggested point can lie on the unit circle.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: At radian angle θ the unit-circle terminal point is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). Every unit-circle point satisfies \(x^2+y^2=1\), so \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\) for all real θ. Here \(\cos^2\theta\) means \((\cos\theta)^2\), not \(\cos(\theta^2)\). If one coordinate magnitude is known, the other has magnitude \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\) or \(\sqrt{1-y^2}\); choose its sign using the quadrant. It is not possible for a unit-circle coordinate to have magnitude exceeding 1.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source quadrant points: \(\theta=\pi/3\) gives \((1/2,\sqrt3/2)\). At \(2\pi/3\), reflect across the y-axis to get \((-1/2,\sqrt3/2)\). Both satisfy \(1/4+3/4=1\). Example 2 — test two proposed points: \((-0.5,\sin(4\pi/3))=(-1/2,-\sqrt3/2)\) lies on the unit circle. However \((-0.5,\sin(5\pi/6))=(-1/2,1/2)\) has squared distance \(1/4+1/4=1/2\), so it lies INSIDE the circle. Example 3: If sinθ=−1/2 in quadrant IV, then cosθ=+\sqrt3/2, not −\sqrt3/2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Begin with equation \(x^2+y^2=1\) for the unit circle. 2. Replace x by \(\cos\theta\) and y by \(\sin\theta\). 3. Rearrange the resulting identity to solve for a missing squared trig value. 4. Take the square root with ± as algebraic candidates. 5. Select the sign using the indicated quadrant. 6. Check the final pair has squared distance exactly 1 and lies in the correct quadrant.
translations.commonMistakes: The identity adds SQUARES of cosine and sine, not the trig values themselves. Do not confuse (sin^2	heta) with (sin(	heta^2)). For (sin	heta=-1/2), cosine could have either sign unless a quadrant is specified. A plotted point with squared distance below 1 is inside the unit circle, not on its circumference.
translations.quickSummary: For every angle, \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\). If \(\sin\theta=-1/2\) in quadrant IV, then \(\cos\theta=\sqrt3/2\), and the point is \((\sqrt3/2,-1/2)\).

translations.title: The Pythagorean Identity (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Use the Pythagorean Identity to find all three trig ratios from one given ratio and the angle's quadrant. Correct solutions require both exact magnitudes and quadrant signs. Critique a worked solution rather than treating a calculator decimal as the only acceptable answer. In particular, a first-quadrant sine and cosine are positive, but both become negative in quadrant III, giving a positive tangent.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For any angle θ, \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\). When \(\cos\theta\ne0\), \(\tan\theta=\sin\theta/\cos\theta\), which is the slope of the terminal ray. Sign patterns for (cos,sin,tan) by quadrant are I (+,+,+), II (−,+,−), III (−,−,+), IV (+,−,−). Thus knowing \(\cos\theta=0.28=7/25\) in quadrant IV gives \(\sin\theta=-\sqrt{1-(7/25)^2}=-24/25=-0.96\) and \(\tan\theta=-24/7\approx-3.42857\).
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source Andre calculation: In quadrant IV with cosθ=0.28, \(1-\cos^2\theta=1-0.0784=0.9216\). The square root is 0.96, and sine must be negative, so sinθ=−0.96. Tangent equals \(-0.96/0.28=-24/7\approx-3.43\). Andre's answers are correct, although the exact fraction −24/7 is more precise. Example 2 — a negative case: A claimed quadrant II angle has \(\cos\theta=3/5\), \(\sin\theta=4/5\). The squares add to 1, but cosine must be NEGATIVE in quadrant II. The same magnitudes with \(\cos\theta=-3/5\) would give \(\tan\theta=-4/3\) and be consistent.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Record the quadrant and signs expected for cosine, sine and tangent. 2. Substitute the known ratio into \(\sin^2+\cos^2=1\). 3. Solve for the missing magnitude with a square root. 4. Choose the sign based on the quadrant; for quadrant IV sine is negative. 5. Divide sine by cosine to calculate tangent if cosine is not zero. 6. Test the squared identity and sign pattern, and critique any rounded answer against the exact fraction.
translations.commonMistakes: A correct sum of squares is necessary but not sufficient for a claimed quadrant: the coordinate signs must also match. Tangent is undefined when cosine equals zero. Do not keep the principal positive square root for sine in quadrant IV. Rounding 24/7 to 3.43 is reasonable, but it is not exact.
translations.quickSummary: Quadrant IV with cosθ=7/25 gives sinθ=−24/25 and tanθ=−24/7. Use \(\sin^2+\cos^2=1\) for magnitudes and the quadrant for signs.

translations.title: Finding Unknown Coordinates on a Circle
translations.explanation: Scale and translate unit-circle coordinates to represent rotating points on clocks and Ferris wheels of different sizes and positions. A radius-one point at angle θ has coordinates (cosθ,sinθ). For radius r and center (a,b), the corresponding point is (a+r cosθ,b+r sinθ), provided the angle is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. Clock hands rotate clockwise starting from 12 o'clock, so their angles must be converted consistently.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A circle centered at (a,b) with radius r has equation \((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2\). The angular parametrization is \((x,y)=(a+r\cos\theta,b+r\sin\theta)\). For a clockwise clock hand of length r at t minutes after the hour, the tip relative to the center is \((r\sin(2\pi t/60),r\cos(2\pi t/60))\), because at t=0 it points upward; this formula treats clockwise movement as positive clock time. On a unit circle, scaling the radius multiplies both coordinate components, and translating the center adds (a,b).
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source minute hand: A five-inch minute hand centered at the origin points left at 45 minutes, so its tip is (−5,0). At 10 minutes, the hand is 60 degrees clockwise from vertical, giving \((5\sqrt3/2,5/2)\) inches. At 40 minutes, the tip is \((-5\sqrt3/2,-5/2)\). A 15-inch hand at the same times has coordinates three times as large.

Example 2 — unknown radius: A third clock tip is approximately (7.5,7.5) inches relative to its center. Its hand length is \(\sqrt{7.5^2+7.5^2}=7.5\sqrt2\approx10.61\) inches. Example 3 — translated circle, original extension: A Ferris wheel centered at (10,20) meters with radius 8 has rider coordinate \((10+8\cos\theta,20+8\sin\theta)\). At θ=π/2 the rider is at (10,28); at θ=3π/2 the rider is at (10,12).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the radius, center and direction from the picture or context. 2. For a given radian angle from the positive x-axis, calculate the unit-circle pair (cosθ,sinθ). 3. Multiply both coordinates by radius r and add the center coordinates. 4. For a clock hand start from the upward direction and account for clockwise rotation. 5. For 10 minutes, calculate the angle 2π(10/60)=π/3 from the top; use x=r sinπ/3 and y=r cosπ/3. 6. Check the resulting point's squared distance from the center equals r².
translations.commonMistakes: A second clock hand three times as long has coordinate components three times as large, not the same components. The clock starts at 12 o'clock and rotates clockwise, not from the positive x-axis counterclockwise. Moving the center changes coordinates but not radius. Do not confuse an angle's coordinate pair with a hand's length in inches or meters.
translations.quickSummary: For a circle with center (a,b) and radius r, use \((a+r\cos\theta,b+r\sin\theta)\). At 10 minutes a five-inch clockwise hand has tip \((5\sqrt3/2,5/2)\), and a 15-inch hand's coordinates are triple.

translations.title: Rising and Falling
translations.explanation: Graphs of periodic relationships repeat patterns over a fixed interval, often with rising and falling output values. Compare a race car's distance from a starting line on repeated laps with a city temperature record whose daily highs and lows may not repeat exactly. The first can have nearly identical laps, while weather contains irregular changes and should not be declared exactly periodic merely because it fluctuates. Identify independent/dependent variables, repeats, maximum/minimum heights and possible periods using graph evidence.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A function f has positive period P if \(f(t+P)=f(t)\) for all relevant t. A smooth wave such as \(w(t)=1-\cos(\pi t)\) has period 2, minimum 0 at even integer t, maximum 2 at odd integer t, and range [0,2]. It can be a simplified model of distance from a starting line over repeated laps, though real distance on a track may not be sinusoidal. Graph features include period (horizontal repeat interval), maximum and minimum outputs, and a midline halfway between extremes. A noisy real-world temperature series is not strictly periodic without additional evidence.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — original Edulytiks stylized race track: Define \(D(t)=1-\cos(\pi t)\), t in minutes. Then D(0)=0, D(1)=2, D(2)=0, D(3)=2, D(4)=0, so the distance pattern repeats every 2 minutes. Its peaks are 2 miles from the starting line and its troughs 0 miles. The source race-car graph has similarly repeated laps, but this exact cosine formula is only an explanatory extension, not an equation claimed by the publisher.

Example 2 — compare a nonperiodic trend: \(T(t)=20+0.3t+2\sin(\pi t)\) has regular short-run ups and downs, yet \(T(t+2)=T(t)+0.6\ne T(t)\); it is NOT periodic because of the increasing baseline. A temperature graph may display rough cycles without satisfying a strict equality for every cycle.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the horizontal input (usually time) and the vertical output, including units. 2. Locate consecutive peaks or corresponding low points in the graph. 3. Compare horizontal spacing to identify a candidate repeat interval P. 4. Check matching outputs at multiple inputs shifted by P. 5. Record max, min and any intermediate baseline, but do not mistake repeating HEIGHTS for a proof of exact periodicity. 6. Describe a physically plausible reason for repetition (laps, rotating wheel) or irregularity (daily weather).
translations.commonMistakes: A graph that rises and falls is not necessarily periodic: the entire pattern must repeat after a fixed interval. A trend term such as +0.3t prevents strict repetition even if a sinusoid is also present. Period is a horizontal time distance, while maximum and minimum are vertical output heights. Do not infer precise measured periods from a schematic diagram without checking its scales.
translations.quickSummary: Periodic functions repeat outputs at regular intervals. A simple lap-distance extension \(D(t)=1-\cos(\pi t)\) repeats every two minutes, whereas a fluctuating temperature function with a rising trend need not be periodic.

translations.title: Introduction to Trigonometric Functions
translations.explanation: Cosine and sine are functions whose inputs are angle measures in radians and whose outputs are the x- and y-coordinates of the matching unit-circle point. As a point moves from (1,0) counterclockwise around the circle, the horizontal coordinate produces the cosine graph and the vertical coordinate produces the sine graph. Both graphs stay between −1 and 1, pass the vertical-line test, and complete one wave in 2π radians. Plot a table of known special angles to explain the waves rather than treating them as arbitrary calculator curves.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: The point at angle θ on the unit circle is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). From 0 to 2π, cosine has values 1,0,−1,0,1 at 0,π/2,π,3π/2,2π; sine has values 0,1,0,−1,0. Both are continuous real functions with range [−1,1], period 2π, and satisfy \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\). Cosine equals sine when θ=π/4 or 5π/4 within this interval; both share the sign in quadrants I and III. The graph of \(\theta+\cos\theta\) is not periodic despite its oscillating part, because adding 2π changes its output by 2π.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source wave table: At θ=0 the point is (1,0); π/2 gives (0,1); π gives (−1,0); 3π/2 gives (0,−1), and 2π returns to (1,0). Thus a graph of cosine plots these x-coordinate values as the VERTICAL outputs against angle input, and a sine graph plots the y-coordinate values. Example 2 — graph predictions: \(y=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\) is a horizontal line, not a wave. \(y=\cos\theta+\sin\theta\) has value 1 at 0 and maximum \(\sqrt2\) at π/4. For equality of cosine and sine, \(\tan\theta=1\) where cosine nonzero, giving π/4 and 5π/4 on [0,2π].
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Mark a counterclockwise rotation angle θ from (1,0) on a unit circle. 2. Record its horizontal and vertical coordinates for several special angles. 3. Plot each coordinate separately against θ, using radians as the input-axis unit. 4. Join the points with continuous sine/cosine curves that have correct maxima and minima. 5. Check the graphs at π/4 and 5π/4 and predict the sum and squared-sum graphs. 6. Explain why each angle has one output for each function and why the Pythagorean squared-sum graph stays at 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Cosine is the horizontal COORDINATE but the vertical output when graphing y=cosθ against θ. Do not label a radian angle as a unit-circle y-coordinate. The equation cos²θ+sin²θ=1 does not mean cosθ+sinθ=1. A graph of θ+cosθ does not repeat after 2π because of the linear θ term.
translations.quickSummary: Cosine and sine map radian angles to unit-circle coordinates and each make a 2π-period wave. They equal at π/4 and 5π/4 on one full revolution; the sum of their squares is the constant function 1.

translations.title: Beyond $2\pi$
translations.explanation: A rotation can go around the unit circle more than once. Extending sine and cosine inputs past 2π does not create new circle points; each extra full revolution returns to the same point. Use coterminal angles and a windmill blade's horizontal and vertical coordinates to evaluate rotations such as 5π/2 or 3π. This shows periodicity directly from the geometry, not only from a memorized equation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For every real θ and integer k, \(\cos(\theta+2k\pi)=\cos\theta\) and \(\sin(\theta+2k\pi)=\sin\theta\). The terminal point at θ on a radius-one windmill is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). Removing full rotations by subtracting multiples of 2π gives a coterminal angle in [0,2π). A rotation of 5π/2 equals one complete revolution plus π/2 and reaches (0,1); 6π/2=3π reaches (−1,0). Between 0 and 5π the windmill completes 2.5 rotations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source marked points: From (1,0), angles π/3, 4π/3, 7π/4, 5π/2, 6π/2 reach \((1/2,\sqrt3/2)\), \((-1/2,-\sqrt3/2)\), \((\sqrt2/2,-\sqrt2/2)\), (0,1), and (−1,0), respectively. For 5π/2 subtract 2π to get π/2. Example 2 — source windmill: With one-meter blades and initial P=(1,0), the point is at the top at θ=π/2, 5π/2 and 9π/2, all separated by 2π. At θ=3π the vertical height is 0 and the horizontal coordinate is −1 meter.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Determine how many whole \(2\pi\)-radian rotations fit in the given positive angle. 2. Subtract those rotations to obtain a coterminal angle in the first revolution. 3. Find the corresponding point using reference-angle values and quadrant signs. 4. Read cosine from the x-coordinate and sine from the y-coordinate. 5. Check the same results by graphing the source windmill over multiple rotations. 6. Explain that periodicity follows because one full revolution returns to an identical physical point.
translations.commonMistakes: The windmill does not have to stop after 2π; its angle input can continue. Do not treat 5π/2 as the same as 5π divided by 2π revolutions without checking the extra quarter-turn. The period is 2π radians, not π for the sine and cosine functions individually. A point at 3π is (−1,0), not the origin.
translations.quickSummary: For any integer k, sine and cosine repeat after \(2k\pi\). Thus 5π/2 has the same coordinates as π/2, and 3π has the same as π; a windmill returns to the same horizontal/vertical position every full revolution.

translations.title: Extending the Domain of Trigonometric Functions
translations.explanation: Negative angles indicate clockwise rotations from the positive x-axis. Sine and cosine remain meaningful for these rotations, as well as for angles exceeding a complete revolution. Use a clock hand or windmill to connect the direction of rotation to the signs of the coordinates; then graph sine and cosine from −4π to 4π. The cosine graph is symmetric about the vertical axis, while the sine graph has symmetry through the origin.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For any real θ, \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\), so cosine is even; \(\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\), so sine is odd. Both have period 2π and range [−1,1]. A negative quarter-turn −π/2 takes (1,0) to (0,−1); a positive quarter-turn π/2 takes it to (0,1). Coterminal angles also differ by 2π, including negative input values: −π/2 is coterminal with 3π/2. The y-axis is a line of symmetry of the cosine graph; it is not a line of symmetry of the sine graph.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source windmill: Priya predicts that rotating the point (1,0) through −π/2 radians reaches the bottom of the unit circle. Clockwise rotation by 90 degrees indeed gives (0,−1), so cos(−π/2)=0 and sin(−π/2)=−1. Example 2 — graph extension: At −π/6, the point has \((\sqrt3/2,-1/2)\), whereas at π/6 it has \((\sqrt3/2,1/2)\). Thus cosine values agree and sine values are opposites. At θ=−4π and +4π, both are (1,0), showing two full revolutions in opposite directions.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Mark positive rotations counterclockwise and negative rotations clockwise. 2. Locate the unit-circle point for a given negative angle by rotating the indicated magnitude clockwise. 3. Use any coterminal positive angle to verify the result. 4. Plot sine and cosine at important negative and positive angles from −4π to 4π. 5. Compare the pairs θ and −θ to establish the cosine even/sine odd relationships. 6. Check the 2π repeating pattern and identify symmetry, maxima, minima and axes intersections.
translations.commonMistakes: A negative angle does NOT mean a negative cosine or sine value automatically; the quadrant determines each sign. Cosine is even, sine is odd; reversing these identities misplaces reflected graph points. Do not assume an angle must be between 0 and 2π to have defined sine and cosine. A clock normally moves clockwise, so align the chosen zero-angle direction before interpreting its hour hand.
translations.quickSummary: Negative radian measures are clockwise rotations. Cosine is even and sine odd: \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\), \(\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\); both are defined for all real angles with period 2π.

translations.title: Tangent
translations.explanation: Tangent extends the unit-circle coordinate relationships to a quotient function, \( \tan\theta=\sin\theta/\cos\theta\). Its value equals the slope of the terminal ray when the horizontal coordinate is not zero. Unlike sine and cosine, tangent becomes undefined at the angles where cosine is zero, and its graph has vertical asymptotes there. A half-turn reverses both sine and cosine signs, leaving their quotient unchanged, so tangent repeats after π radians.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(\cos\theta\ne0\), \(\tan\theta=\sin\theta/\cos\theta\). Tangent has real domain excluding \(\theta=\pi/2+k\pi\), integer k, and range all real numbers; it has period π and zeros at \(\theta=k\pi\). The vertical asymptotes occur precisely where cosine=0, with sine=±1. At π/6, tan=1/√3=√3/3; at π/3, tan=√3; at 2π/3, tan=−√3; at 7π/6, tan=√3/3. These exact values follow from sine/cosine ratios; approximate classroom table values may differ by rounding.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source tangent table: At θ=−π/3, cosine=1/2, sine=−√3/2, so tangent=−√3. At θ=0, tangent=0/1=0. At θ=π/2, the denominator is 0, so tangent is UNDEFINED (not 0 or infinity as a number). At θ=4π/3, both sine and cosine are negative, giving tangent=√3. Example 2 — repeat after half a turn: \(\tan(\pi/6)=\sqrt3/3\) and \(\tan(7\pi/6)=\sqrt3/3\). Since both sine and cosine negate after adding π, their quotient is unchanged; the graph must repeat after π. The line x=1 through the origin's terminal ray at θ=π/6 intersects at y=√3/3, giving tangent as a slope.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Find sine and cosine from the unit-circle point. 2. Check whether cosine is zero before attempting the quotient. 3. If it is nonzero, calculate sine divided by cosine. 4. List zero inputs at integer multiples of π and excluded inputs at odd half-π angles. 5. Compare tanθ with tan(θ+π), explaining the simultaneous sign reversal. 6. Draw tangent between vertical asymptotes, with the curve passing through the origin and rising without bound near the next asymptote.
translations.commonMistakes: The tangent graph does not have a 2π fundamental period: it repeats after π. Do not assign a numerical output at π/2, where cosine=0. On quadrant II tangent is negative because sine positive and cosine negative; on quadrant III tangent positive because both are negative. A vertical asymptote is not an intersection of the graph with that line.
translations.quickSummary: Tangent is sine/cosine where cosine is nonzero; it has period π, zeros at kπ and vertical asymptotes at π/2+kπ. For example tan(π/3)=√3 but tan(π/2) is undefined.

translations.title: Amplitude and Midline
translations.explanation: Amplitude measures how far a periodic graph rises above its middle height, and the midline represents the average of its high and low outputs. A windmill blade moves symmetrically around its center, so the center height is the midline and blade length is the amplitude. Multiply sine by a vertical factor to adjust the up/down distance, then add a constant to change the center height. Use graph and equation representations to verify actual maximum and minimum outputs.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(\theta)=a\sin\theta+b\) or \(a\cos\theta+b\), with a≠0, amplitude is \(|a|\), midline is \(y=b\), maximum is \(b+|a|\), minimum \(b-|a|\), and the period remains 2π. Conversely given maximum M and minimum m, midline \(b=(M+m)/2\), amplitude \((M-m)/2\). In the source windmill example, \(g(\theta)=5\sin\theta-1\) has midline −1, amplitude 5, maximum 4 and minimum −6; the negative midline is a mathematical coordinate unless context gives a different ground reference.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source functions: \(f(\theta)=\cos\theta\) ranges from −1 to 1, midline 0, amplitude 1. \(g(\theta)=5\sin\theta-1\) ranges from −6 to 4: \((-6+4)/2=-1\), \((4-(-6))/2=5\). Example 2 — original model: For a 3-meter blade centered 8 meters above ground, \(h(\theta)=8+3\sin\theta\) has high point 11 meters, low point 5 meters, and midline 8 meters. At θ=π/2 the tip is at 11, at 3π/2 it is at 5, and at 0 it is at 8. Reversing rotation changes the sign of sine but not the blade length.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify maximum and minimum outputs from the source graph. 2. Average them to calculate the midline. 3. Take half their difference to calculate amplitude. 4. Write an equation by multiplying sine/cosine by the amplitude and adding the midline. 5. Verify predicted highs and lows using sine or cosine equal to ±1. 6. Interpret scale factors as blade radius and the constant as center height when this suits the physical context.
translations.commonMistakes: Amplitude is always nonnegative even if the coefficient a is negative; use |a|. The midline is not automatically the horizontal axis. Maximum minus minimum is TWICE the amplitude. A sign reversal may switch which quarter-turn is high without changing amplitude or midline. For a real windmill, negative height can indicate an unsuitable model or coordinate reference.
translations.quickSummary: Midline \(b=(M+m)/2\) and amplitude \((M-m)/2\). For \(5\sin\theta-1\), midline is −1, amplitude 5, maximum 4 and minimum −6.

translations.title: Transforming Trigonometric Functions
translations.explanation: Combine vertical scaling, vertical translation and horizontal shifts of sine and cosine to model different rotating windmills. A coefficient outside the trig function controls radius/amplitude; an added constant controls the wheel-center height; an input shift moves the phase of the motion. Describe how a point positioned at the far right of a blade moves upward or downward immediately after angle zero to infer the sign of sine. Translate graph equations carefully rather than confusing the different roles of constants.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(h(\theta)=a\sin(\theta+\phi)+k\), amplitude is |a|, midline k, and the graph shifts LEFT by positive \(\phi\). With \(a<0\), the vertical output is reflected about the midline. Since sin0=0 and sinθ initially increases for positive θ, the source windmills \(h_1=2.5\sin\theta+10\), \(h_2=0.8\sin\theta+3\), and \(h_3=-1.5\sin\theta+5\) all begin at midline but the third moves downward as θ increases. Their blade radii are 2.5, 0.8, 1.5 feet and their centers are at heights 10,3,5 feet.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source windmill comparison: \(h_1=2.5\sin\theta+10\) ranges from 7.5 to 12.5 feet. \(h_2=.8\sin\theta+3\) ranges from 2.2 to 3.8. \(h_3=-1.5\sin\theta+5\) ranges from 3.5 to 6.5 and initially descends from height 5 as θ increases. The negative coefficient does not mean a negative blade length. Example 2 — source shift context: \(g(\theta)=3\cos(\theta+\pi)-5=-3\cos\theta-5\), so its graph is cosine shifted left π, vertically stretched 3 and shifted down 5; its range is [−8,−2]. By contrast \(f(\theta)=3\cos\theta-5\) starts at −2, while g starts at −8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Rewrite the given source equation in a recognizable sinusoidal form. 2. Read absolute outside coefficient as amplitude, and the constant outside as midline. 3. Compare the sign of the sine coefficient with the initial upward/downward motion when θ=0. 4. For an expression inside the trig input, identify the horizontal phase shift. 5. Calculate maximum and minimum from midline ± amplitude. 6. Evaluate θ=0 and π/2 to check the physical motion and distinguish radius from center height.
translations.commonMistakes: A negative sine coefficient reflects the outputs but does not create negative blade length. Adding π INSIDE cosine shifts the graph, while adding π OUTSIDE raises all heights. The minus five in (3cos(	heta+pi)-5) controls the midline, not the phase. Do not assume every windmill has the same rotation direction simply because all models use θ.
translations.quickSummary: For \(h=a\sin(\theta+\phi)+k\), radius/amplitude is |a|, center/midline is k, and \(\phi\) shifts phase. The source windmills have different blade lengths, heights and initial movement directions.

translations.title: Features of Trigonometric Graphs (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Read amplitude, midline and horizontal shift from trig equations and graphs, and begin examining how a factor INSIDE the input changes a wave's period. In the source sound-wave comparison, one curve has a shorter repeat interval and a different height. Match multiple equivalent equations to the same graph by using trig identities and anchor points, rather than assuming one graph can be represented by only one expression.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For \(f(\theta)=a\sin(b\theta+c)+d\) with a≠0 and b≠0, amplitude is |a|, midline d and period \(2\pi/|b|\). Positive b>1 shortens the period; 0<b<1 lengthens it. A horizontal phase shift is \(-c/b\), not simply −c when b≠1. Standard identities include \(\cos(\theta+\pi/2)=-\sin\theta\), \(\sin(\theta-\pi/2)=-\cos\theta\), \(\sin(\theta+\pi)=-\sin\theta\). They can make two expressions share exactly the same graph.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source matching: \(y=2\sin\theta-3\) has amplitude 2 and midline −3, with range [−5,−1]. \(y=3\sin\theta-2\) has amplitude 3 and midline −2, range [−5,1]. Both have period 2π. The expressions \(-\cos\theta\) and \(\sin(\theta-\pi/2)\) are equivalent and have identical graphs; likewise \(\cos(\theta+\pi/2)\) and \(\sin(\theta+\pi)\) both equal \(-\sin\theta\). Example 2 — source \(y=\sin(2\theta)\): It reaches 0 at θ=0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π and completes TWO full cycles on [0,2π], so its period is π, half of \(\sin\theta\).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Find the graph's maximum, minimum and central height or read a and d from the equation. 2. Compute amplitude and midline, then infer range. 3. Determine the input coefficient b and calculate period \(2\pi/|b|\). 4. Find an x-value where the curve crosses its midline and note its direction. 5. Use special-angle identities or tabulated points to test graph/equation matches. 6. Explain when different expressions define the SAME graph, without changing the physical interpretation of a source sound wave.
translations.commonMistakes: Amplitude is the absolute value of the outside coefficient, not the inside coefficient. The period of sin(2θ) is π rather than 4π. The expression (cos(	heta+pi/2)) equals (-sin	heta), not (sin	heta). A horizontal translation in (asin(b	heta+c)) depends on division by b.
translations.quickSummary: For \(a\sin(b\theta+c)+d\), amplitude |a|, midline d and period \(2\pi/|b|\). Source equations can be equivalent: \(-\cos\theta=\sin(\theta-\pi/2)\), and \(\sin(2\theta)\) has period π.

translations.title: Features of Trigonometric Graphs (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Use the horizontal scale factor in a trigonometric equation to determine its repeat time. This matters in a real windmill: blade length controls amplitude, tower height controls the midline, and rotation speed controls period. Compare different sine graphs and explain how a multiplication on the input can increase or decrease the time for one complete cycle. Interpret a period in seconds or minutes, not merely as a number of radians.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: The function \(f(t)=A\sin(\omega t)+k\), \(\omega\ne0\), repeats when the angle \(\omega t\) increases or decreases by \(2\pi\), so its positive fundamental period is \(P=2\pi/|\omega|\). In the source \(f(t)=4\sin(2\pi t/3)+15\), t in seconds, the amplitude is 4 feet, midline 15 feet and period 3 seconds. The windmill blade is 4 feet long, its center is 15 feet above ground, and its tip ranges from 11 to 19 feet. In contrast \(y=\sin(\pi\theta)\) has period 2, \(y=\sin\theta\) period 2π, and \(y=\sin(\theta/2)\) period 4π.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source windmill: \(f(t)=4\sin(2\pi t/3)+15\) gives f(0)=15, f(0.75)=19, f(1.5)=15, f(2.25)=11 and f(3)=15 feet. The path is one cycle of length 3 seconds; the radius is 4 feet and tower-center height is 15. Example 2 — compare periods: \(g(\theta)=\sin(\pi\theta)\) repeats after 2 input units because \(\pi(\theta+2)=\pi\theta+2\pi\). \(h(\theta)=\sin(\theta/2)\) repeats only after 4π radians of input, twice as slowly as \(\sin\theta\). A graph's horizontal axis must show what its input represents.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the coefficient \(\omega\) multiplying the time or radian input. 2. Find the change in input that makes its inner angle differ by 2π. 3. Calculate period \(P=2\pi/|\omega|\), preserving correct time units. 4. Read amplitude |A| and midline k separately. 5. Evaluate the model at quarter-period intervals to verify one entire cycle. 6. Explain how changing \(\omega\), A or k affects rotation speed, blade radius or center height without mixing the transformations.
translations.commonMistakes: For the source function, 3 is the period in SECONDS; 2π/3 is an angular coefficient in radians per second, not the period. An amplitude of 4 does not mean a 4-second period. The graph (sin(	heta/2)) has a LONGER period than (sin	heta), not a shorter one. Always distinguish the input's physical unit from the angle used inside sine.
translations.quickSummary: A sinusoid \(A\sin(\omega t)+k\) has period \(2\pi/|\omega|\), amplitude |A| and midline k. The source windmill \(4\sin(2\pi t/3)+15\) completes one rotation in 3 seconds and ranges 11–19 feet.

translations.title: Comparing Transformations
translations.explanation: Read how a source graph was changed and ask for missing information before creating its new equation. Function transformations may happen in a particular order: reflect, translate or scale, and each changes the resulting expression. This first-edition information-gap lesson is not a single numerical exercise; justify why the data needed include original function, horizontal scale, shift, vertical scale and offset. A mathematical example shows how to reconstruct a trig transformation once those quantities are supplied.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a base function f, a transformed expression can be written \(g(x)=a f(bx-h)+k\). Its horizontal shift is \(h/b\) if b≠0, not h in general; horizontal scale factor is \(1/|b|\), and a negative b reflects the input direction. If f=cos, amplitude |a| and midline k, period \(2\pi/|b|\) for nonzero a,b. Transformations in different orders can produce different equations: reflect f across x-axis, shift it one LEFT, and three DOWN gives \(g(x)=-f(x+1)-3\), for example.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source sequence across function families: Let \(h(x)=x^2-4\). Reflect over the x-axis to get \(4-x^2\); shift one left to get \(4-(x+1)^2\); shift three down to get \(H(x)=1-(x+1)^2\), which has vertex (−1,1). The same operations on \(f(x)=\cos x\) give \(F(x)=-\cos(x+1)-3\), amplitude 1 and midline −3. Example 2 — transform cosine using a data card: Suppose a cosine graph has amplitude 2, midline 3, period 4π and its maximum occurs at input π/4. One valid equation is \(g(x)=2\cos((x-\pi/4)/2)+3\), since b=1/2 gives period 4π and the cosine input is zero at x=π/4. Its range is [1,5]. A graph matching those conditions is also described by many equations with coterminal phase shifts.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify which original function and transformations are known and which are missing. 2. Ask for the scale factors, horizontal shift and vertical offset needed to determine the new graph. 3. Apply the operations in the stated sequence, writing a new expression after each one. 4. If starting from \(a\cos(bx-h)+k\), translate the phase properly as h/b and period \(2\pi/|b|\). 5. Verify a maximum/minimum input and the resulting range. 6. Explain your reasoning and any nonuniqueness; information-gap communication needs a rubric, not only string equality.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not assume (-f(x+1)-3) equals (f(-x+1)-3): input reflection differs from output reflection. When (b=1/2), the shift in (acos(bx-h)) is 2h, not h. A single graph can have many equivalent trig equations due to periodicity, so one matching written expression is not the only valid answer. Do not auto-grade a partner's explanation as one number.
translations.quickSummary: A transformation can be expressed as \(g(x)=a f(bx-h)+k\). Read amplitude, midline and period from the trig case, ask for any missing information, and apply transformations in the correct order.

translations.title: Modeling Circular Motion
translations.explanation: Trigonometric functions model a carousel rider's position over repeated revolutions. The horizontal and vertical coordinates each follow sine or cosine, but their phase differs depending on where the rider begins. Use the radius, period and direction to find an angular rate, choose the correct starting angle and calculate arc distance. Unlike a model of height above ground, this carousel model initially uses coordinates relative to its center, so the midlines are zero.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For counterclockwise circular motion with radius r, angular speed \(\omega=2\pi/P\) radians per second and starting angle \(\phi\), the coordinates are \(x(t)=r\cos(\omega t+\phi)\), \(y(t)=r\sin(\omega t+\phi)\). In the source carousel, radius=20 feet, period P=10 seconds and Jada starts at (20,0), so \(J(t)=(20\cos(\pi t/5),20\sin(\pi t/5))\). Noah starts at (0,20), so \(N(t)=(20\cos(\pi/2+\pi t/5),20\sin(\pi/2+\pi t/5))\). Arc distance for angle θ is \(s=r\theta\), with θ in radians; one full ride revolution travels 40π feet.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — carousel arcs: Jada at angle 0 reaches Noah's initial position (angle π/2) after a quarter revolution, so arc distance is \(20(\pi/2)=10\pi\) feet, and time is \(10/4=2.5\) seconds. Starting from Jada's initial angle, Elena begins \( \pi/2+2\pi/3=7\pi/6\) counterclockwise away, so Jada's forward arc to Elena's initial position is \(20(7\pi/6)=70\pi/3\) feet. Example 2 — ride duration: 3.25 minutes is 195 seconds, or 19.5 turns at 10 seconds per turn. Jada has traversed \(19.5\cdot40\pi=780\pi\) feet. Elena finishes at the point opposite her start after half a turn beyond 19 full turns. Example 3 — graph relationship: \(\sin(\pi/2+x)=\cos x\), so Noah's vertical coordinate equals Jada's horizontal coordinate at the same angle.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Convert the period to angular speed \(\omega=2\pi/P\). 2. Identify the initial position on the circle and set its starting phase. 3. Write x(t) and y(t) with a radius outside the trig function. 4. For a quarter-circle from Jada to Noah, calculate θ=π/2, distance rθ=10π and time P/4=2.5 s. 5. Convert the total ride duration into seconds and number of turns. 6. Check the final point by the leftover partial turn and distinguish arc distance traveled from straight-line displacement.
translations.commonMistakes: The quarter-carousel distance is 10π feet, not 10 feet or the chord length 20√2 feet. A 195-second ride at 10 seconds per revolution is 19.5 turns, not 19.5 radians. Sine and cosine describe relative coordinates, not a rider's height above the floor without a separate vertical reference. Distance traveled does not reset after each revolution even though position does.
translations.quickSummary: For a 20-foot-radius carousel rotating every 10 seconds, \(J(t)=(20\cos(\pi t/5),20\sin(\pi t/5))\). Jada reaches Noah's starting point in 2.5 seconds, traveling a circular arc of 10π feet.

translations.title: Beyond Circles
translations.explanation: Periodic models also describe noncircular data, such as the fraction of the Moon's illuminated face visible at a particular time. Use a monthly data table to estimate a midline, amplitude, period and horizontal shift before constructing a cosine model. The measured data are approximately rather than perfectly sinusoidal, and one month alone cannot determine a unique precise astronomical period; check the proposed model against several days and explain uncertainty before predicting later dates.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a modeled fraction \(M(d)=a\cos(2\pi(d-h)/P)+k\), physical outputs must stay within [0,1]. When observed extremes are approximately 0 and 1, a reasonable midline is 0.5 and amplitude 0.5. In the first-edition January 2018 table, visible fraction is 1 on day 2, 0 on day 17 and 1 on day 31, suggesting a cycle of about 29 days from peak to peak. A plausible initial model is \(M(d)=0.5+0.5\cos(2\pi(d-2)/29)\). This is not a claim that the actual lunar cycle is precisely 29 days, and it does not capture every observed fraction.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — source Moon data: On day 2 the observed illuminated fraction is 1.00, on day 17 it is 0.00, and day 31 is 1.00. With estimated period 29 days and peak at day 2, \(M(2)=1\), \(M(16.5)=0\) and \(M(31)=1\). On day 10 the model predicts \(0.5+0.5\cos(16\pi/29)\approx0.419\), while the source table reports 0.37. The mismatch is evidence that this is an approximation.

Example 2 — original tide application: A simplified tide oscillation of three-foot amplitude and twelve-hour period can be \(T(h)=3\sin(2\pi(h-1)/12)\) feet relative to a chosen zero level, with midline 0. It repeats each 12 hours even if the real tide heights or timing fluctuate. It is not valid to infer one universal ocean tide equation from a short graph.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Record the source table's maximum and minimum illuminated fractions and the days they occur. 2. Compute midline=(max+min)/2≈0.5 and amplitude=(max−min)/2≈0.5. 3. Estimate a peak-to-peak interval, noting that one month is insufficient for an exact period. 4. Choose cosine shifted to a near-full moon: \(M(d)=0.5+0.5\cos(2\pi(d-2)/29)\). 5. Evaluate the model at known dates and compare with observations. 6. Use the model for tentative predictions only, naming phase error, daily observation rounding and real astronomical irregularities.
translations.commonMistakes: A 29-day fitted period is an estimate, not proof of the exact astronomical lunar period. The physical visible fraction cannot be below zero or above one. A day of zero illumination fraction and a peak date are only approximate when observations are rounded. A sinusoidal curve that nearly fits the table is not identical to the real Moon's orbit; keep prediction uncertainty explicit.
translations.quickSummary: A fitted Moon model may use midline 0.5, amplitude 0.5, period about 29 days and peak near January 2. A model \(M(d)=0.5+0.5\cos(2\pi(d-2)/29)\) matches the extremes approximately, but other days reveal residual error.

translations.title: Being Skeptical
translations.explanation: Statistical claims depend on how information was collected, not just on the percentages in a headline. A survey asks questions, an observational study records outcomes without assigning a treatment, and an experiment deliberately imposes a treatment or condition. Before accepting a claim, identify the population and sample, ask how participants were selected, assess whether wording and nonresponse can bias results, and decide whether the study supports association or a causal conclusion.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A population is the full group about which a conclusion is desired, while a sample is the observed subset. A survey collects responses; an observational study observes existing behavior or conditions; an experimental study changes a treatment to compare outcomes. Random selection supports generalization to the sampled population when the selection frame and response process are adequate. Random assignment to treatments supports causal comparison by reducing systematic confounding, though execution and measurement still matter. Association by itself is not proof of causation. A percent without sample size, denominator and design cannot be used to evaluate precision or representativeness.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source headline: “80% of Dentists Recommend Acme Toothpaste” does not establish how many dentists were approached, how the recommendation was defined, whether respondents were representative, or who paid for the survey. If only 8 of 10 dentists answer positively, the observed proportion is indeed 80%, but it cannot be presented as a well-established rate among all dentists without further evidence. Example 2 — source absences: Randomly select 300 students across a district and mail questions about missed days. This is a survey with a random invitation, but nonresponse and inaccurate parent recall may bias estimates. Taking absence records from ONE selected elementary school is observational administrative data, but it may not represent the entire district. Example 3: Scientists assign equal sweetener concentrations to bowls and count fly visits; as a controlled intervention it can form an experiment, but bowl location and unequal exposure can still confound results.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the statement or graph carefully, including what the axes measure and any truncated time range. 2. State the population and observed sample; for headlines ask for sample size and selection method. 3. Classify the investigation as survey, observation or experiment by HOW data are generated. 4. Check randomness of selection separately from randomness of treatment assignment. 5. Identify nonresponse, confounders, vague wording or limited observation windows. 6. Write a qualified conclusion at the level of evidence supported rather than automatically inferring causation.
translations.commonMistakes: A random mailing list does not guarantee random RESPONSES. One school's records cannot automatically estimate districtwide patterns. Eight out of ten is 80%, but the exact percentage alone says little about the margin of error. Two correlated variables need not cause each other. A deliberately misleading graph axis or headline can omit context even if all shown numerical values are true.
translations.quickSummary: Distinguish surveys, observational studies and experiments by how data are collected. Evaluate claims using population, sampling, response, design, confounding and correct causal language; percentages alone do not prove reliability.

translations.title: Study Types
translations.explanation: Choose a study design that answers a statistical question and be clear about what the design can establish. Asking people's preferences is well suited to a survey; describing naturally occurring differences generally calls for an observational study; testing a controllable intervention for a causal effect generally calls for an experiment with fair assignment. Some proposed interventions are unsafe or unethical, so observation is preferable even if it limits causal conclusions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A statistical question anticipates variation across units or observations. Surveys estimate opinions or self-reports; observational studies compare conditions without assigning them; randomized experiments compare deliberately assigned treatments. Confounding occurs when another variable is associated with both the explanatory factor and the outcome. Random selection and random assignment answer different design problems. Without treatment assignment, measured association—such as between hours of television and energy—does not uniquely identify a causal mechanism. Study interpretation also depends on whether measurements are valid and groups are representative.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source question matching: “What sport do students at this school prefer?” is an opinion question suited to a representative survey. “Do smokers have more car accidents than nonsmokers?” is suited to an observational study; it would be unethical to assign smoking as a treatment. “Does chewing gum while studying and testing change scores?” might be evaluated with a randomized experiment when permitted, with equal testing conditions except for the treatment. Example 2 — source television: A survey of 1,000 people aged 20–30 finds a lower reported evening energy among those watching at least two hours of TV. That is an association from self-reported data; sleep patterns, jobs or health might explain some of the difference. A randomized and appropriately approved TV-time intervention with a pre-specified outcome would better test causality, but its results may still be limited to the participating population.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the statistical question, outcome and possible explanatory variable. 2. Check whether the question is about preference, naturally occurring association or an intervention's effect. 3. Choose a survey, observational study or randomized experiment accordingly. 4. State who should be sampled and how measurements will be made. 5. For experiments, assign eligible participants at random while keeping other conditions comparable. 6. Explain what conclusion would be defensible and identify important ethical or practical limitations.
translations.commonMistakes: A survey asking about TV habits is not automatically a randomized EXPERIMENT merely because 1,000 people were asked. Confounding can make two groups differ for reasons other than TV. Never randomly assign a harmful activity such as smoking in an experiment. A numerical mean difference does not by itself prove causation, even with a large sample.
translations.quickSummary: Study design follows the question: surveys for reported preferences, observations for existing conditions, randomized experiments for appropriate interventions. The television-energy source provides association, not automatically a causal effect.

translations.title: Randomness in Groups
translations.explanation: Random selection and random assignment protect different parts of statistical reasoning. Selecting participants at random from a population can reduce selection bias, while assigning participants at random to treatment groups can reduce pre-existing differences between those groups. A sample is still a subset of the population; even perfectly randomized assignments do not guarantee the study's volunteers represent everyone. Simulations help reveal how random selection differs from convenience sampling.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: In a simple random sample of size n, every possible n-person subset of a finite sampling frame has equal selection probability. In the simpler source lottery description, each listed individual has equal probability of selection, but equal marginal probabilities alone do not guarantee every subset is equally likely. A randomized experiment assigns treatments with a chance mechanism, keeping assignment independent of known traits. This strengthens causal comparison within the recruited sample; generalizing to the entire population additionally requires a suitable sampling frame, nonresponse control and study context. Random assignment does not mean the realized groups must be exactly equal in every characteristic.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source governor survey: A reporter asks 100 people about a governor. Choosing only politically interested people at the capital introduces selection bias. Choosing 100 names randomly from a statewide frame is preferable for estimating statewide opinion, provided the frame and responses are reliable. Taking 50 known supporters and 50 nonsupporters may deliberately distort the true population proportions. Example 2 — source music/memory experiment: A study recruits 200 volunteers and compares memory after hip-hop versus orchestral music. Randomly drawing 100 names into the hip-hop treatment and assigning the other 100 to orchestral music is preferable to grouping by favorite genre or age. This assignment makes the treatment groups more comparable, but the 200 volunteers need not represent all students or adults. Example 3 — synthetic simulation: From numbered names 1–100, a random draw of 10 distinct labels estimates a population average; repeated random draws give different means despite identical selection rules.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Name the target population and the people who can actually be selected. 2. Inspect a proposed sample-selection method for convenience or systematic inclusion bias. 3. Choose a fair random mechanism with a defined sampling frame. 4. For an experiment, separately assign sampled or recruited volunteers randomly into treatment groups. 5. Describe which comparisons are causal within the participants and which generalizations require representative sampling. 6. Repeat a simulation and explain why outcomes vary while the fairness of the design is maintained.
translations.commonMistakes: Random selection is NOT the same as random assignment. A study may randomize treatments among volunteers but still fail to represent the population. One individual having an equal selection probability does not alone prove every sample subset is equally likely. Random groups may differ by chance; balance is expected in aggregate but not exact for every assignment.
translations.quickSummary: Use random selection to support population inference and random treatment assignment to support causal comparison. The source's random 100-of-200 music-group assignment reduces systematic confounding, but volunteers may not represent everyone.

translations.title: Describing Distributions
translations.explanation: Describe a distribution through shape, center and spread rather than a single average. Histograms and dot plots of repeated glass-crack lengths can show clusters, skewness, several modes or outliers. The mean measures an arithmetic center; the median is the middle ordered value; standard deviation measures how widely values vary about the mean. Compare two distributions using the same horizontal units and scale, and explain when an unusual outlier makes the mean less representative.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For observations \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), mean \(\bar x=\sum x_i/n\). The median is the middle value of sorted data or the average of two central values when n is even. Population standard deviation is \(\sigma=\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\mu)^2/N}\); sample standard deviation is \(s=\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2/(n-1)}\) for n>1. They are not the same denominator, so state which is being used. A symmetric distribution has balanced sides, skewness indicates a longer tail, bimodal indicates two prominent peaks, and a bell-shaped distribution has one roughly symmetric central peak. Standard deviation is nonnegative and uses the same measurement units as the observations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — original teaching data inspired by source glass-crack measurement: In millimeters, lengths 8,9,9,10,14 have mean \(50/5=10\) mm and median 9 mm; the 14-mm observation creates a right-side tail. The population variance is \((4+1+1+0+16)/5=22/5=4.4\) mm², so population standard deviation is \(\sqrt{4.4}\approx2.098\) mm. The sample standard deviation would be \(\sqrt{22/4}\approx2.345\) mm. Example 2 — compare spread: Data sets A={8,9,10} and B={2,9,16} both have mean 9, but B has far larger spread. For population standard deviation, A has \(\sqrt{2/3}\) while B has \(\sqrt{98/3}\), confirming that identical means do not imply identical variability. These numerical lists are Edulytiks examples, not transcribed publisher glass samples.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the dot plot or histogram's horizontal variable, vertical counts and bin boundaries. 2. Describe number of modes, symmetry/skewness and any outliers. 3. Compute mean from the original values when available and median from their sorted order. 4. Find deviations from the mean, square them and average with the correct population/sample denominator. 5. Take the square root to obtain standard deviation in original measurement units. 6. Compare both center and spread and qualify any conclusion when only binned counts are provided.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not determine an exact mean from a coarse histogram without assumptions about within-bin values. The standard deviation is not measured in squared units—that is the variance. Use n−1 for sample standard deviation when estimating a population variability from a sample and n for a defined population set. A bell-shaped distribution need only be approximately normal; skewed or bimodal data do not fit one bell well.
translations.quickSummary: Compare distributions by shape, center and spread. Mean and median describe central tendency; standard deviation quantifies variability around the mean and requires correct sample/population denominator and original measurement units.

translations.title: Normal Distributions
translations.explanation: The first-edition lesson compares body-temperature histograms for groups of 500 healthy people and collects class handspans for a piano-key reach question. Decide whether a distribution is approximately unimodal, symmetric, and bell-shaped rather than assuming that every histogram is normal. A normal curve is a mathematical probability model, not a literal picture of all observed histograms. For the model, its mean locates the center and its standard deviation controls width. A relative-frequency histogram reports the proportion of observations in each interval, which differs from raw counts. This lesson introduces those ideas before calculating detailed areas in subsequent lessons.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Relative frequency for an interval is the count in that bin divided by the total number of observations; for 500 people, a bin containing 75 people has relative frequency 75/500=0.15. For equal-width bins, the heights of a relative-frequency histogram sum to 1; when bin widths differ, the histogram must be interpreted carefully because areas, not arbitrary heights, represent comparable proportions in a density display. A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean μ, has a single bell-shaped peak, total area under the density curve 1, and a horizontal asymptote at y=0. Its positive standard deviation σ controls spread; larger σ at fixed μ creates a lower, wider peak. Real samples may be approximately rather than exactly normal.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — body temperature: In a group of 500 people, 65 readings fall in one half-degree interval. Its relative frequency is 65/500=0.13 (13%). If two adjacent equal-width bins contain 65 and 85 people, their combined relative frequency is (65+85)/500=0.30. A symmetric-looking center is supporting evidence for a normal model, but obvious separated peaks or strong skew argue against it. Example 2 — piano reach: In a class of 25, suppose handspans are grouped into bins with counts 3, 7, 10, 5. Relative frequencies are 0.12, 0.28, 0.40, 0.20, which sum to 1. If the first three bins contain handspans below 21.5 cm, then 5/25=20% reach the 21.5-cm span, provided the fourth bin starts at or above that cutoff. These counts are an original Edulytiks demonstration, NOT the publisher's measured class data. Example 3 — model shape: Curves with μ=10 and σ=1 or σ=2 are centered at 10; the second is more spread out, not shifted to a new mean.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Inspect axes: identify temperature or handspan, units and whether bars show counts or relative frequencies. 2. For each class, count observations and divide each bin count by the sample total to get relative frequency. 3. Check that equal-width relative frequencies sum to 1, and do not confuse a bin's proportion with a continuous curve's point height. 4. Describe shape, center and spread; look for approximate symmetry, a single peak, skew and outliers. 5. Compare a proposed normal curve with the data, naming its mean μ and standard deviation σ and stating why its fit is approximate. 6. For the 21.5-cm piano threshold, count observations whose measured handspans meet or exceed the cutoff and divide by the class total; do not infer counts from a smooth fitted model without an area calculation.
translations.commonMistakes: A bell-shaped histogram is not proof that observations were generated by an exactly normal distribution. The height of a normal density at a point is not the probability of that exact value; probabilities are areas over intervals. Divide class bin counts by total observations to obtain relative frequencies, not by the number of bins. A different mean translates a normal curve horizontally; a larger standard deviation spreads it without changing its mean. The 21.5-cm piano threshold is a length, not the number of keys.
translations.quickSummary: Use relative frequencies to compare histograms fairly and check whether observations are roughly unimodal, symmetric and bell-shaped. A normal curve is a continuous probability model with total area 1, center μ and spread σ; it may approximate real temperature or handspan data but does not automatically describe every sample.

translations.title: Areas in Histograms
translations.explanation: Area provides the bridge from a histogram to a probability model. The first-edition lesson starts with a piecewise straight-edged bell-shaped figure: find the area shaded between x=1 and x=2 and divide by the TOTAL area under the same figure. In a relative-frequency display, a shaded interval represents the proportion of observations in that interval. The lesson then uses a set of 200 short-story word counts with mean 2,600 words and standard deviation 400 to explore intervals described relative to the mean. Distinguish exact geometric area from a normal-model estimate.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: The area of a trapezoid of width w and endpoint heights h1 and h2 is w(h1+h2)/2; rectangles contribute width times height. The area proportion is selected area divided by total nonnegative area, not selected height divided by maximum height. A continuous probability density has total area 1; a frequency histogram requires division by its total area before interpreting arbitrary geometric areas as proportions. A normal model has roughly 68% within μ±σ and 95% within μ±2σ, with percentages approximate for approximately normal empirical data. If μ=2600 and σ=400 words, μ±σ is 2200–3000 words and μ±2σ is 1800–3400 words.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — original source's piecewise curve has heights 0,1,3,4,4,3,1,0 at integer x=0,...,7. Its seven unit-width trapezoids have areas 0.5,2,3.5,4,3.5,2,0.5, totaling 16 square coordinate units. The shaded strip from x=1 to x=2 has area (1+3)/2=2; its proportion of the total is 2/16=1/8 or 12.5%. Example 2 — source story submissions: In a collection of 200 stories modeled as approximately normal with mean 2600 and SD 400 words, the one-SD interval is 2200 to 3000 words. About 68%, or approximately 136 stories, would be expected inside that interval under the normal approximation; this is not an exact observed count. At 200 words per page, the mean length corresponds to about 13 pages, subject to layout and rounding.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read x-coordinates and heights from the source polygon rather than assuming the maximum bar height is a probability. 2. Split the region into unit-width trapezoids. 3. Sum all seven trapezoid areas to obtain 16. 4. Compute the shaded trapezoid as (1+3)/2=2. 5. Divide shaded area by total area to report 1/8=12.5%. 6. For story lengths, mark μ=2600 and one/two SD boundaries 2200,3000 and 1800,3400, then use approximate normal coverage only if the data shape justifies that model.
translations.commonMistakes: The unnormalized source graph has total area 16, not 1; do not call its shaded area 2 a probability. If raw bar heights are frequencies, divide counts by total observations to get relative frequencies. For normal-model statements, 'about 68%' is approximate; a real dataset of 200 stories is not guaranteed to contain exactly 136 in the interval. Units for story lengths are words; pages require converting with the given words-per-page assumption.
translations.quickSummary: For a nonnegative curve or histogram, proportion is shaded area divided by total area. The first-edition polygon's x=1 to 2 strip has area 2 of total 16 (12.5%). For approximately normal story lengths μ=2600, σ=400, the one-SD interval is 2200–3000 words.

translations.title: Areas under a Normal Curve
translations.explanation: The area under a normal curve represents the proportion of values in a range. The publisher gives a curve with mean 40 and standard deviation 2, along with cumulative area 0.3085 to the left of 39 and 0.9332 to the left of 43. Use these known areas, symmetry and complement reasoning to answer questions without recalculating every area. In the same lesson, compare LED and incandescent bulb lifespans using standardized distances from their distinct means and standard deviations.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A normal density has total area 1 and symmetry about μ, so P(X<μ)=0.5. For cumulative area F(a)=P(X≤a), the proportion between a and b is F(b)−F(a), and the right-tail proportion above a is 1−F(a). The z-score z=(x−μ)/σ, for σ>0, measures distance from the mean in SD units. Comparable standardized positions have identical ideal normal proportions even when the underlying units and distributions have different means. A normal random variable is continuous, so including or excluding a single endpoint does not change the probability.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — given source areas for μ=40, σ=2: P(X>39)=1−0.3085=0.6915. P(39<X<43)=0.9332−0.3085=0.6247. Symmetry yields P(X<40)=0.5, while P(39<X<40)=0.5−0.3085=0.1915. Example 2 — light bulbs: LED lifespan μ=2300 days, σ=230; incandescent μ=100 days, σ=10. The cutoffs 2070 LED days and 90 incandescent days each have z=−1; both lower-tail model areas are approximately 0.1587. Above 2530 LED days or 110 incandescent days is also about 0.1587; between ±1 SD is about 0.6827. These are model expectations, not individual product guarantees.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the curve mean, SD and any PROVIDED cumulative areas. 2. Sketch the target interval and mark its two endpoints. 3. Use a complement to find a right tail, or subtract left cumulative areas to find a bounded interval. 4. Check that probabilities lie between 0 and 1 and that symmetry yields 0.5 at the mean. 5. For bulb comparisons compute z=(cutoff−μ)/σ separately for each type. 6. Interpret the resulting common normal area in the original units (days) and say it is a model-based approximate proportion.
translations.commonMistakes: Area to the left of 39 (0.3085) is not the right-side area; its complement is 0.6915. Subtract cumulative areas in the correct order: larger cutoff F(b) minus smaller cutoff F(a). Don't compare 2070 and 90 days directly without recognizing different bulb populations; both are one SD below their own means. Never describe an approximate normal-model expectation as an exact percentage of observed bulbs.
translations.quickSummary: For a normal model, bounded-interval area is F(b)−F(a) and a right-tail area is 1−F(a). With F(39)=0.3085 and F(43)=0.9332, area between them is 0.6247. One SD below a mean corresponds to roughly 15.87% below that cutoff.
