translations.title: Not Always Ideal
translations.explanation: Random data are rarely identical to their expected percentages. This lesson tests the plausibility of a probability model using repeated trials, beginning with three students each shooting 100 free throws at a hypothesized 60% success chance. Compare observed counts with typical variation rather than expecting exactly 60 makes every time. Next use repeated sets of 20 coin flips to understand how unexpectedly low numbers of heads can occur by chance and when they warrant more evidence about fairness.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For n independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability p, the count X has mean np and standard deviation sqrt(np(1−p)). This binomial calculation is an original Edulytiks extension; the source emphasizes classroom simulation and argument. Under p=0.6, n=100, the expected count is 60 and SD=sqrt(24)≈4.90, making 63 near expectation but 75 and 35 unusually far. For a fair coin flipped 20 times, E(heads)=10 and SD=sqrt(5)≈2.24; a count of two heads is POSSIBLE but unlikely. Evidence of an unlikely outcome calls for replication and careful evaluation, not categorical proof that a coin is unfair.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — first-edition free throws: Lin makes 63/100=63%, Kiran 75%, and Diego 35%, compared with a proposed 60% shot probability. Relative to expected count 60, differences in SD units are 3/√24≈0.61, 15/√24≈3.06 and −25/√24≈−5.10. Lin's count is unsurprising under the model; Kiran's and Diego's warrant questioning whether all three share the same ability. Example 2 — repeated 20-flip experiments: The chance of two or fewer heads in 20 fair independent flips is [C(20,0)+C(20,1)+C(20,2)]/2^20=(1+20+190)/1,048,576≈0.000201. This probability is small, NOT zero; a single such result should prompt checking the coin and repeating experiments. Classroom dot plots will vary between trials.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define the proposed probabilistic model and its assumptions of independence and fixed p. 2. Calculate the expected count np and, if useful, a model SD. 3. Convert observed totals into proportions (63/100, 75/100, 35/100). 4. Compare differences to simulated or theoretical variation, not only to the expectation. 5. For coin trials, run several independent sets of 20 flips and draw a dot plot of head counts. 6. If an outcome looks unusual, assess how many simulated values are as or more extreme and describe what additional evidence would distinguish natural randomness from a flawed model.
translations.commonMistakes: A 60% shot chance does not force exactly 60 successes in 100 attempts. A very unlikely event can still occur under a fair model; one unusual sample does not prove cheating or bias. The binomial SD formula assumes independent identical success probabilities, which real players' shots may violate. Do not conflate expected variation with evidence that every student's true shooting probability equals 0.6.
translations.quickSummary: Compare observed data to expected sampling variability. Under 60%-success independent shots, expected makes from 100 attempts equal 60, with SD near 4.9; results 75 and 35 are unusual. Two or fewer heads in 20 fair flips is possible but rare (~0.0201%).

translations.title: Variability in Samples
translations.explanation: Different random samples from the same population give different sample means and proportions. Use the first-edition collection of 36 coins to draw small samples of five and compare estimated mean mint years and the proportions stamped D (Denver). Then interpret a histogram made from many volunteers' campaign-support samples. A sampling estimate should be reported with a plausible uncertainty interval; the width depends on sample size, selection process and variation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For a sample of n numerical observations, sample mean is their sum divided by n; for a categorical property, sample proportion p-hat is its count divided by n. Random selection does not guarantee identical statistics across repeated samples, but it helps reduce systematic selection bias when the frame is valid. A source campaign histogram of 30 random-sample proportions has mean 0.55 and SD 0.15; about two SDs from the center gives an exploratory span 0.25 to 0.85. This is a descriptive interval for the observed DISTRIBUTION OF SAMPLE STATISTICS, not an automatically certified 95% confidence interval for a population parameter. The source introduces margin of error conceptually; formal inference needs sampling-design and coverage assumptions.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — synthetic five-coin sample: Coin mint years 1999, 2000, 2002, 2004, 2005 have mean (1999+2000+2002+2004+2005)/5=2002.0. If 2 of these 5 were minted in Denver, p-hat=2/5=0.40. A second five-coin sample can easily give different results although both came from the same jar; these coin values are Edulytiks examples, not asserted source-jar measurements. Example 2 — source campaign simulation: Thirty samples of ten voters each give sample-proportion center 0.55 and SD 0.15. A band within two SDs is 0.55±2(0.15)=[0.25,0.85]. The band describes typical sampled estimates under an approximately bell-shaped distribution; it does not mean the candidate's true support must be between 25% and 85% with 95% confidence based on this single summary.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Clarify whether the target is a population mean year or a population proportion minted in Denver. 2. Select a sample of coin labels using an actual chance process rather than favorites. 3. Average the five years for a sample mean. 4. Divide Denver counts by five to obtain a proportion. 5. Repeat samples and build histograms of estimates to inspect variability. 6. From the campaign distribution center 0.55 and SD 0.15, compute illustrative center ±2 SD values, then explain the assumptions and why a formal margin-of-error statement cannot be inferred from one display without sampling-method details.
translations.commonMistakes: One sample does not identify a population statistic exactly; another random sample can give a different mean or proportion. A proportion must be between 0 and 1, not the number of Denver-marked coins by itself. The source's SD=0.15 describes the distribution of SAMPLE proportions, not the SD of all individual voter choices. A two-SD band is not automatically a guaranteed or formally calibrated population confidence interval; consider model assumptions and how data were collected.
translations.quickSummary: Use sample means and proportions to estimate population characteristics, and examine many random samples to judge variability. For the first-edition campaign sample-proportion distribution μ≈0.55, SD≈0.15, the exploratory ±2-SD range is 0.25–0.85, not a guaranteed population interval.

translations.title: Estimating Proportions from Samples
translations.explanation: A sample proportion estimates the corresponding proportion in a population, but that estimate varies from one random sample to another. The source begins by calculating blue-chip proportions, then uses paper slips marked Pass and Fail to explore the sampling variability of pass rates. Identify the population, sample design, sample size, successful count and experimental spread before reporting a margin of error. A simulated margin is empirical evidence conditional on the simulation's assumptions, not proof that the population parameter equals the point estimate.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For x successes in n observations, p-hat=x/n with 0≤p-hat≤1. The sample contains 20 marked slips, 14 Pass and 6 Fail, so the known illustrative bag population proportion is 14/20=0.70. For an independent random sample with replacement of size n, the approximate standard error for a sample proportion is sqrt(p(1−p)/n); a commonly used approximate 95% half-width is 1.96 times an estimated standard error, when a normal approximation is appropriate. The source focuses on the width of many simulated proportions, not on claiming a universally valid 95% interval. Sampling without replacement from only 20 slips needs finite-population considerations and may not follow the replacement formula.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source mental proportions: 17 blue of 50 chips is 17/50=0.34, 28 of 50 is 0.56, 17 of 20 is 0.85, and 21 of 60 is 0.35. Express each as a fraction or percentage, not as the number of blue chips. Example 2 — source Pass/Fail bag: With 14 Pass and 6 Fail slips in a 20-slip bag, the bag's pass fraction is 0.70. If a sample of 10 draws with replacement yields 8 Pass results, p-hat=0.80; if another sample gives 6 Pass, p-hat=0.60. The two sample estimates differ even though the bag proportion is unchanged. Original Edulytiks extension: using p=0.7 and n=100 independent WITH-REPLACEMENT draws, standard error is sqrt(0.21/100)≈0.04583 and a normal two-SD half-width is about 0.0917. Never apply that figure automatically to a source finite-bag draw without checking its selection method.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the event and the number of observations in the sample. 2. Divide its success count by sample size to find p-hat, checking it lies in [0,1]. 3. Repeat the stated random selection process several times using the same population or simulation model. 4. Plot the distribution of sample proportions and describe its center/spread. 5. Estimate a margin of error from the simulated distribution under a stated coverage convention, or use an appropriate theory only when its sampling assumptions are met. 6. Report the estimate plus/minus the contextual margin with units in percentage points and identify any selection/nonresponse limitations.
translations.commonMistakes: A sample with 8 of 10 successes estimates 80%; it does not prove the entire population is 80% successful. A margin of error is not the observed difference between two arbitrarily chosen sample proportions. Finite-population sampling without replacement differs from independent draws with replacement. An interval can extend outside [0,1] under naive normal formulas; then another statistical method may be required. Report percentage points for an absolute margin, not percent relative increase.
translations.quickSummary: The sample proportion is successes divided by the number sampled. Original chip proportions are 0.34, 0.56, 0.85 and 0.35; the source Pass/Fail bag has true 14/20=0.70. Simulated sample proportions vary and can support a qualified margin-of-error estimate.

translations.title: Reducing Margin of Error
translations.explanation: A larger random sample usually yields a more stable estimate of a population proportion than a small sample. Compare the source's repeated simulations about female leads in children's movies, then examine why the distribution of sample proportions becomes narrower as sample size increases. This lesson is about SAMPLING precision; collecting many systematically biased observations does not fix a flawed sampling frame or a leading question.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For approximately independent random observations and population proportion p, the standard error of p-hat is sqrt[p(1−p)/n]. A confidence half-width using the same method and coverage is approximately proportional to 1/sqrt(n). Quadrupling n approximately halves that half-width; doubling n reduces it by factor 1/sqrt2, not by one half. This describes expected precision across repeated samples, not the exact error of any one sample. Source classroom simulations may give different widths from this idealized formula. More observations cannot by themselves remove systematic bias, nonresponse or confounding.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — original Edulytiks illustration: Suppose the proportion of children's movies with female lead roles is about 0.4 and sampling can be treated as independent. At n=100, plug-in standard error sqrt(0.4·0.6/100)≈0.04899; a rough two-standard-error margin is 0.09798, or about 9.8 percentage points. At n=400, SE≈0.02449, and the two-SE margin≈0.04899, about 4.9 points. A fourfold sample increase halves the modeled margin. Example 2 — failure of scaling to cure bias: If all 400 movies come from one studio's catalog, a precise estimate for that catalog cannot automatically represent all children's movies regardless of small sampling error. This is a logical counterexample, not a claim about the publisher's actual sample.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Read the source table to identify the sampling method, movie counts and simulated sample-proportion distributions. 2. Compare their centers, spreads and potential outlying values. 3. Identify which samples are larger and whether their histograms look more concentrated. 4. Use approximate relationship MOE∝1/sqrt(n) to predict changes when n doubles or quadruples, explicitly stating model assumptions. 5. For a worked p=0.4, compute the SE at n=100 and 400 and compare. 6. Distinguish smaller random sampling variation from persistent systematic selection or response bias.
translations.commonMistakes: Four times as many observations does NOT reduce standard error to one fourth; it reduces it approximately to one half. A large sample does not automatically represent the intended population. A lower margin of error concerns uncertainty from sampling, not guaranteed closeness of every specific estimate. Do not compare two margins with different coverage or sampling methods as though sample size alone explains their difference.
translations.quickSummary: For comparable random sampling methods, the typical variability of a sample proportion shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(n). Quadrupling the sample size about halves the margin of error, but cannot correct a biased study design.

translations.title: Estimating a Population Mean
translations.explanation: Estimate a population MEAN rather than a population proportion. The first-edition lesson rolls a fair six-sided number cube 35 times per sample, then compares sample averages from many repetitions. Each set of 35 results varies; so does its sample mean. The center of the distribution of sample means should be close to the population mean, and its spread supports a qualified estimate with margin of error. The mean of a large collection of single-roll outcomes and the spread of 35-roll sample means are different quantities.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: The sample mean is x-bar=(x1+...+xn)/n. The population mean of a fair standard die is (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5. Its variance is (1²+...+6²)/6−3.5²=35/12, so population SD=sqrt(35/12)≈1.708. For n independent rolls, the standard deviation of the SAMPLE MEAN is σ/sqrt(n); for n=35 this equals sqrt((35/12)/35)=sqrt(1/12)≈0.288675. A rough 95% model interval for the sample mean's fluctuation around 3.5 is 3.5±1.96(0.288675), or approximately 2.934 to 4.066. This describes a MODEL for repeated fair-die samples, not an automatically valid confidence statement from an actual unspecified experiment.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — five toy die results, clearly an Edulytiks miniature example: 2,4,6,1,5 have sample mean 18/5=3.6. Another sample 1,1,2,4,4 has mean 12/5=2.4; both are possible even with a fair die. Example 2 — source 35-roll design: Across many repetitions of 35 fair independent rolls, sample means should cluster near 3.5 with theoretical SD ≈0.2887. A simulated set with sample mean 3.8 is about (3.8−3.5)/0.288675≈1.039 sampling SD above expectation, not evidence of an unfair die on its own. A mean outside the rough interval is possible, just less common under the stated model.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Define the population of possible die outcomes and verify the assumed fair distribution. 2. Roll 35 times and compute x-bar by summing outcomes and dividing by 35. 3. Repeat with a random process and graph the sample means, not the individual face outcomes. 4. Observe the center near 3.5 and estimate the SD of the sample-mean distribution. 5. Use an explicit margin convention with empirical or theoretical spread to report an interval. 6. Check units, sampling assumptions and whether the estimate concerns a population MEAN or an event PROPORTION.
translations.commonMistakes: The six faces of a fair die have equal probabilities; the 35-roll sample mean need not be exactly 3.5. The population SD ≈1.708 is NOT the SD of 35-roll sample means ≈0.289. A proportion formula sqrt[p(1−p)/n] is inappropriate for means of numbered outcomes. The approximate sampling interval is not a guarantee that every sample mean lies inside. Keep one sample's mean distinct from the average of many simulated means.
translations.quickSummary: Random sample means fluctuate around the population mean. For a fair die μ=3.5 and for 35 independent rolls the theoretical SD of the sample mean is sqrt(1/12)≈0.2887. Use repeated sample means and a stated margin convention to quantify uncertainty.

translations.title: Experimenting
translations.explanation: An experimental comparison uses RANDOM ASSIGNMENT to separate a treatment's effect from preexisting group differences. The first-edition lesson begins with two product-satisfaction dot plots and then creates a randomization distribution by pooling the observed scores, reassigning them to groups by chance, and recomputing the difference between means. The original statistic should be compared with that distribution, not only with the two raw sample averages. This reasoning differs from a survey of voluntary users, which cannot by itself establish a product's causal effect.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A treatment is the experimental condition intentionally changed between groups; random assignment makes confounding differences less systematic in expectation. Define a signed statistic, for example D=mean(A)−mean(B), and retain that sign throughout. Under a 'no treatment effect' randomization model, pool the outcomes, randomly reassign labels while preserving original group sizes, then calculate D for every simulated reshuffle. The randomization distribution shows which differences would be common or unusual if treatment labels did not influence outcomes. A two-sided randomization p-value is the fraction of equally likely reassignments (or simulated fraction) with |D_sim|≥|D_observed|, with finite-simulation limitations. Statistical significance is not a guarantee of clinical or practical importance.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source satisfaction dot plots: Product A ratings are 3,4,5,5,5, giving mean 22/5=4.4; Product B ratings are 2,3,4,4,5, giving mean 18/5=3.6. The observed mean difference A−B is 0.8 rating points. Because these groups were surveyed from existing users, the difference does NOT alone demonstrate that product A CAUSED higher satisfaction. Example 2 — original miniature randomization demonstration: Four observed outcomes are 1,2,3,4. Put two in group A, two in B. For observed A={1,2}, B={3,4}, D=−2. The six equally likely assignments of two to A give differences −2,−1,0,0,1,2. Two of six have |D|≥2; the exact two-sided randomization proportion is 1/3, not strong evidence against the no-effect assignment model.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. State the research question, assigned treatment and how participants entered the study. 2. Compute both group means and define the difference direction A−B. 3. Under the no-effect model pool the measured outcomes from BOTH groups. 4. Randomly reassign outcomes to groups of the same sizes or enumerate all assignments when small. 5. Recalculate the difference in means after each assignment and form a dot plot of those differences. 6. Count simulated differences at least as extreme as the observed |D|, report their proportion and discuss causal limitations, randomization and sampling uncertainty.
translations.commonMistakes: Surveying five product users in each group is not equivalent to randomly assigning the products. The mean difference direction must not switch from A−B to B−A midway. Pooling outcomes and resampling within each original group would test a different question from randomizing labels. A large-looking raw gap is not necessarily unusual under the randomization distribution, and a low p-value cannot prove a treatment is the unique cause.
translations.quickSummary: Use randomized group assignment, then compare the observed difference in group means with differences obtained by random reassignment under a no-effect model. The source survey averages 4.4 and 3.6 differ by 0.8, but causal conclusions require a genuine experimental design.

translations.title: Using Normal Distributions for Experiment Analysis
translations.explanation: Random assignment can create differences between groups even when a treatment has no effect. This lesson asks whether an observed experimental mean difference is unusually far from the center of a distribution created by randomly regrouping the same outcomes. The first-edition material examines exhaustive regroupings for small datasets and then uses a fitted normal distribution to approximate tail areas for larger simulations. Decide using the model and data, while keeping the distinction between a rare assignment and proof of a treatment effect.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For an experiment with groups T and C, define D=mean(T)−mean(C). Under a no-treatment-effect randomization assumption, repeatedly shuffle outcome labels into new groups of the same sizes, compute D, and describe the resulting null distribution. To assess an observed difference without a specified one-sided alternative, the source intends a TWO-sided analysis: estimated p=P(|D_sim|≥|D_obs|). If a roughly normal null distribution has mean μ0 and SD σ0>0, an exploratory standardized statistic is z=(D_obs−μ0)/σ0; approximate two-sided normal tail is 2[1−Φ(|z|)] when μ0≈0 and the model is suitable. A low p-value indicates observed data are unusual under the no-effect model, but is neither the probability the null is true nor proof of causal certainty.
translations.workedExamples: Source activity 14.1 — notice and wonder: Compare the center, spread, symmetry, and frequency near zero in several dot plots of random treatment-minus-control mean differences. Record what you notice and wonder; support a graph-based claim with actual plotted or tabulated frequencies, not only a mean. Source activity 14.2 — all possible regroupings: Control C={1,3,4,6,8,10} has mean 32/6; treatment T={2,5,7,9,11,12} has mean 46/6. The observed difference D=mean(T)-mean(C)=14/6=7/3≈2.333. Choosing any six of the twelve values gives C(12,6)=924 equally sized regroupings. Exactly 143 yield D≥7/3, another 143 yield D≤-7/3, and the two-sided extreme proportion is 286/924≈0.3095, not below 5%. Random regrouping remains a plausible explanation for this difference; it does not justify a treatment-effect conclusion. Source activity 14.3 — birds raised in captivity versus wild: The observed difference is 0.27 grams; the distribution from 1,000 simulated regroupings has mean 0.0021 grams and SD 0.112 grams. Under a suitable approximate normal null model, z=(0.27-0.0021)/0.112≈2.392 and the two-sided area beyond this magnitude is about 0.0168 (1.68%). At a predeclared 5% threshold, the outcome is unusual under regrouping alone, but a causal claim requires a defensible assignment design and model assumptions; an observed p-value is not the probability that the treatment worked. Optional smaller exact-enumeration check: For T={3,4} and C={1,2}, the six allocations yield D=-2,-1,0,0,1,2, giving 2/6≈0.333 in both tails.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Name the treatment and control groups and define the sign of the statistic D. 2. Calculate the original observed D. 3. Under the no-effect assumption generate repeated random regroupings of the pooled outcomes while preserving group sizes. 4. Plot or tabulate the simulated D values and locate the observed value. 5. If using an approximately normal model, estimate its mean and SD and convert D to a z-score. 6. Compute the area in BOTH tails beyond the observed absolute difference when using the source two-sided analysis, then interpret the result conditionally on the randomization design.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not mistake a p-value for the probability that a treatment has no effect. The tail area for a two-sided test is not just one extreme tail. An approximately normal fit can be poor for tiny or highly discrete randomization distributions; exact reassignments may be preferable. Statistical significance should not be confused with a large practical effect or generalization to people outside a convenience sample.
translations.quickSummary: A randomization distribution measures how extreme a mean difference is under reassignment with no treatment effect. For the source 12-value experiment, the original D=7/3 has two-sided p=286/924≈0.3095. For the bird simulation, a suitable normal model with mean 0.0021 and SD 0.112 gives two-sided p≈0.0168 at D=0.27 grams. Tail-area significance is conditional on the study design, not automatic proof of causality.

translations.title: Questioning Experimenting
translations.explanation: An information-gap activity is successful only when students ask for the details needed to judge an experiment. In the source greenhouse study, 30 strawberry plants are randomly assigned: 15 grow in standard soil and 15 in a different soil, while other conditions are held as similar as possible. After six weeks, compare average strawberry weights and the differences generated by random rearrangements of the two group labels. Identify precisely what must be known before calling the observed difference unusual.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For the first-edition strawberry experiment, the control mean is 238.67 grams and treatment mean is 347.47 grams, so observed treatment-minus-control difference D=108.80 grams. The simulated null randomization differences have mean −0.540 grams and SD 29.83 grams. An approximately normal standardized position is (108.80−(−0.540))/29.83≈3.665. If the simulated null distribution is reasonably normal, a two-sided tail beyond ±3.665 SD is very small (around 0.00025), so ordinary group assignment alone is an implausible explanation under that null model. Such a statement relies on the experimental assumptions and is not a claim that no alternate cause exists; exact significance should be determined from the source simulation or appropriate statistical technology.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source soil experiment: Compute difference 347.47−238.67=108.80 grams. Using null mean −0.540 and SD 29.83 gives z=(108.80+0.540)/29.83≈3.665. The observed gap is over three null-distribution SDs above its center and deserves strong scrutiny of random assignment, measurement conditions and repeatability; it is unlikely to arise from label reassignment alone if the model fits. Example 2 — information-gap question set: Ask how many plants were in each group, which treatment varied, what was measured, what average and dispersion each group showed, whether plants were randomly assigned, how many randomization trials were simulated, and whether the reported tail uses both directions. A ratio or p-value without these details is not sufficient for an academic argument. Original source activity 15.2 is a teacher-observed PARTNER information gap: the problem-card student must ask specific questions and explain why each datum is needed; the data-card student must provide only requested information and ask why it matters, then both compare their independent reasoning. A list of questions alone cannot substitute for observing this interaction or assigning a defensible teacher rubric. Example 3 — optional source activity 15.3, baseball normal-table check: Assume baseball weight X is approximately normal with mean 145 grams and SD 2 grams, with official allowable weights from 142 through 149 grams. The lower-bound z=(142-145)/2=-1.5 and upper-bound z=(149-145)/2=2; z=1.45 represents weight 145+2(1.45)=147.9 grams. Using a standard-normal cumulative table, Phi(-1.5)≈0.0668 and Phi(2)≈0.9772, so P(142≤X≤149)=0.9772-0.0668≈0.9104 (about 91.04%). Shade the LEFT-of-142 and LEFT-of-149 cumulative regions separately, then subtract them to get only the interval area. Optional extension: a value 70 in N(55,8) has z=1.875, whereas 10 in N(6,1.6) has z=2.5, so 10 is relatively farther above its own distribution mean.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Ask for the treatment/control definitions and confirm the same growing period and measurement units. 2. Ask how 30 plants were divided and whether assignment was random. 3. Collect each group's mean and calculate observed signed difference. 4. Ask how the null randomization distribution was generated, how many repeats, and its mean and SD. 5. Standardize D with the null center and spread, then compare with the actual simulated distribution or a justified normal approximation. 6. State what the evidence suggests and which unverified assumptions, confounders, measurement errors, and sampling limitations prevent an absolute causal guarantee.
translations.commonMistakes: The greenhouse has 30 plants total, not 30 in each group. Subtract treatment minus control consistently: 108.80 grams is a difference in average strawberry weight, not a percentage increase. A z-score of approximately 3.665 is not itself the p-value. A small randomization tail does not remove the need to check assignment integrity, soil treatment definition, other growing conditions and measurement quality. Asking and defending the information needed requires a reasoning rubric.
translations.quickSummary: For 15 control and 15 treated plants, the source average weights differ by 108.80 g. Relative to a null regrouping distribution mean −0.540 g, SD 29.83 g, the standardized gap is about 3.665, unusually large under that assignment model; verify all study assumptions.

translations.title: Heart Rates
translations.explanation: Finish the statistics unit by designing and interpreting a real classroom comparison of two conditions using measured heart rates. The first-edition activities ask students to estimate beats per minute from a timed pulse, record changes after a breathing or flapping/counting condition, randomly assign students to groups, and simulate regrouping to determine whether observed mean differences might plausibly reflect chance assignment. This is a statistical learning activity, not personal medical advice or a diagnosis. Participation, physical comfort, consent, and measurement limitations matter.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: A count of h beats in 10 seconds corresponds to 6h beats per minute (bpm), provided the rate is roughly stable over the measurement window; longer intervals can improve precision. Define each participant's baseline and follow-up before computing a within-person change, or compare group means at a consistent measurement point. Randomly assign consenting participants to conditions and preserve sample sizes when simulating shuffled group labels. The observed treatment difference D=mean(T)−mean(C) is compared with the no-effect randomization distribution; estimate a two-sided proportion of simulated |D| at least as extreme as observed. This method is statistical, not a substitute for clinical assessment or a proof that short-term heart-rate differences have a unique cause.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — source measurement conversion: A person counts 12 beats in 10 seconds, equivalent to 72 bpm; a later count of 15 beats over 10 seconds estimates 90 bpm, an increase of 18 bpm. Check interval timing carefully. The numbers here are teaching examples, not measured student health data. Example 2 — original small randomization oracle: Four recorded changes in bpm are 1,2,3,4, split randomly into groups of two. If treatment receives 3,4 and control 1,2, D=3.5−1.5=2 bpm. All six equally likely choices of two treatment values give D=−2,−1,0,0,1,2, so a two-sided exact randomization tail for |D|≥2 is 2/6≈0.333. Even an observed two-bpm gap can easily arise from group assignment in this tiny experiment; actual class results require their own randomization simulation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Explain the measurement, research question and any voluntary participation/safety accommodations. 2. Measure an agreed baseline over the same timed interval and convert a 10-second beat count to bpm by multiplying by 6. 3. Randomly assign participants to treatment and control or two conditions, record which variable differs and hold timing consistent. 4. Collect follow-up values; define whether comparing bpm levels or changes from baseline, and compute each group mean. 5. Reassign the recorded outcomes at random to equal-size groups many times to build a null distribution of mean differences. 6. Compare |D_observed| against simulated |D|, report the proportion and explain sampling, timing, volunteer and physiological limitations without diagnosing individuals.
translations.commonMistakes: A 10-second beat count is not already a bpm rate; multiply it by six. Do not claim all changes are caused by breathing, movement or counting if assignment or other conditions were uncontrolled. An unusual sample statistic can occur by chance; a low model tail probability is conditional on design and assumptions. Never publish student pulse data or identifying medical information as example fixtures. A classroom heart-rate investigation should allow non-participation and should not encourage medically risky exertion.
translations.quickSummary: The final first-edition lesson uses measured beats per minute and randomized group comparisons to practice inference. Convert a 10-second pulse count by multiplying by six, then assess group mean differences with a randomization distribution and careful study-design caveats.
